# POPE LEO X.

<note>Pope Leo X (reigned 1513–1521), born Giovanni de' Medici, was a massive patron of the arts and literature. His papacy was defined by the flowering of the High Renaissance in Rome.</note>

### To Our Beloved Son, Francesco de Rossi of Ravenna.

<image-desc>A large ornate woodcut initial letter 'D' decorated with swirling acanthus leaves and floral patterns within a square border.</image-desc>

**BELOVED** Son, greetings and apostolic blessing. Since many—and indeed the most outstanding—writers, who were lying hidden to the gravest loss of the Latin language, have in our time come forth into the light as if from the deepest darkness, we cannot but congratulate scholars in the greatest measure. For among the other cares that we undertake (in this stewardship of human affairs granted to us by God), we consider this to be not among the least: that the Latin language may be said to have been enriched during our Pontificate, and that no small assistance has been brought to those who desire the liberal arts <note>original: "bonarū artiū." Refers to the "Good Arts" or Humanities, the core of Renaissance education.</note> for the greatest progress in their studies. 

Therefore, we believe no expense should be spared so that ancient writers may be most diligently sought out among all nations and brought to us. For in this way, no one shall regret their labor; many will take up this burden of their own accord to penetrate into the most remote regions to rescue from the darkness the monuments of the ancients—which were suppressed either by human envy or the damage of time—knowing they will receive excellent rewards for their efforts. 

As you have recently done, beloved son, who through so many barbarian and foreign nations reached even into Syria at the greatest expense and not without danger to your life; and for no other reason than to rescue from neglect—or rather from total loss—several writings of the most outstanding philosophers. Among these is a certain work titled *The Theology of Aristotle* or *Mystical Philosophy* (for so the title of the book indicated). Since it is filled with excellent doctrine, you discovered it written in Arabic characters, having been translated from the Greek. This work, now rendered into Latin, you have offered to Us as a most welcome gift, and [intended] it for the use of the printing presses...

<note>The text ends mid-sentence as it continues on the next page. This letter serves as a formal endorsement from the Pope, validating the "discovery" of the manuscript in Syria and its importance to the Christian scholarly world.</note>

<note>faded text at bottom: The fading mentioned in the warning likely obscures the closing lines of the address or the start of the next section, but the primary message of papal patronage remains clear.</note>

<summary>A formal letter from Pope Leo X to Francesco de Rossi, praising him for traveling to Syria to recover lost philosophical works, specifically the "Theology of Aristotle" found in Arabic.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the formal Papal Brief from Pope Leo X to Francesco de Rossi. <page-type>preface</page-type>
<sig>A ii</sig>

...you have undertaken the printing for the public good, even at our encouragement. So that this labor of yours may not be in vain—as might happen if others were to print it immediately after your edition—we command each and every person throughout the entire world to whom these letters may come, under the penalty of <term>automatic excommunication</term> <note>original: "excommunicationis latæ sententiæ." A formal ecclesiastical censure that takes effect immediately upon the commission of the forbidden act without the need for a specific trial.</note>. For those, however, who live within the jurisdiction of this, our **Holy Roman Church** <note>original: "S. R. E." abbreviated for Sancta Romana Ecclesia.</note>, we add the penalty of a fine of two hundred <term>ducats</term> <note>A gold coin used throughout Europe; 200 ducats was a substantial sum, roughly equivalent to several years' wages for a skilled artisan.</note> (to be applied to the appropriate causes) and the forfeiture of the books they have printed: that no one should dare to print [this work] without your consent for the next <gloss>ten-year period</gloss> <note>original: "decennium." This was a standard duration for a printing privilege in the 16th century.</note>.

We reserve to ourselves alone the power of absolution for each and every person who contravenes this our will; and we wish both those printing and those selling the printed volumes to be held under these same penalties. Furthermore, so that no one may dare to stubbornly rise up against this our prohibition, we command and enjoin each and every Legate of the Apostolic See, Nuncios, Orators, Patriarchs, Archbishops, Bishops, Abbots, and all ecclesiastical Prelates—as well as their Lieutenants, the Governors and Presidents of all places, and the commanders of troops—in the virtue of holy obedience and under the penalty of incurring the same excommunication, that when requested by you, they shall provide every assistance to prevent anyone from daring to <insert>reprint</insert> <note>original: "innovare," literally "to innovate," but in this legal context referring to an unauthorized new edition.</note> against our edict during the aforesaid ten-year period.

Moreover, if anyone should be so bold and reckless as to either prohibit these our letters from being published, or to remove them from sacred or secular places once published, let him be guilty of these same penalties, Apostolic constitutions and ordinances and any other things to the contrary notwithstanding.

Given at Rome, at St. Peter’s, under the **Ring of the Fisherman** <note>original: "annulo Piscatoris." The personal signet ring used by the Pope to seal official briefs, depicting St. Peter fishing from a boat.</note>, on the 30th day of December, 1517, in the fifth year of our Pontificate.

# To the Most Blessed and Most Pious Pope Leo X, the Most August/
# Prince, Francesco de Rossi of Ravenna [wishes] happiness.

<image-desc>A square woodcut decorative initial 'Q' with an intricate interlaced strapwork design in white on a black background.</image-desc>WHEN, three years ago, I was living in Damascus,
Most Holy Pontiff—as a constant devotee of good literature,
I devoted all my effort,
sparing no expense or labor,
so that I might enter the city's famous library
(accompanied by a friend somewhat skilled in
the Arabic tongue, so as to read the inscriptions sufficiently)
to explore the countless and precious manuscripts
arranged there. Among these, one in particular, an ancient
volume, caught my eye: it was labeled *The Theology of Aristotle*, or *Mystical Philosophy* <note>original: "Aristotelis theologia, seu Phia Mystica." At the time, this text was believed to be by Aristotle, though modern scholars identify it as a collection of ideas from the Neoplatonist philosopher Plotinus.</note>,
which, since I had heard it was composed by Aristotle and
had been lost and longed for, the impulse to possess this work immediately
occurred to me. I thought how much value it would hold
among all philosophers and theologians,
especially in this century, in which Aristotle himself stands
as the most renowned of all and the master of wisdom to everyone.
Therefore, having paid a not insignificant sum and through secret dealings,
I achieved my wish and moved on to Cyprus with the business,
where—since I despaired of finding a man in Italy
knowledgeable in the literature of this work,
or at least I doubted it—Moses Rovas <note>A Jewish physician and translator active in the early 16th century.</note>, a physician
most expert in the Arabic language
and a consulted philosopher, was sought out.
And because he approved of the book in no small measure,
upon my request and having been paid a fee <term>minervali</term> <note>original: "mineruali." A classical term for a teacher's pay or a reward for scholarly labor, named after Minerva, the goddess of wisdom.</note>,
he even translated it into such common Italian as
he knew—quickly indeed, but with total faithfulness,
rendering it word for word.
When I then handed this over for review to the
distinguished philosopher and physician, Pietro Nicola de
Castellani of Faenza—a man devoted to wisdom,
highly active in the Academy but most of all in the <term>Peripatetic</term> <note>original: "peripatetico." Referring to the school of philosophy founded by Aristotle; literally "those who walk about."</note> school—he, having read the work
accurately and with reverence,
praised it without ceasing. He judged that it should be
refined at the first opportunity and translated into Roman oratory <note>Refers to formal, classical Latin.</note>.

<meta>This page continues Francesco de Rossi’s dedication to Pope Leo X. On the previous page, de Rossi described discovering an ancient manuscript titled "The Theology of Aristotle" in Damascus and bringing it to Cyprus to be translated from Arabic into Latin by the physician Moses Rovas.</meta>

...led and took it up. Therefore, this golden work, most precisely corrected, will not hesitate to come forth into the light; otherwise, it would be absurd. For according to the opinion of Plato, books ought not to go out into public unless they have first been approved by the judgment of a censor. 

But I have most willingly dedicated this to you, most clement and most munificent Pontiff, both because you alone in this our time imitate that most famous Tuscan Maecenas <note>Gaius Maecenas was the legendary Roman patron of the arts under Emperor Augustus. The author is comparing Pope Leo X—a member of the Florentine Medici family—to this archetypal patron.</note> of yours; for indeed, from your very tenderest years <note>original: "ab teneris quippe unguiculis," literally "from tender little nails," a Latin idiom for early childhood.</note>, you have always stood as a true protector and bulwark of all virtues. Also because I hope that I will do something pleasing not only to all philosophers and theologians, but also to the Most Reverend Cardinal de' Medici, Legate of Bologna and most worthy Apostolic Vice-Chancellor—Lord Giulio, from your most illustrious family of the Medici <note>Giulio de' Medici, the future Pope Clement VII, was Leo X's cousin and a powerful figure in the Roman Curia.</note>, who, following the footsteps of your elders and of your Holiness, has never hesitated to cherish all men of letters. 

And finally because you, most noble Pontiff, were deservedly elected as the Angelic High Priest of the most holy Church, so that in the future, with your most sacred Cardinals and your most warlike nephew Lorenzo de' Medici <note>Lorenzo de' Medici, Duke of Urbino, to whom Machiavelli famously dedicated *The Prince*.</note>, you might most fiercely defend the Christian Republic. Indeed, under the auspices of your Majesty, the rebels against the Christian name shall be utterly cast down. 

Wherefore, it is not without reason that this *Mystical Philosophy of Aristotle*, or if you prefer, this theological work, is dedicated to your most august Highness; since in almost all respects (except for a very few things), it harmonizes with theological dogmas and most holy institutions, so that it might now be said of Aristotle—as Augustine said of Plato—that by transposing certain things, a Christian is made here of Aristotle <note>St. Augustine famously argued that Platonic philosophy was the most compatible with Christian thought; de Rossi is claiming this "newly discovered" Aristotle is even more aligned with the Church.</note>. 

Therefore, most clement Pontiff, with that most serene countenance which is your custom, deign to receive into the sacred patronage of your majesty this volume of the Philosopher—himself accustomed to the life of royal courts—now discovered, translated, and adorned. It is a handbook small in its number of pages, but in its immense meanings, it can scarcely be embraced by human arms; so that what the entire...

--- Page 10 ---
<meta>This page continues Francesco de Rossi’s dedication to Pope Leo X. On the previous page, de Rossi described discovering an ancient manuscript titled "The Theology of Aristotle" in Damascus and bringing it to Cyprus to be translated from Arabic into Latin by the physician Moses Rovas. Here, he explains the metaphysical content of the work and the historical reasons for its fragmented state.</meta>

...as the Preface specifically sets forth) it sheds light upon: God, the Intellect, and the Soul, exploring them most deeply. And since—just as Alexander [the Great] wrote to Aristotle himself—I would prefer a Prince to excel in letters more than in arms, these books, so long desired, have never before been cherished in an open Latin translation. I rejoice that these have emerged in your age, just as Philip the Great <note>Philip II of Macedon, Alexander the Great's father, famously rejoiced that Aristotle was alive to tutor his son.</note> rejoiced that the author lived in his own time.

I would not, however, want anyone to dare to belittle or set aside these fourteen golden books if the ninth book is found to be mutilated and crippled in its first chapter alone. For Strabo <note>A Greek geographer and historian whose "Geography" contains the famous account of what happened to Aristotle’s library after his death.</note> wrote thus concerning the books of Aristotle and Theophrastus: when Neleus—having come into possession of the library of both philosophers—had carried them to Scepsis, his descendants, out of fear of the kings <note>original: "Regum." Historical context suggests the Attalid kings of Pergamum, who were aggressively collecting books for their own library, though the text says "Italian Kings."</note>, buried them in the earth, where they were weakened by moths and worms. Then, because Apellicon desired to repair the damage, they were filled with errors. Although several people later attempted to correct these—especially when the victor Sulla <note>Lucius Cornelius Sulla, the Roman general who took the library to Rome as war booty in 84 BCE.</note> carried them to Rome upon his return from Athens—it is nevertheless difficult to say whether they were restored to their former integrity or remained corrupted. 

That this manuscript was among that number, our own book can bear witness, for it is mutilated and crippled at the beginning of the ninth book. It comes from a very ancient translation made from Greek into the Arabic language by Abenamam the Saracen <note>Likely Ibn Na'ima al-Himsi, a 9th-century scholar involved in the translation of the "Theology of Aristotle" in Baghdad.</note>, which is in my possession for all to inspect. 

Therefore, let this foremost work, deservedly dedicated to the divinity of your Majesty, most Holy Pontiff, be placed in your Palatine—and indeed most worthy—Library. As for me, Roleus <note>The author, Francesco de Rossi.</note>, your humble servant, long since most devoted to your Holiness from the heart: I pray that you might mercifully bestow your grace upon me and not disdain to count me among your flock. 

Farewell, and live happily, most Blessed Father, Most Radiant Star of the entire Christian Commonwealth. 

Ravenna, on the Kalends of January <note>January 1st</note>, 1519.

<meta>This page transitions from Francesco de Rossi’s dedication to the specific editorial work of Pietro Nicola de' Castellani. While the previous page discussed the manuscript’s journey from Damascus to Cyprus and its initial literal translation by the physician Moses Rovas, this preface introduces Castellani's role in polishing that raw translation into elegant, "Roman" Latin suitable for the court of Pope Leo X.</meta>

# The Preface of Pietro Nicola de' Castellani of Faenza, Philosopher and Physician, to the *Theology of Aristotle*, addressed to the reader.

<image-desc>A large decorative woodcut initial 'F' featuring a complex white-line interlaced knotwork pattern on a dark square background.</image-desc>FRANCESCO Rossi of Ravenna, studious reader, recently brought from the Renowned Library of Damascus to Italy a codex of reliable antiquity, titled the *Theology of Aristotle*, which was translated long ago from the Greek language into Arabic by Abenama the Saracen <note>This refers to 'Abd al-Masih ibn Na'ima al-Himsi, a 9th-century scholar who translated Neoplatonic texts into Arabic under the name of Aristotle.</note>. When this work was presented to me for evaluation—having been interpreted by Moses Rovas <note>A Jewish physician and translator who worked with Rossi.</note> in a style that was unpolished, following the Arabic idiom, and unlettered due to a lack of Latin skill—I was nonetheless greatly pleased by its sublime theorems. Above all, I noted many sentiments that are in perfect agreement with the Christian religion and are exceptionally useful against its detractors. Therefore, I felt moved to clothe the work in the toga of a Roman translation <note>original: "Romanæ ecphraseos toga donare." Castellani uses the metaphor of giving the book a Roman citizen's toga to describe turning a rough translation into elegant, scholarly Latin.</note>, lest such a precious book—stripped of its Greek cloak as if by pirates and dressed in a barbarian’s rough coat—should flee from the public eye out of shame. I was mindful of his own Theophrastus <note>Aristotle’s successor as head of the Peripatetic school.</note>, who said that an unorganized speech should be trusted no more than an unbridled horse. For this reason, I have employed a more refined Latin dialect than that used by the philosophers who came slightly before me. I have done so that the book might speak more elegantly (as far as the technical subject matter allowed) before the man to whom it was dedicated: Pope Leo X. He is a most eloquent Roman Pontiff, living in an age where eloquence has flourished again even among the wise, aided by the immense support of the most illustrious family of the Medici <note>original: "Medicor[um] Prosapiæ." A pun on the Pope's family name, which means "physicians."</note>. This was done so that no injustice might occur—of which Boethius complained—if wisdom were to be divorced from eloquence. Yet, I have not applied so much rhetorical splendor as I might have, for that was not permitted, lest Musonius <note>Musonius Rufus, a Stoic philosopher who argued that philosophy should be practical and plain-spoken rather than a display of oratorical skill.</note> cry out that it is not a philosopher speaking, but a [shouter of words]...

<summary>Pietro Nicola de' Castellani explains his decision to rewrite Moses Rovas's literal Arabic-to-Latin translation into a more elegant, classical style. He argues that the text's profound theological insights, which align with Christian doctrine, deserve a presentation worthy of its dedicatee, Pope Leo X.</summary>
<keywords>Pietro Nicola de' Castellani, Francesco Rossi, Abenama the Saracen, Moses Rovas, Pope Leo X, Boethius, Musonius Rufus, translation theory, Neoplatonism, Damascus manuscript</keywords>

--- Page 12 ---
<meta>This page continues the translator’s preface by Pietro Nicola de' Castellani. The previous page ended with Castellani describing his decision to provide a refined Latin translation ("Roman toga") for this text, which had arrived in Italy via a rough Arabic-to-Latin version. The catchword "opinionibus" from the previous page suggests the sentence began by discussing the various opinions of scholars.</meta>

...to sing of their opinions. <margin>What this work of Aristotle's was.</margin> Furthermore, that these were the genuine books of Aristotle is testified first and foremost by the divine Thomas <note>St. Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the most influential scholastic philosopher and theologian.</note> in his defense *On the Unity of the Intellect* <note>original: "De Unitate Intellectus." A work where Aquinas argues against the Averroist view that all humans share a single intellect.</note>. He declared that he had seen them written in Greek in exactly the same number of books, though they were not yet translated into Latin at that time. He added that they were necessary works, serving as if they were appendices to the *Metaphysics* <note>original: "Methaphisicæ appendices." Castellani is trying to give the text legitimacy by linking it to Aristotle's known masterwork.</note>. Indeed, these books were promised by Aristotle himself in the second book of the *Physics* and in the twelfth book of the "First Wisdom" <note>Aristotle often referred to what we call "Metaphysics" as "First Philosophy" or "Wisdom."</note>. To this, one might add that it is by no means likely that any other philosopher would have written a work of such mystery with so much "consumption of oil" and "throwing of dust" <note>These are classical idioms for the exhaustive labor of a scholar working by lamplight ("oil") and the intense effort of an athlete in the arena ("dust").</note> only to attribute it to another man. In fact, no such deed is recorded to have ever been done before and preserved for so long.

<margin>Solution to objections.</margin> Furthermore, let no one argue that this work should not be counted among Aristotle’s writings, for to do so would be to prove a falsehood. Indeed, Diogenes Laertius <note>A 3rd-century biographer of Greek philosophers.</note> reports in his *Life of Aristotle* that he composed one book on the Pythagorean decrees; and this is that very work, encompassing the mystic philosophy of the Egyptians which was surely drawn from them by Pythagoras and brought into Greece. 

Truly, it is no obstacle that Laertius calls it "one book" while these are fourteen, since it was divided by later scholars for the sake of teaching and easier memory—just as the book *On the Soul* <note>original: "De Anima."</note> was named as one by the same author but split into three, and the book of *Physics* was also called one but divided into eight. Nor is it forbidden by the fact that the opinion that "the soul is a harmony" is condemned here, when (as Themistius <note>A 4th-century Greek rhetorician and commentator on Aristotle.</note> says in his first book *On the Soul*) that was not the opinion of Pythagoras himself, but rather of certain of his followers. 

Neither should it be objected that the author here contradicts assertions he wrote in other works in several, or at least some, instances. For Aristotle here openly prefaces (as he does nowhere else) that he is not collecting his own wisdom, but the foreign wisdom of the Egyptians. And this is not without reason, since in the fourth book he confesses that such things are not discovered by human means, but revealed by the divine—which happened to Pythagoras, as historians have recorded among other things. Nor does he truly oppose his own [opinions] elsewhere as many times here...

<summary>Castellani defends the authenticity of the "Theology of Aristotle," citing Thomas Aquinas and Diogenes Laertius to argue that while it contains "Egyptian" or Pythagorean wisdom, it is a genuine Aristotelian project. He addresses potential objections regarding the book's length and its apparent contradictions with Aristotle's other known works.</summary>
<keywords>Aristotle, Thomas Aquinas, Theology of Aristotle, Neoplatonism, Pythagoras, Egyptian wisdom, Metaphysics, De Anima, Diogenes Laertius, authenticity, scholasticism</keywords>

--- Page 13 ---
<meta>This page continues Pietro Nicola de' Castellani’s preface. He is addressing potential criticisms regarding the authenticity of the text by discussing the apparent contradictions between this work (the "Theology of Aristotle") and Aristotle’s canonical works like the Physics and Metaphysics. He argues that these discrepancies arise from Aristotle’s intellectual evolution over time.</meta>

...opinions than they seem at first glance, which we will teach separately soon in our own commentaries on these books.
And so that we may now assist those who are impatient with delay, we shall review certain points. Therefore, he denies the physical production <note>The creation or origin of the universe</note> of the world in his lectures *On Nature* <note>Aristotle's *Physics*</note> and *On the Heavens*, whereas here he posits it and explains it as metaphysical. He clearly testifies that Plato seems to assert in his speech a temporal <note>beginning at a specific point in time</note> creation of the world, even though he [Plato] understands it to be instantaneous. 

Here he confesses that there is one true principle of things; elsewhere he denies a single mathematical principle. The Ideas, which here he grants as subsisting <note>having independent existence</note> and formative, he elsewhere seems to reject as not existing within things as essences and forms. Heat, which he here admits to be the substance of fire, he elsewhere accepts as the form itself (otherwise unnamed), and yet elsewhere rejects it, considering it a quality. Averroes <note>Ibn Rushd (1126–1198), the influential Islamic philosopher and commentator who reconciled Aristotelianism with Islam.</note> does the same thing repeatedly. 

He allows here that irrational souls <note>the souls of animals, which lack human reason</note> are immortal according to their substance, but he openly says they are corruptible "according to accident" when the physical functions of the animals are corrupted. Reciting elsewhere, however, in the tenth book, tenth chapter, correcting this and following his own opinion, he writes that the rational soul is immortal, but the sensitive <note>pertaining to the senses</note> soul is mortal. 

One thing especially vexes the reader: that he denies in the *Metaphysics* that the rational soul precedes the physical composition of the animal, yet here he clearly asserts it. But in response to these objections, we say that the soul of this species is, according to him, uniquely perpetual; such a Being, according to the same author, existed eternally, and he observes that the intellect comes to the animals from the outside <note>original: "exteriusque accedere intellectum." This refers to the controversial Aristotelian idea that the "Active Intellect" enters the human from a divine or external source.</note>. Therefore, he is not so much in conflict with this work as he is with his other writings in the twelfth book of the *Wisdom* <note>The *Metaphysics*, which Aristotle often called "First Wisdom."</note>. 

From this, it could be said—and it is common to others (if it must be said)—that nothing is more likely, and certainly not impossible, than for even a philosophical man to hold different opinions at different times; this is an argument for his progress and a lack of stubbornness. Indeed, this often happens to wise men who change their minds until their death—of whom it would be tedious to list everyone. Furthermore, regarding the character of the style...

<summary>Castellani defends the text's authenticity by arguing that contradictions between this work and Aristotle’s other books are evidence of the philosopher's intellectual growth and shifting opinions over his lifetime. He specifically addresses conflicting views on the creation of the world, the nature of "Ideas," and the immortality of the soul.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the translator's preface by Pietro Nicola de' Castellani. Having just discussed contradictions in Aristotle’s various works, he now addresses the style of the translation and the tradition of harmonizing Aristotle with Plato.</meta>

...[interpreta]tion is more expansive and open than the usual Aristotelian style, it is no hindrance, since his eloquence is not the same in all his other works; and this style also exists because of the Arabs, from whom this work was transferred through paraphrase. As can be seen, they "taste" of their own interpretations. Therefore, we have expressed the meanings rather than the literal words of those authors, quite boldly, following the precept of Saint Jerome <note>original: "Hieronymi præceptum"; Jerome was a 4th-century scholar who famously advocated for "sense-for-sense" translation</note> and the example of Cicero. 

Furthermore, the title’s attribution to the author should not be weakened by the fact that Aristotle, imitating Plato here, frequently cites "the Judge" <note>This likely refers to a specific philosophical authority or a stylistic device used in the text</note>, whom the younger Peripatetics <note>original: "pipateticis"; the followers of Aristotle’s school of philosophy</note> consider a perpetual adversary. For there is a constant opinion among the ancient and wise—as witnessed by Augustine in the fifth book of *The City of God* and Thomas Aquinas in the second book of *On the Heavens*—that although these two [Plato and Aristotle] disagree in many things by mouth, they do not disagree in their heart. 

<margin>
Reason for the Title.
</margin>

Regarding the harmony between them: among the Greeks, Porphyry completed it and Simplicius began it; among the Latins, Boethius and Pico della Mirandola <note>Pico was a famous Renaissance philosopher who sought to unify all schools of thought</note> promised it. This harmony we ourselves have conceived in our mind, and in due time, it is to be explained with principal notes which we have already prepared and touched upon.

The title of this work offers the name "Theology"; yet as it progresses, it is called "Mystical Philosophy." This is because, among the ancient sages, divine secrets such as those noted here were not to be made public to the common people—partly because they cannot be fully grasped by them, and partly so that, being insufficiently understood, they are not held in contempt. It is also so that "holy things are not given to dogs" <note>A reference to the Gospel of Matthew 7:6, warning against sharing sacred knowledge with those who won't appreciate it</note>. 

For this reason, the image of the Sphinx was fashioned at the Temple of Delphi, signifying that divine matters are to be kept hidden. Pythagoras also first entrusted such things to the souls of his listeners rather than to letters. The Egyptians, lest they perhaps fall into oblivion, committed their secrets to signs, but mystical ones (which are called Hieroglyphs). Plato, moreover, left things written in enigmatic words, which the Hebrews also observed in their Kabbalah <note>original: "caballa"; the ancient Jewish tradition of mystical interpretation of the Bible</note>. 

The general subject of this work is the Universe; the principal subject, however, is incorporeal substance, which is called "spirit." It encompasses God, the Intelligences <note>In medieval philosophy, these are the divine or angelic minds that move the celestial spheres</note>, and Souls, which are the three things primarily considered in this work. Among these, however, God is the primary subject; hence the work is named "Theology" after Him. It stands among the parts of philosophy such that the work should be read after the *Metaphysics*, since many things are assumed in this work that were proven in that one. Indeed, it belongs to Metaphysics itself, which otherwise (as [pre]...

<meta>catchword: præ (pre)</meta>

<summary>The translator defends his "sense-for-sense" translation style and explains that the "Theology of Aristotle" uses a mystical, veiled language common to ancient sages like Pythagoras, the Egyptians, and Plato. He argues that the work aims to harmonize Plato and Aristotle's core beliefs and focuses on incorporeal substances: God, Intelligences, and Souls.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the translator's preface by Pietro Nicola de' Castellani. Having just mentioned the efforts of Boethius and Pico della Mirandola to harmonize the philosophies of Plato and Aristotle, Castellani now argues that this particular work—attributed here to Aristotle—serves as the necessary completion of his system.</meta>

<page-type>text</page-type>
<sig>B ii</sig>

...fate) it seemed to Thomas Aquinas <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274) was the most influential scholastic philosopher and theologian of the Middle Ages</note> a supplement to the mutilated parts [of Aristotle's corpus]. For which reason, since young men are not to be imbued with supernatural doctrines according to the judgment of Aristotle, they are all the less to be admitted to this kind of reading. For indeed, divine matters among the followers of Plato also are not to be learned except at an advanced age, in which the passions cease; just as the so-called Kabbalah <note>original: "Caballica"; the mystical tradition of Judaism</note> among the Hebrews was not heard before the fortieth year. 

The style is for the most part narrative, since supernatural things, according to Plato, ought to be narrated rather than proved; and thus they are sufficiently known through themselves among the wise—especially those of the highest rank illuminated by a clear natural light—just like axioms or "prologues" <note>original: "prologa"; fundamental principles that precede an argument</note> (as Boethius said). But if any proof is offered at any time, it exists as more Dialectical than Apodictic <note>In Aristotelian logic, "apodictic" refers to absolute, certain demonstration, while "dialectical" refers to reasoning from probable or accepted opinions</note>, because in matter of this kind, demonstrations are rare and dialectical reasons frequent, as seen in the seventh book of the *Metaphysics* and observed by Averroes <note>A 12th-century Islamic philosopher whose commentaries on Aristotle were central to Western thought</note>. Therefore, Plato calls Theology "dialectical"—that is, proceeding through dialectical reasons.

<margin>Proportion.</margin>
The proportion of this work to the rest of philosophy is as the end (the goal) is to those things which lead to the end; to philosophy simply, it is like its most powerful part, since it has the most noble subject, and for that reason is to be greatly desired. For Aristotle judged it better to contemplate sublime things with probability than lowly things with absolute certainty. 

<margin>Utility.</margin>
The benefit of this book is very great, especially for the Catholic faith, to which, I say, it is in most things agreeable; and although in a few things it is discordant, nevertheless, just as Origen <note>referred to here by his nickname "Adamantius"</note>, Cyprian, and Lactantius were prudently admitted into Christian schools by the advice of Jerome and Basil, it will be highly conducive for those wayward minds which cannot be drawn to piety except by the reasons and authorities of outsiders. 

Here indeed are read so many theological and orthodox opinions—more than anywhere else in a single pagan volume—that if those few which go astray did not exist among them, we would rightly consider Aristotle not a pagan or anyone else, but rather a Christian philosopher (as Dionysius <note>Dionysius the Areopagite, a Christian Neoplatonist</note> and Philoponus do). Since indeed here is [the knowledge] of God...

<meta>This page continues the preface by Pietro Nicola de' Castellani, transitioning from the historical context of the work to a profound theological and metaphysical description of God as the "First Cause," consistent with the Platonic-Aristotelian synthesis mentioned previously.</meta>

a most singular unity and a most separate essence—indeed, a most eminent super-essence <note>original: "supcentia" (superessentia); a term used in Neoplatonic theology to describe God as existing beyond the category of "being" or "essence"</note> and indivisible. An uncreatable and most constant Existence. A necessity greatest and beyond all dispute. The purest actuality; the highest simplicity; a Subsistence everywhere independent and entirely solitary. A priority beyond time. The most excellent Truth. A primary Goodness, dearer than all others. Here is the infinite power of God: absolute Wisdom, and indivisible knowledge, an all-encompassing providence, an Intellect most full of Ideal Reasons <note>The "Ideal Reasons" (rationū Idealiū) refer to the Platonic Forms as they exist within the divine mind</note>. A Will that cannot be moved from without and is by no means envious. An incomprehensible and ineffable depth; an essential action without time or subject. Here in God is the Word <note>original: "uerbū" (Verbum); referring to the Logos, the second person of the Trinity, through whom all things were created</note> conceived and produced: coessential and coequal, through whose command all things are made. Here in God is the containment of the preeminence of all things. Here in God is the efficacy of faith for acting; here from God is the production of all things and their constant preservation. 

The emanation of spirits; the foundation of matter; the creation of the world—new, voluntary, and perfect. Here from God is the dependence and efficiency of all things; here under God all things lie; here toward God all things tend. Here through God is the understanding and illumination of all. Here is the number and placement of spirits: their consensus, conscience, and conversation. Here is the multitude of souls: their incorporeality, immortality, and momentary understanding; their translation, purification, and the true clarity of those who have emerged, through the reward of merits and the punishment of demerits; the commendation of virtues and the detestation of vices. Therefore, since all Philosophy leads to Happiness <note>original: "Fœlicitatē" (felicitatem); the classical goal of human life, often identified with the vision of God</note>, this work leads there insofar as, by proclaiming so many signs concerning God, it draws one into His love. 

This kind of love is followed by attainment; attainment, moreover, by enjoyment, from which whole beatitude <note>original: "beatitudo"; the state of perfect blessedness or supreme happiness</note> consists—which was the single opinion of the Princes of Wisdom. This beatitude we shall hasten to complete with the rest, if this present industry, such as it is, does not displease learned minds, and especially those to whom it pertains. This will be no small encouragement for the edition also of the paraphrase of the whole of Logic <note>original: "logicam uniuersam"; likely referring to the *Organon* of Aristotle</note> already completed, and for the finishing of the rest of Philosophy.

<summary>Castellani provides a dense metaphysical description of God as the ultimate source of all being, intellect, and morality, arguing that the study of these divine attributes leads to human happiness and beatitude. He concludes the preface by seeking the approval of scholars to continue his series of philosophical paraphrases.</summary>

<meta>This page transitions from the end of a detailed index (concluding with definitions of Universals and Divine Unity) to the formal beginning of the treatise itself. It establishes the philosophical framework for the work, moving from the categorization of terms to the primary investigation of the "Theology of Aristotle"—a text known historically to be a Neo-Platonic adaptation of Plotinus, though attributed to Aristotle in the Renaissance.</meta>

->**BOOK THE FIRST**<-
->a<-

# THE THEOLOGY,
# OR MYSTICAL PHILOSOPHY
# OF THE MOST WISE MAN
# ARISTOTLE THE STAGIRITE,
# ACCORDING TO THE EGYPTIANS:
# INTERPRETED BY PIETRO NICCOLÒ
# OF THE CASTELLANI OF FAENZA,
# PHILOSOPHER AND 
# PHYSICIAN.
<note>original: "Ecphraste." This term implies more than a literal translation; it suggests the author has interpreted or "brought out the meaning" of the text. While titled "according to the Egyptians," this work is actually a 9th-century Arabic synthesis of Plotinus’s "Enneads," which was mistakenly attributed to Aristotle for centuries.</note>

### Chapter one of the First Book, regarding which Theorems of the Preface are to be treated, according to which Authors, and in what style.

Likewise, we will consider the **sublunary nature** <term>Sublunary: The region of the universe below the Moon (the Earth), which—unlike the "perfect" heavens—is subject to change, decay, and death.</term>, how the power of Heaven imitates that divine power which is manifested in sensible, material, alterable, and corruptible things. 

Then we shall write of the disposition of **rational souls** in their descent and ascent, and we will give the cause of their union to bodies. We will also speak of the honorable Soul, which possesses intellectual character and is not submerged in worldly desires and the filth of the body...

### Chapter Two. How the Soul is United to the Body.

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'C' featuring floral and vine motifs within a square border.</image-desc>

Since it is already clear (as has been proven in the books of the ancients) that the **Soul** is not the **Body**, nor does it die, but remains forever, let us now ask how, having departed from the **intellectual world**, it descended to this **sensible world** and was joined to this dissolvable body. Indeed, no purely intellectual substance admits motion. But being fixed in the intellectual world, it is not torn away from it, nor likewise does it approach elsewhere, since it has no place to which it might be transferred. To this we say: that every secondary intellectual substance has within itself a certain **desire** for another. Moreover, when the **Intellect** has conceived something by appetite, it moves toward it, just as a pregnant woman strives to give birth. Thus, therefore, the Intellect, conceiving a desire, endeavors to achieve it. For truly, the Intellect desiring a lower state becomes the **Soul**. Whence the Soul is the Intellect desiring and yearning with a universal desire; and the **Universal Soul** itself is not separated in substance from the Intellectual world, but desiring particulars under universal work, it withdraws from it <note>This "withdrawal" is not a physical movement, but a shift in focus or state—from contemplating the divine whole to managing the material parts.</note>. It orders these things and moderates the accidental sin <note>original: "peccatum accidēns." In this Neoplatonic context, "sin" refers to the falling away from divine unity into the fragmentation of the material world.</note> according to the law of the proximate celestial cause. The **particular soul** <note>The individual human soul as opposed to the World Soul.</note> is not in the Body as it seems, but outside of it. First, therefore, it moves toward the primary World, then to the secondary, and afterward returns for a third time to the primary—and appropriately to each of them.

### Chapter Three. That <term>quod: used here to introduce a factual statement</term> every soul is immortal, and for what reason, according to Pythagoras.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'I' containing scrolling vine and leaf motifs.</image-desc>

The **Active Intellect** <note>original: "Intellectus agens"; in medieval philosophy, this is the power of the mind that transforms sensory experiences into abstract thought</note> is never separated from the soul, but always works together with it appropriately in all things. Therefore, the soul truly works continually, because it exists perpetually. And although the souls of other animals—such as the **Lion**—have withdrawn from the higher world through sin <note>Likely referring to the 'fall' or descent into material bodies</note>, they are nonetheless not destroyed in their **substance**, but only in their **accidents** <term>Accidentia: properties that can change or be lost without the thing itself ceasing to exist, like color or weight</term>. And therefore, they do not return to that higher world in a simple or direct way. For the accidents in this world are distinct from the soul, yet they are natural to the animal itself, since they arise from its very nature.

In a similar way, all the souls of plants arise from a single principle, since they agree in the possession of life; they are **substances**, not accidents, and are incorporeal and indivisible. Therefore, they are not destroyed either. But the soul of man has three parts: namely, the **Vegetative** <note>the faculty of growth and nutrition</note>, the **Sensual** <note>the faculty of perception and movement</note>, and the **Intellectual**, which is separated from the body when it is dissolved. And this intellectual part—being free from the defilement of the body (inasmuch as it does not sin)—is unlike the other part submerged in matter. That lower part was made for this purpose: so that the bodily condition and its various physical accidents (acting like bonds or chains) are **prevented** <term>prohibetur</term> from ascending to the other world. The soul does not reach that world except with difficulty, and only after the power of these accidents is stripped away and it is purged from the filth of the body; then it returns as something incorruptible. For it is not as some who are strangers to truly divine science believe. Indeed, the soul is sustained by its authors <note>referring to the divine sources or creators of the soul</note>, even when separated, and it exists as a **True and Perfect Being**. Therefore, the soul does not die, as we have said many times.

These probable reasons ought to be repeated here for those who do not believe otherwise. Let us speak briefly. We establish that principle in which all have agreed—the Ancients and the Moderns, theologians, philosophers, prophets, and whole peoples—namely, that when the **Soul** is snatched away by the desires of the body and the intellect is subjugated, it immediately incurs the wrath of the Lord. Therefore, one must abstain from sins and set aside bodily desires; for in this way, the Lord will have mercy. 

Again, if our ancestors had not believed in the **immortality of the soul**, they would not have established laws according to the dictate of nature that affirm it. No one has contradicted this except those entangled in vices. They also said that many who prayed did not lack the help of souls that had returned from bodies to the other world. For one exploring the truth, this is manifest through the experience of revelation, and the construction of temples dedicated to them for these reasons. Wherefore it is evident that the **Soul**, having departed from this world and attained the other, is not destroyed at all. This is because it was created perpetual on account of the nobility of life. 

And **Plato** held this same opinion concerning the **universal soul** <note>The 'Anima Mundi' or World Soul, which in Platonic thought animates the entire universe</note>, saying:

"Often, while contemplating according to the soul and leaving behind the cast-off skin of the body, I seemed to myself to enjoy the highest good with admirable joy; whence I remained somewhat astonished. Then, recognizing that I am a part of the superior world, I attained **eternal life** under a great light—unutterable, unheard of, and unthinkable <note>original: "ienarrabili inaudibiliq ac icogitabili". However, when the intellect fell away from that contemplation into imagination due to weariness, that light deserted me, leaving me sad. Again, having left the body and returned, I found the soul full of light, at once flowing into the body and yet elevated above it."

Plato says, therefore: "He who, having attempted to ascend to the highest world, understands **divine substances** and **universal causes**, will surely obtain the greatest reward." Wherefore no one ought to neglect this, however much labor it may require; certainly

### Chapter five. Why the Soul descended into the lower world.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'D' with floral or leaf scroll patterns inside a square border.</image-desc>

Regarding the **Universal Soul** <note>the 'Anima Mundi' or World Soul, which animates the entire cosmos</note>, we must understand why it descended into this Body—whether it did so willingly out of obedience, or was compelled by some other cause. We will gain more benefit from the study of the Soul than from any other science, for by it we shall ascend to the Intellect, and even to God the Most High. Through this, we learn whether God created all things rightly and with perfect **wisdom**, or through some other design. In the past, **Plato** assigned many attributes to the Soul, to which we have borne witness, though he did not record every one; otherwise, a reader might have easily grasped his entire mind. These attributes of the Soul are varied. For instance, the Intellect is joined to the Sense, and it does not entirely despise it; yet through its union with the **body**, it is bound and suffocated within it,

For indeed, the **Body** is to the **Soul** as a **Place**. It is impossible, however, for this World to attain **Intellect** unless it first possesses a **Soul**. For this reason, the sublime **Creator** joined the Soul to it. And He entwined other species with the **Rational Soul**. Indeed, the operations of the Soul do not appear at all without purpose. Of these operations, there are few in **Plants**, more in **Beasts**, and the most in **Man**, so that this World may be perfect—though not as perfect as the higher world, because it is an effect of it, and also stands as the origin of all corruption. Therefore, it is necessary for the sensible World to also contain the kinds of living beings that exist in that intellectual world.

### Chapter Six. Concerning the error of the Ancients, and how every Being is good because of God.

<meta>This page continues from the previous discussion on the Soul's relationship with the body. Although the catchword from the previous page was "q omnis" (that all), this page begins with the suffix "pus," likely the conclusion of the word "corpus" (body), maintaining the focus on the physical versus the spiritual realm.</meta>

->**BOOK**<-

[...Bo]dy. The ancients indeed debated this, holding various opinions. Let us begin, however, with the opinion of the **Old Man** <note>original: "Senis"; a reference to the "Sage," typically identified as Plotinus in the Neoplatonic tradition</note> whom we recently cited, who said that he perceived the ancient natural philosophers <note>original: "physicos"</note> erred in their understanding of **imperceptible Beings** <term>Entium insensibilium: spiritual or formal realities that cannot be grasped by the physical senses</term>. They sought these things through the lower world; for this reason, they were of the opinion that hidden **Beings** were not present in it, setting aside the **Intellect** and following the **Senses**. By considering the world through the senses, they attempted to find eternal things among those that are subject to change.

When he noticed that they were wandering from the path of truth because of the prevailing power of the senses, he took pity and led them back to it. He distinguished the **Intellect** from the **Senses**, and **Intelligible things** from **Sensible things**. He established that the former are found to be eternal and unchanging, while the latter are changeable and corruptible. He added that there is a single author of both: the **First and True Being**, namely the sublime **God**, the maker of worlds. He further added that such a **First Agent** is the highest good, and that no other thing is good of itself, but everything is good only through Him.

He also asserted that this **World** consists of **Matter** and **Form**; and that which forms primary matter into a state of nature is more noble than the matter itself. Likewise, the **rational soul** forms primary matter because of a power sent into it from the wonderful **Intellect**; and the **Active Intellect** <term>intellectus agens: the faculty that transforms potential knowledge into actual understanding</term> assists the soul in forming primary matter through the power of the **First Being**. This is the principle of all three **Beings**: namely, the **Intellect**, the **Soul**, and **Nature**. Thus, sensible things were made beautiful by the power of the **First Agent**, acting through the intermediaries of the **Soul** and the **Intellect**. Fittingly also, the **True First Being**—the sublime **God**, good, simple, and the most perfect of all—inspires life first into the **Intellect**, then into the **Soul**, and afterward into **Nature**, making the **Intellect**, **Soul**, and **Nature** the principles of all other things.

### Chapter Seven. That God creates without time.

¶ All priority exists in time <note>original: "omnis prioritas est in tempore"</note>, since it is impossible for the **Agent** <term>Agens: the active cause or creator</term> not to exist before the **Effect**. However, this is not truly the case, because the **Intellect** discerns things without time, and the **Senses** do likewise. Hence, the intention of **Plato** was to follow the manner of speaking of the ancients, who, when describing generation, were forced to introduce the concept of Time. Of **Creation**, however, there is no Time, because the first and highest Agent, who creates anew, differs from the second, inferior, and shadowy agent. Therefore, if you wish to learn whether the **Patient** <term>Patiens: the thing being acted upon; the recipient of an action</term> suffers or is changed within time, explore whether its Agent acts within time. For a Patient acted upon by an Agent in time is changed in time, but a Patient acted upon by an Agent in a moment, is changed in a moment.

### Chapter two: That the Soul does not use recollection.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'D' at the beginning of the main text block, set within a square frame with a dense foliate and floral background pattern.</image-desc>

We say likewise that all knowledge <note>original: "scientia"</note> in the **higher World** <term>Mundo superiori</term> is perpetual. For whatever exists there is without time. Therefore, the Soul there gazes upon forms without time. Because they remain evident to it—both the highest and the lowest—and because it does not proceed from one thing to another by discerning from genera to species and individuals, or from species to higher genera and universals. Therefore, it does not even need the **recollection** <term>reminiscentia: the process of actively retrieving or "calling back" a memory</term> of them. 

And if someone, doubting this, should say that this condition belongs only to the **Intellect** <term>intellectus: the faculty of direct, intuitive understanding</term>—because all things are present to it in act simultaneously, and therefore it does not need recollection—while the Soul seems to behave differently (namely, that many things are not present to it in act at once, as in primary matter, but that it understands naturally one thing after another); and if it were so, it would be necessary for it to remember, whether it be in this lower World or in the higher. 

To this we shall respond that nothing prevents the Soul in the higher World from knowing many things at once. Indeed, such a thing is observed even here: that although it is simple, it knows many things in a single act—as sight perceives various colors. Therefore, the Soul also knows many things at once, without time, because it is above time, being indeed the cause of it. But if someone should say: the Soul distinguishes between the first and the last, why does it seem to be divided one after another? When, however, in this way...

# BOOK TWO

...knows; therefore it does not know all things at the same time <note>original: "sciat/non igitur simul cognoscit"</note>. We say that the **Soul** discerns by **Intellect** <term>Intellectu: a faculty of direct, immediate understanding</term>, not by **thought** <term>cogitatione: sequential reasoning or mental calculation</term>. When it performs this through the Intellect, it does not exclude the differences between things, but a greater union occurs. Indeed, the Intellect discerns without time, nor does it have (since it is simple and unified) a "before" or an "after," because no gap of succession flows between them. For the beginning exists simultaneously with the end. Furthermore, if it were said that it is well known that when the Soul discerns, it knows the beginning, the end, and the middle: we say that this is true, but it knows these things not through a temporal middle, but only through an ordinal one. This is evident in the way the eyes see a tree; for although one sees the roots and the branches at the same time, yet one recognizes the roots "first"—by an order of arrangement, not an order of time—rather than the branches. If physical sight knows in this way, how much more will the Intellect know the beginning, the end, and the middle with their proper order, yet without the passage of time.

For the universal is not taken away when its particular is removed; for example, if individual animals are taken away, the concept of **Animal** is not removed. But if the universal is taken away, all things beneath it—the particulars—are taken away as well.

### Chapter four: that the intellect is not subject to change, and in what way the Soul is subject to change.

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'E' set within a square frame with foliated scrollwork and floral motifs.</image-desc>

And if anyone should say: if the Intellect encounters in its contemplation sometimes its own substance and sometimes external things, it is surely altered or changed. Yet we have said that it is unalterable and impassible <term>impatibilem: a philosophical term meaning "incapable of being acted upon" or changed by outside forces</term>. 

Let us respond: if the Intellect encounters things in its contemplation at different times, this happens in different states. Namely, in the **Intellectual World** <note>Mundo Intellectuali: the realm of pure, eternal ideas</note>, it encounters in its contemplation only its own substance. Therefore, its act of understanding is its own substance. But in the other, the **Sensible World** <note>Mundo sensibili: the physical world perceived by the senses</note>, it encounters in its contemplation sometimes its substance and sometimes things themselves. This happens by reason of the "particular," whose essence is turned back into a universal when it is with the Intellect, once the physical impediment is removed. Indeed, the particular has...

It explains that while individual things may perish, the universal concepts within the Intellect remain eternal and unchanging.</summary>

## BOOK TWO

# SECOND

...for the universal remains. For it accepts the predication of that which is defined by it, and it differs from it only in that the particular is subject to the universal. This likewise occurs because of the bodily disposition impressed upon it by means of the **Soul** <term>Anima: the vital principle that links the physical body to the higher mind</term>. For the **Intellect** <term>Intellectus: the highest capacity of the mind for direct spiritual understanding</term>, when it is heavily entangled with the Body and united with the senses, encounters things as objects of **speculation** <term>speculationi: from 'speculum' (mirror), meaning to see the reflected images of things rather than their essence</term>. However, once it has emerged a little from the physical, it encounters even the substance of things as an object of **contemplation** <note>The author distinguishes between 'speculation' (observing outward forms) and 'contemplation' (grasping the inner reality or substance).</note>. Therefore, the Intellect does not change except in the manner we have previously described. 

The Soul, however, is said to move by the act of learning things, because it is situated on the boundary of the **Intellectual World** <term>Mundus intellectualis: the realm of pure, eternal truths above the physical world</term>. Its motion is "reflexive" <note>original: "reflexus," meaning a motion that turns back upon itself</note>, because in the act of knowing, it first encounters a thing as an object of speculation and then returns to its own essence. Truly, it is said to move because it changes its focus around an unchanging thing. 

The Intellect, on the other hand, remains unchanging and even unmoved. It is impossible for the Soul to be unmoved when it is subject to the Intellect. That which is subject to another is changeable; otherwise, it would be identical to that which is predicated of it. One thing must be known, however: that in the Intellectual World, the Soul moves in a **straight** <term>recte: direct or forward motion toward truth</term> rather than a reflexive manner. In the lower world, it is the opposite. 

But if someone were to object that even the Intellect moves—arguing that it changes from one thing to another, and if it changes, it undoubtedly moves—we shall say that the Intellect never moves unless its **primary Author** <note>original: "Autore eius primario," referring to God or the Creator</note> wills it; and even then, it moves directly and without ceasing. For such motion is actually a kind of rest. Indeed, the Intellect is a perpetual and **impassible** <term>inoffensibilis: incapable of being harmed, hindered, or changed by external forces</term> Essence; for this reason, it exists as more worthy than all other creatures. 

And if someone still protests, saying that the Intellect moves while speculating because it encounters sometimes a thing and sometimes the substance of that thing, we respond that if the Intellect moves, it moves from itself and toward itself, and not otherwise. Therefore, it does not move toward things outside of itself, nor from them back to itself. Since it contains all things, and brings forth the things it contains into **existence** <term>existentia: the state of being manifest in the world</term>, whenever it moves, its motion is entirely uniform and essentially unchanging. Such motion is similar to rest.

...indeed motion is from one thing to another, but this [motion of the Intellect] is not **subtractive** <note>original: "ablativus," implying a change where something is lost or taken away to gain a new state</note> or divisible. For if the Intellect were altered, it would not truly know, nor would it possess knowledge firmly. But the Intellect, having all things present before it, is not moved at all, because it contains them all—having proceeded from itself and being destined to return to itself, as we have said many times.

### Chapter Five: That the Soul is not moved in the Intellectual World

<margin>a</margin>
Furthermore, likewise, the **Soul** <term>Anima: the vital principle that connects the physical body to the higher mind</term> will not be altered in the **Intellectual World** <term>Mundus Intellectivus: the eternal realm of pure truth above the physical world</term>. This is because there, the Soul is pure and abstracted from all **husks** <note>original: "corticibus," referring to the "shells" or outer layers of physical matter and sensory experience that coat the soul in the material world</note> and compositions. It exists **in act** <term>in actu: fully realized and functioning, rather than just having the potential to act</term>, since no corporeal matter is then mixed with it, and it knows lower things truly and perfectly. Indeed, in that place, it is joined to the Intellect without any medium. Here below, it had been united to the senses; therefore, without undergoing any death, but rather becoming clearer, it is joined to the Intellect and shaped by it. For how could it be thinkable that the Soul itself should die while other substances are **incorruptible** <note>original: "incorruptibiles," meaning they cannot decay or be destroyed</note>? Since the Soul itself preserves others and is preserved by the Intellect. The Intellect, however, is preserved by the **First Author** <note>original: "autore primo," referring to the Creator or the first cause of all things</note>, who exists by His own power. The Intellect is the **face of the Soul** <note>original: "facies Animae"; a metaphor suggesting the Intellect is the higher "visage" or mirror that the Soul looks toward to find its own divine form</note>, toward which the Soul is inclined and with which it contemplates. The Intellect was produced before other creatures without a medium, and it is the medium through which the Soul was produced, just as that medium was produced as Nature. Through this medium, the Body was made; and through this medium again, all things that are born and decay were made. The Soul, therefore, in the higher World is entirely unalterable and **impassible** <term>impatibilis: unable to be affected or changed by external influences</term>. It knows its own substance and the whole of reality with a single, entirely **undifferentiated** <note>original: "indifferente," meaning a direct, holistic knowledge that does not need to be broken down into separate parts</note> knowledge. This is because of its union; for then the Soul, the thing known, and the Intellect are all a certain unity.

<summary>This page explains that neither the Intellect nor the Soul undergoes change or "motion" in the higher realm, as they exist in a state of pure actuality and unity. It details a hierarchy of existence where the First Author sustains the Intellect, which in turn sustains the Soul, which sustains the physical world.</summary>

# SECOND

### Chapter Six: That the Soul has Memory in the Sensible World, and what kind it is.

<image-desc>Large decorative woodcut initial 'D' featuring a seated figure, possibly a scholar or saint, within a classical architectural frame with floral patterns.</image-desc>

When the **Soul** <term>Anima: the vital, animating principle of a person</term> turns away from the **Intellect** <term>Intellectus: the highest faculty of the mind, capable of direct spiritual truth</term> and is sent down into this World, it contemplates things beyond the Intellect and possesses memory. Yet, it does not remember the superior beings for that very reason—otherwise, it would not have descended here in the first place. Just as it is mindful of lower things when it departs from the higher realm and descends here, so too, if it had first fallen to the Heavens and kept a memory of them, it would have remained within them. Therefore, just as the Soul, while existing here, has memory only of lower things, so also when it is ascending to Heaven, it does not remember anything other than itself, and it becomes almost identical to that higher state. Indeed, when the Soul remembers certain things, it becomes similar and identical to those very things; otherwise, it would not truly remember them.

For there is a kind of **Memory** that is similar to the Intellect, and another that is similar to **Sense** <term>Sensus: the ability to perceive the physical world through the body</term>. The Understanding of **substances** <term>substantia: the essential reality or "being" of a thing</term> is a firm and steady reason. **Thought** <term>Cogitatio: the discursive process of thinking about things one by one, rather than seeing the whole truth at once</term>, however, is weak and not singular but varied, changing according to the earthly or Heavenly things being thought about. Through imitation, the Soul becomes similar to—and almost the same as—the things it thinks about, which are mostly lifeless bodies (since they are secondary things). In truth, Thought can hardly be truly similar to both [the physical and the intellectual] at once in the way that pure Understanding is, because it is the middle point between the Intellect and Sense. It inclines equally toward both, and without them, it preserves nothing perfectly.

It is clear, then, that the Soul, when remembering, joins either a noble or an ignoble thing to its **Imagination**. Returning to our point, we say that the Soul in the higher World—where it is not forbidden—desires perfect good. It understands that good (presented by the medium of the Intellect) as something unoccupied and ungrasped, from which the **Universal Soul** <term>Anima Universalis: the "world soul" that governs the entire cosmos</term> and the **Rational Soul** <term>Anima Rationalis: the individual human capacity for logic and reason</term> are distant only by the medium of the Intellect. Indeed, once the Soul has turned away from the first good and turned toward lower things, it desires what it contains according to its memory. For it does not desire such things unless it first thinks of them; and as we have already stated, Thought is a kind of Memory.

### Chapter Seven: How the Intellect is "ignorant" of its Superior Author and of Inferior Creatures.

<image-desc>An ornate woodcut initial letter 'Q' featuring symmetrical scrolling foliage and floral patterns within a square border.</image-desc>
Now, if someone were to suggest <gloss>that</gloss> the **Soul** <term>Anima: the vital, animating principle of a person</term> gazes upon this World before it descends into it, then by that same logic, once it has returned from this world to the higher realm, it would look back upon the lower world and would undoubtedly remember it. However, it has already been said <gloss>that</gloss> in the **Intellectual World** <term>Mundus Intellectivus: the realm of pure spiritual truth, above the physical world</term>, the Soul remembers nothing of this physical world. We say <gloss>that</gloss> the Soul considers this World <gloss>through</gloss> intellection before it inhabits it; this, however, is a kind of **ignorance** <term>ignorantia: here used in a mystical sense, meaning a state of being that is "beyond" or "above" ordinary human knowledge</term>, not **science** <term>scientia: structured, logical knowledge or "book learning"</term>. Yet this ignorance is nobler than all science, and this is because the **Intellect** <term>Intellectus: the highest part of the mind, capable of direct spiritual insight</term> is "ignorant" of its superior acting cause and of lower things. And being mindful of lower things (by another means), it descends from that honorable state to this World.

Furthermore, the Intellect is "ignorant" of its superior **First Author** <note>original: "Autor primus," referring to God or the ultimate Source</note> because it does not know Him perfectly. If it did know Him perfectly, it would be superior to its own Author, and thus the **Effect** would be the **Efficient Cause** <term>Efficiens: the agent or force that brings something into being</term> of its own Creator. This is false and highly improbable.

Again, it is said to be ignorant of lower things (as we said before), not <gloss>that</gloss> it lacks knowledge of them—since it actually contains them—but rather, while the cause of *our* ignorance is a great deficiency, the reason for the Intellect's "ignorance" is its supreme perfection and highest loftiness. This is because it contemplates those things not according to what they are in themselves, but in a higher way, since it is their cause. A thing is always higher when it exists within its cause than when it exists in itself.

Even the **First Creator** knows these things, but not in the same way as the Intellect; He knows them more loftily still, knowing them insofar as He creates them. Therefore, the knowledge of the Intellect is, in a sense, "ignorance," because it is not the true, divine kind of knowledge. This is also why we said <gloss>that</gloss> the Intellect is "ignorant" of the subjects below it. Again, this ignorance is called knowledge, since it is a perfect consideration of such things, even if it is not according to their physical essence. Nor does the Intellect need a "science" of them, because it is their cause, <gloss>containing</gloss> all things "as the wise man said."

It establishes that the Intellect contains the essence of all lower things as their cause, while remaining humbly "ignorant" of the full perfection of its own Creator.</summary>

...it has been said. The sublime **Creator** <term>Conditor: God as the "Founder" or "Architect" of the universe</term> preserves all things in the **Intellect**, which He brought forth into the **Soul** <term>Anima: the mediating spirit between the physical and the divine</term> by the medium of the Intellect alone; and into nature, by the medium of the Soul; and into this World by means of both, in an orderly fashion, until it reaches particular, individual things. When, however, God created the Intellect as the cause of things, it follows that He Himself is the Author of them, and He does not require a "science" or structured knowledge of them <note>original: "nec indiget earum scientia"</note>. And if the Intellect is said to be "ignorant" of things, it is because it did not produce them from nothing, nor as the primary cause. 

Instead, God is called "Knowing" <note>original: "Sciens"</note> insofar as He created them, whereas the Intellect is "ignorant" in comparison to the knowledge of things in themselves. Thus, even the Intellect’s knowledge of its own essence is called a kind of **ignorance** <term>ignorantia: here meaning a lack of total comprehension compared to the absolute knowledge of God</term> when compared to the knowledge of God. For knowledge of oneself as one truly is, is not a state of total ignorance. How indeed could it be so, since it is the same as other **Sciences** <term>Scientiis: formal systems of knowledge</term> and things known, and through it the Soul gazes upon truth, as we have said before. 

We assert, however, that its Knowledge is ignorance in respect to the Creator; just as the Soul is "ignorant" of its own "caused" effect <note>The physical body or the results of its actions in the world</note> in the manner we previously explained regarding the Intellect; otherwise, it would not require a higher, first Author. 

Therefore, let us return to our view that the Soul, when separated from this dwelling <note>The physical body</note> and existing in a higher state, does not remember any of the things previously known—especially those things that are **sensible** <term>sensibilium: things perceived by the five senses</term> and **corruptible** <term>corruptibilium: physical things that decay or change</term>. Instead, it deals with "Intellectualized" concepts derived from sensible things. Otherwise, it would receive images in the same way it did here before. This is absurd, for it would then be "thinking" <note>In the sense of human discursive reasoning</note>; and when one thinks, one **imagines** <term>imaginatur: the process of forming mental pictures of physical objects</term>. As we have taught: if the Soul were to use imagination in that higher realm, the things there would be exactly like the things here, which is a great inconsistency. They only receive knowledge by means of the united Intellect. Therefore, the Soul does not use imagination in the **Intellectual World**. It was proved before that, having fallen from that realm, the soul requires memory of sensible, changeable, and corruptible things. We have shown through this inductive discourse how its "ignorance" stands in comparison to the higher author and the lower effect.

It also explains that in the spiritual realm, the Soul perceives pure truths rather than mental "images" or sensory memories of the physical world.</summary>

## Chapter eight: how the Soul
## admits division.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'I' with intricate floral and scrollwork designs within a square frame.</image-desc>

**At present**, it must be stated why division occurs in the human **Soul** <term>Anima: the vital, animating principle of a human being</term> and what follows from division in its own right. It is necessary, moreover, to know whether the Soul admits division at all, and whether it does so by its own nature <note>original: "per se"</note> or by association <note>original: "accidentariam"</note>. We say, therefore, that the Soul joined to the **Body** is divided accidentally <term>secundum accidens: a philosophical term meaning something happens to a thing not because of what it is, but because of what it is attached to</term> when the Body is divided. For anything indivisible that is joined to a divisible thing is said to be "divisible by association." 

Division, however, is also spoken of according to "form" <note>meaning the different functions or powers of the soul</note>, as when it is said that the **imaginative** faculty <term>imaginatiua: the power to form and retain mental images</term> is beyond the **vegetative** <term>uegetalem: the basic biological power of growth and nutrition</term>, and the **concupiscible** <term>concupiscibilis: the faculty of desire and seeking what is pleasant</term> is distinct from the **irascible** <term>irafcibilem: the faculty of spirit, often associated with anger or the drive to overcome obstacles</term>. 

We likewise say that one part of the body primarily contains the imaginative faculty, another the concupiscible, and yet another the irascible. Thus, the Soul is divided "by association" when the underlying Body is divided, but not by its own nature, since a substance <note>referring here to a spiritual essence</note> receives no division. 

Furthermore, seeing that living Bodies require a Soul spread through all parts of the Body so that the Animal may feel everywhere in the Body, we assert that the Soul is divisible. It is clear that every limb feels as long as it contains the **sensitive** soul <term>sensitiuam: the faculty responsible for perception and feeling</term>. We say, then, that this power is divided when a limb is divided; yet, even though it is spread through all the limbs, it is not divided within itself, but is **perfect** <note>meaning "complete" or "whole"</note> in every part. 

If anyone should say that the Soul is divided according to the sense of touch, but follows different rules for the other senses, it must be said that the Soul is not divided even when touch is divided—though this is less evident—in the manner we have described. The **vegetative** power is similar. The **appetitive** <term>appetitiua: the faculty of longing or hunger</term> and the **fugitive** <term>fugitiuaq;: the faculty of avoidance or fleeing from harm</term> powers, which are extended throughout the Body, are less divided among themselves. These are indeed part of the sensitive faculties, but are "below" the others, and for that reason appear more divided. These are less distinct within the Body because they do not operate through instruments <note>original: "instrumenta," referring to specialized physical organs like the eyes or ears</note> located in separate places; otherwise, they would be hindered from performing their work.

<summary>This chapter explains that while the Soul is a single, indivisible spiritual substance, it appears "divided" because it is joined to a physical body with different parts and organs. It details how various faculties—like imagination, desire, and growth—relate to the body's physical structure.</summary>
<keywords>Soul, division, Body, sensitive faculty, vegetative faculty, concupiscible, irascible, philosophy of mind, Aristotelian psychology</keywords>
