### Chapter nine: that one common sense encompasses all the organs of sensing.

A single sensitive power unites all the organs of sensing, flowing into them through the specific intermediary senses <note>the five physical senses of sight, hearing, smell, taste, and touch</note>, whose objects it recognizes and distinguishes. And it exists as something indivisible, nor does it operate through one single instrument because of its great spirituality. Therefore, all the senses terminate at it, just as all lines from the circumference of a circle lead to the center; and it knows simultaneously and in an instant all things to which the senses themselves are directed. 

For every specific sense distinguishes only the appearances <note>original: "species"; here meaning the sensory information or "mental image" of an object</note> of its proportioned object. Just as **sight** distinguishes whiteness, blackness, and other colors; **hearing** distinguishes sounds sharp, soft, deep, and slow; **smell** distinguishes stench and other odors; **taste** distinguishes sweetness and other flavors; and **touch** distinguishes roughness and smoothness. 

But this spiritual power, common to the senses, distinguishes their sensible things and the forms of each, and reports them to the **Imaginative** faculty, which shapes and composes them at will. Then it also reports to the **Memory**, which preserves them for opportune use; then the **Thinking** faculty <term>cogitatiua: the power that processes and arranges mental images before they reach the intellect</term> draws them toward another arrangement, until it leads them to the **Intellect**. And all these are spiritual powers, and they operate by themselves, without obvious physical organs.

**O**ne must know whether these aforementioned **powers of the Soul** <note>original: "uirtutibus Animæ"; refers to faculties like memory, reason, or sensation</note> and others have specific locations in the **Body** <note>original: "Corpore"</note> or not? For we say that the site of a power of the Soul is understood to be in that part of the Body where its **operation** <note>original: "operatio"; meaning its active functioning or work</note> is manifested. And certain powers of the Soul do not at all require locations in order to exist within them, but rather so that they might show the operations drawn out through them, as if through suitable receptacles. It is the Soul itself which adapts a limb for an operation, and the powers of the Soul are distinct according to the different dispositions of the limbs; yet they are not simply different from one another, nor is the Soul composed of them. Instead, it is **simple** <note>meaning indivisible and not made of parts</note>, and those noble powers it possesses it grants to the parts of the Body through a continuous **influx** <note>original: "influxu"; a philosophical term for the way spiritual energy flows into physical matter</note>. Because of this, the powers are not merely instruments of the Soul. Indeed, the more noble they are, the more they exist within the Soul itself than in the limbs.

Returning, therefore, to the primary matter, we say that if every power of the Soul lacked a location, the external power would not differ from the internal, nor would the part of the Body responsible for **movement** <note>original: "motiua"</note> be made distinct from the **sensitive** part <note>the part that feels or senses</note> through the endowed influx of power—which would be entirely inappropriate. Likewise, it would follow that it would be unknown in which instruments the operations of the Soul reside. 

But if someone should respond that certain powers of the Soul do have locations—namely, those limbs in which their operations appear—we would say in turn that if it were so, the whole Soul would not be within us, but some part would remain outside of us; and this is highly improbable. Therefore, in our account, we assert that no part of the Soul exists in a place by any logical reason, whether the Soul is within the Body or not. For a **place** <note>original: "locus"</note> surrounds and contains that which is located within it, and whatever is contained by a place is a physical **Body** <note>original: "Corpus"</note>. Yet neither the Soul nor any power of it is a Body. And when we say the powers of the Soul are within certain limbs, we do not mean they are in them as if in a physical location, but that they manifest their operations in them. For the Body relates to place in a different way than the Soul relates to place. If any...

### Chapter Three: That God is, and what He is like. ###

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial "Q" featuring floral and scrolled leaf motifs within a square frame.</image-desc>
That God exists is shown by this noteworthy demonstration: since nothing exists in **potentiality** <note>original: "in potentia"; the possibility of being or doing something</note> unless something else exists **in act** <note>original: "in actu"; the actualization or reality of that possibility</note>; otherwise, a thing would not emerge from potentiality into act. For indeed, potentiality is nothing other than the possibility of act, nor can it exist in act by itself; for it is not fitting that anything else should be the **Agent** <note>original: "Agens"; the active force that makes something happen</note> of its own existence. For the Agent is prior in act. It is false for something to be both prior and posterior to itself in the same respect; therefore, if potentiality is to be led into act, it is necessary for something to exist in **pure act** <note>original: "actu mero"</note>, since there is no other by which it could be actualized. And this is the **Necessary Being** <note>original: "Ens necessarium"; a being that cannot not exist</note>: perpetual, unchangeable, undiminishable, unalterable, and all-...

->[header] BOOK THREE<-

He Himself remains unchangeable, because He is unproduced; and this is because He exists by necessity in actuality from His own essence. Indeed, He is **True Being** <note>original: "Ens uerum"; a fundamental philosophical term for that which truly exists in the highest sense</note>, and even above Being. For this reason, all existence depends on Him, is preserved in Him, and returns to Him. It is impossible to imagine Him having any potentiality; otherwise, He would require another to bring Him into actuality. Every other thing besides Him is thought to be in potentiality before it is in actuality. For a lack of being precedes existence, and potentiality precedes necessity. 

He is, however, undiminishable, as the most absolute True Being. He does not share any common quality with any other thing, but is a Being prior to any immediate cause. Since He is the agent of all things, He is the **Necessary Being** by which all else is described. He knows all things—past, present, and future—under a single, unchanging logic, because He knows them insofar as He is their **Author** <note>original: "Autor"; the source or creator</note>. Other things, however, are known by another insofar as they are perceived. Likewise, He leads something from potentiality to actuality by contemplating Himself, not by looking at anything outside Himself. He is always unchanged because He is the supreme act. 

The creature, however, is impermanent because it is corruptible, and also capable of returning to potentiality; and this is because it is capable of being generated. That which exists in actuality is more noble than that which exists in potentiality, for it exists in act after it was in potentiality. Being in potentiality is not True Being; and even if such a "possible" thing is called "Being" in a broad sense, it is not truly called so. Therefore, it is proven that **actuality** is better and more universal than **potentiality**, and that it differs from physical nature, as it is unchangeable. Thus, the **Intellect** and the **Soul** are prior to **Nature**, since Nature is the work of both.

We say that since the Soul is a **Being in actuality** <term>Ens actu: something that fully exists and is "in act"</term>, it is impossible for it to be called a **Being in potentiality** <term>Ens potentia: something that has the capacity to exist but is not yet realized</term>, unless we consider it to be so called because it was produced, as was said before. For in every produced thing there is Actuality and Potentiality, and because Being in actuality is diminished [compared to the source] / God Himself is the principle of a thing that is transitioned from potentiality to actuality. Furthermore, the Intellect and the Soul are not said to be in actuality and potentiality because they are produced with a temporal delay, or alternating like physical bodies that are born and then corrupted; for they remain, and exist perpetually.
Hence, for this reason, the Soul is not **breath** <note>original: "spiritus"; here referring to a physical vapor or wind</note>, nor any other kind of Body at all, just as was proved above; and although it may be described differently by some, nevertheless what we have recently written should be sufficient. But if anyone should still say that the Soul is something beyond the nature of the Body, let us also explore this / and what such a composition of the Body might be through which the Soul is described. For certain members of the **Pythagorean Sect** <note>Followers of Pythagoras who believed the soul and the universe were structured according to musical and mathematical ratios</note> said that the composition of the Body is similar to the composition of a **Lyre** <term>Cythara: a stringed musical instrument</term> / since just as (when the strings of the Lyre are tightened correctly and according to proportion) the Lyre receives a harmony, [so too the Soul...]

Likewise, the Soul rules over the Body and prevents it from performing many actions according to its physical nature; a mere composition, however, neither rules over the Body nor prevents it from acting according to its physical nature. Furthermore, when the composition of the Body is at its best, the Body is consequently healthy and free of pain; however, it is not always the case that the same holds when the Soul is at its best <note>The author observes that a morally "perfect" soul can exist in a sickly body, proving they are different things.</note>. Additionally, if the Soul were a composition, then because various members of the body have various compositions, many Souls would exist within a single Body. This is exceedingly absurd.

Furthermore, if the Soul were the composition of the Body, it would be made by itself, for the composition of the parts of the Body is made by the Soul, not by the parts themselves. This is because a composition must be made by something prior—just as the arrangement of strings, which the harmony of a musical instrument <term>Organum musicum: a term for any complex musical instrument, like a lute or an organ</term> follows, is not made by itself but by the musician. For the strings are indeed arranged, but they do not arrange themselves, which would be an undignified <note>original: "ignobilis": implying a lower or impossible order of operation</note> operation. 

Similarly, if the Soul is a composition of the Body, since this composition is produced by the Body, it follows that the Soul is produced by something that is not a Soul. It would also follow that Beings are only prior to one another by simple comparison. However, no form is produced without a **Formative Soul** <term>Anima Formatrix: the soul's power to shape and organize physical matter into a living being</term>; otherwise, it would happen by chance, which is impossible in both specific and universal things. Therefore, the Soul is not the composition of the Body.

<meta>This page continues the philosophical inquiry from Book III. The previous page discussed the soul's priority over the body's composition and its role as a governing substance. This page moves into the formal definition of the soul using Aristotelian terminology, specifically addressing whether the soul is a 'substance' or an 'act.'</meta>

->BOOK [III]<-

If it is said that the ancient Philosophers unanimously asserted that the **Soul** is the **Act of an Organic Physical Body**, and because an act is not a substance (since it inheres within a substance), will the Soul therefore not be a substance? We respond that it is necessary to examine this kind of reasoning.

This **Act**, then, certain Athenians <note>Referring to the Greek philosophers, particularly Aristotle and his school.</note> called by another name, **Entelechy** <term>Entelechia: a Greek term for the actualization or "completeness" of a potential; the state of a thing having reached its full purpose.</term>. The Philosophers likewise said that the Soul is to the Body in a certain proportion, just as **form** is to **matter**, which constitutes the Body; except that the Soul is not the form of the Body insofar as it is a body alone. Rather, it is the act of an **Organic Physical Body** <note>original: "Actus Corporis Physici organici"</note> which has the potential for life.

And it has already been proven that the act of the Body is a substance and not an **accident** <term>Accidens: a philosophical term for a property or quality that can change or be lost without the thing itself ceasing to exist.</term>. Moreover, it is called a "Physical Body" to distinguish it from an artificial one (such as one that is painted); likewise, it is called "potential for life" to distinguish it from inanimate things, such as stone, iron, and the like, which, although they are physical bodies, do not possess the potential for life. The term "Organic" was also added—that is, having instruments to carry out the works of life, such as the **Brain**, **heart**, and **Liver**, which are the principal organs.

Furthermore, an **Act** is of two kinds: one is **separable**, such as a sailor from a ship or a rider from a horse; the other is **inseparable**, such as heat from fire or cold from snow. A separable act, therefore, is not destroyed when the subject is destroyed, whereas an inseparable one is destroyed. Thus, the Soul is a separable act of the Physical Body; for it is not destroyed when the Body is destroyed, as has already been shown.

Again, one kind of act is the perfection of its matter, such as the heat of fire through which it exists; another kind *performs* a perfection, as a builder [is the act] of a house. The Soul is the act of the Physical Body; its perfection does not rest, but rather because it performs perfection within it—namely sensation, **Intellect**, **Imagination**, and other works. Indeed, before animation, the Body is imperfect. However, the Soul is not a **bodily perfection**; otherwise, it would be divisible (if the Body were divided), just as if...

The author uses the metaphor of a sailor and a ship to illustrate how the soul remains intact even after the body's destruction.</summary>

# Chapter Seven: That the Soul is a Separable Act.

<margin>a</margin>
The **Soul** is not the perfection <note>original: "perfectio"; in this context, it refers to the "completion" or the full realization of a thing's potential.</note> of a single limb, in the way that sight is the perfection of the eye. This is because the Soul brings about the perfection of every individual limb; even when the perfections of these individual limbs are destroyed, it is not necessary for the Soul to be destroyed. Rather, it is an **act** <term>Actus: the state of being active or functional, as opposed to mere potential.</term> that is separable from the subject in which it resides. Moreover, it is not subject to decay, because it possesses operations that it performs by itself without the use of bodily organs—namely, the upright actions of good morals which are often contrary to the desires of the Body. It also discerns all the limbs of the body without any intermediary. It carries out these "inorganic" <note>Meaning functions performed without the use of a physical "organ" or tool, such as abstract thought.</note> operations while existing in a pure state, contemplating incorporeal things. Therefore, the **Essence of the Soul** undoubtedly remains as a survivor after the Body has decayed; otherwise, its operations would be more noble than its very essence. This would be a great absurdity, since Essence is the cause of action, and it is false to claim that an effect is better than its agent.

Even if the Soul were an inseparable act—like a natural form—how is it that in **sleep** it is elevated from the Body without being torn away from it, in order to receive **prophecy** and **revelation**? In this same way, it also emerges from the body during wakefulness, returning to its own essence once material distractions have been removed. This is most apparent at night, due to the rest of the **senses** and the cessation of their labors.

Furthermore, if the Soul were merely the perfection of the Body by which it exists as a Body, it would not move the body against its own physical impulses, nor would it know the body. Although the Soul discerns sensible things, it is not similar to the senses themselves; for it knows a thing even when it is dissimilar to it. According to the order of nature, the senses themselves receive the "simulacra" <note>Images or sensory impressions of external objects.</note> of things, but it is the Soul that truly discerns them. Likewise, the Soul would not be able to speculate upon incorporeal things if it were itself merely a bodily form. But even if the Soul were a natural perfection, it would not [move...]

In truth, humans are directed by a Soul shaped by instruction, which was previously unformed and merely capable of being formed.

Like the Beasts themselves, he would not seek out **Forms** <term>Forms: In Aristotelian philosophy, the "essence" or "shape" of a thing that makes it what it is.</term> that are foreign to the Body, nor would he be a spectator of hidden things.

Furthermore, just as air, when receiving every color, must lack any color of its own—for if it possessed even one specific color, it could not admit another—the same is true of water. The eye, too, if it contained one color within itself, would not comprehend the rest; and so it is with hearing, smell, and the other senses. In this same way, since the human Soul receives and discerns all bodily forms, it cannot be one of those forms itself. Nor does the human Soul receive and know bodily forms in the way a Beast does—commonally and without discernment—but it distinguishes them specifically. It comprehends them clearly through its own **reason** <note>original: "rationem"</note>, just as it distinguishes a color or a scent with definition. Therefore, it is sufficiently proven that the Soul of a man is not a natural Form like that of a beast, especially since if it were...

## Chapter two: That even matter is produced by God, although it is moved toward Him, and how this is proved.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'D' featuring a lattice of vines and floral patterns within a square border.</image-desc>
**P**erhaps someone might say that the substance to which every natural **Form** is reduced does not possess such a movement of its own, since **Motion** <note>original: "Motus"</note> occurs through desire, and in that [substance] no desire exists. Therefore, if it is not mobile, it is also not produced according to essence, but is a composite. And yet it is the cause of all motion. To this we shall respond that whoever thinks this is mistaken. For the first simple thing to which all others are reduced never lacks every proper form through which things exist; otherwise, being void of **Forms**, it would not subsist. But when one **Form** is taken away, another succeeds it; therefore, by repeatedly receiving Form from the **First Mover**, it is also brought into being. On this account, the wise have already said that **Prime Matter** <note>original: "materia prima"; the most basic, formless substance of the universe.</note> is moved by a **Motion** which is the reception of **Form**, and that it desires **Form** as the **Imperfect** <note>original: "Imperfectum"</note> desires **Perfection** <note>original: "perfectionem"</note>: just as the eye desires sight, or the female desires the male <note>A traditional Aristotelian analogy used to describe how formless matter 'seeks' a defining shape or nature.</note>.

It is imaginable, however, as a successive transformation into infinity: from one **Form** to another, nor is there any principle except with the reception of a **Form**. An example of this evidence is: the various shaping of solid things for every purpose. Wherefore it has already been proven that every other substance has its efficient cause in **Essence**, existence, and permanence: the **First Agent**, which is the first universal **Mover**, and that every mobile thing is moved toward it, and that everything made by **Motion** also remains through motion, because motion is the act of a **Being** in potentiality <note>A classic Aristotelian definition: motion is the process of a possibility becoming a reality</note>, that is, the perfection and the drawing out of that which is proceeding into act.

...more in materials <note>original: "materiebus"; the text picks up from the previous page's discussion of how many things exist in matter</note>, and they are corrupted, while the universal forms remain incorruptible. Therefore, the art is more noble in the artist than in the finished work; nor is that **Form** <term>Form: In this context, the "Form" is the ideal blueprint or perfect mental concept of a thing, rather than its physical shape</term> which exists in the stone the same in **Essence** <term>Essence: The fundamental nature or "soul" of an object</term> as that which resides in the artist. Instead, the ideal remains firm in the artist, and from it, another proceeds into the material. The works of the sculptor are less noble and less beautiful, never reaching perfection despite the artist's efforts, but are limited by the capacity of the material itself, which exists as a more or less true imitation of that ideal Form. 

Furthermore, a Form within matter is singular and inseparable; if it were transferred from one subject to another, it would be diminished all the more. Briefly, therefore, we conclude that every **Agent** <term>Agent: The active force or person that causes something to happen or be created</term> is more noble than the subject it acts upon—for the subject is overcome, while the agent overcomes. Even the internal model is better than the physical copy, since individual good Forms come from prior and higher universals. Artificial things come from the Form that dwells in the Mind of the artist, which is superior to the one fashioned in marble. 

Indeed, art itself looks toward the Intellect, since it remains perpetual by emulating nature. Nature, in turn, necessarily perseveres in a similar way because it imitates another: namely, the higher Intellect. For the artist, in his work, does not merely follow a finished craft; rather, by ascending in thought, he takes an image from nature through which he makes his work more beautiful. And if by chance the natural Form which he portrays is imperfect, he himself perfects it by imitating the Intellectual ideal, adjusted for the suitability of the material receiving it. For example, if an Artist wishes to create an image of **Jupiter** <note>original: "Iouis"; the Roman king of the gods</note>, he does not look at any physical or sensible Form. Instead, having transcended in thought, he paints the god with the most beautiful appearance imaginable. Hence, if Jupiter himself were to make himself visible to human eyes, he would express himself in no other likeness than that which the artist had already conceived.

### Chapter Two: That God does not act through deliberation.

If God created the senses along with the Soul when He first created it, it seems that the capacity for sensation is inherent to the Soul before it descends into the physical structure of a living creature. If this is so, the descent of the Soul would be natural, and the foundational beginning of the senses would have been in the **Intellectual World** <term>Mundo Intellectuali: The realm of pure, divine thought and perfect forms</term>, while their final completion occurs in the **Elementary World** <term>Elementario: The physical world composed of the four elements—earth, air, fire, and water</term>.

Therefore, if the Soul had been produced not for its own sake, but so that it might dwell in a lowly and despicable habitation full of afflictions, it would follow that it was directed there by the first Author through consultation or thought. But we say that God does not act through consultation, or deliberation and thought; otherwise, He would have something "prior" to Him <note>The author argues that if God had to "think through" a problem, the problem or the principles used to solve it would be older or more fundamental than God Himself</note>. Since He is the **First Being** <term>Ens primum: The ultimate source of all existence</term>, there is nothing prior to Him, just as nothing exists after the "last" thing. For one who thinks always thinks based on something that came before. 

Furthermore, one thinks of conclusions derived from principles. Principles are knowable through the senses, but the Divine Intellect knows nothing of sensible things through the physical senses, because...

It also argues that God acts by His very nature rather than through human-like reasoning or deliberation, as He is the ultimate source of all principles.</summary>

...remaining within the **Intelligible things** <term>Intelligibles: In Platonic philosophy, these are the ultimate realities or "Forms" that can only be understood by the mind, not the senses</term> themselves. So much less, therefore, the first **Founder** <term>Conditor: The Creator or Architect of the universe</term> undoubtedly does not need thought, nor deliberation, to govern **Living Creatures** <note>original: "Animalia"; in this philosophical context, this refers to any ensouled being, including humans</note>, or anything of the lower and upper World. 

For things produced through deliberation and thought happen in this way: when all things were brought forth in the wisdom of the **First Being** <note>original: "Entis primi"; a reference to God as the source of all existence</note> under their own proper nature and in a species that cannot be communicated to another. Nor will any other wise person, no matter how much they think, make a thing equally similar and right. 

Thought serves as an aid for making those things which do not yet exist, occurring while someone thinks before they act. Because, indeed, one cannot look upon a thing directly before it is made, it is necessary for the agent to know beforehand what kind of thing is fitting to be made; thus, when it is eventually made, it will not be different from what was foreknown. But when something effects another thing by its **Essence** <term>Essence: The internal nature or "being" of a thing, rather than its outward actions</term> alone, it is not necessary for it to foreknow what kind of thing ought to be made, since it produces such a thing simply because it is fitting for it to be. For this reason, it does not require another helper, nor thought, to produce anything. 

Whence, returning to our proposal, we say that **Souls** <term>Anima: The life-force or animating principle</term> in their own World, before they descended into the physical structure of Living Creatures, were already sensitive, but with an **Intellectual Sense**. However, once they exist within the established Living Creatures, they are also sensitive, but with a **Corporal [physical] Sense**. Being positioned in the middle between the **Intellect** <term>Intellectus: The higher, spiritual mind</term> and **Bodies**, they receive from the Intellect a sensitive power, which they then transmit into the Body. Yet, once it is transmitted into the Body, it exists in another way—namely, as a physical sensation. For the Soul, whenever it is turned away from the Sense and turned toward the Intellect, will make **Corporal things** <note>original: "Corporalia"; physical or material matters</note> become spiritual, preparing them to be known by the Intellect. Sometimes, however, the reverse happens, and it causes spiritual things to become Corporal.

### Chapter five: That God does not act through another, and that in spiritual things, the "what" and the "wherefore" do not differ.

<margin>a</margin>
The First **Mind** <note>original: "Mens"</note> does not act for the sake of something else, since there is nothing more noble for which it could act. Hence, he is the true agent. And the Beings produced by him other than the Intellect are prefigured in the first product, which is the **First Form** <note>original: "Forma prima"</note>—for example, the Soul is prefigured in the Intellect. It is necessary, however, to know him as he knows himself—which we cannot do—since in him, the understanding power and the Essence understood are then one and the same thing. Therefore, we who think recognize essences different from him through the Intellect better than we recognize him. Furthermore, when something other than the Intellect and the **Intelligible** <term>Intellectibile: A thing that can be grasped by the mind rather than the senses</term> is known through the Intellect, it is known by *what* it is, beyond *why* it is <note>original: "quid sit / ultra quid sit"; a distinction between a thing's identity and its purpose/cause</note>. For these two differ in natural, material things, because these are but images of the Intellect and the Intelligibles. For example,

<meta>This page continues the discussion of spiritual hierarchies, transitioning from the general nature of the "Author of Causes" to the specific relationship between the "Sensible Man" (the physical human) and the "Intellectible Man" (the spiritual or ideal archetype of humanity).</meta>

<sig>g</sig>

The **Sensible Man** <term>Homo sensibilis: Man as he exists in the physical world, perceived through the five senses</term> is a likeness of the **Intellectible Man** <term>Homo Intellectibilis: The ideal, spiritual form of humanity existing in the divine Mind or Intellect</term>. For the Intellectible Man is spiritual, and none of his members are separated from one another. Indeed, the position of the eye is not outside the position of the hand. Similarly, the rest of the members do not stand apart; rather, all are present together. Therefore, *what* the eye is does not differ from *why* it was made. Such a distinction between essence and purpose occurs only in things that can be divided into different parts. 

Furthermore, even in the world of the senses, the same knowledge sometimes encompasses both *what* something is and *why* it is. For example, what a solar eclipse is and why it happens are expressed in a single definition: the obscuring of light due to the moon being placed between <note>original: "obscuratio ob lunam interpositam"</note>. Now, if in the matters of the lower world the "what it is" and the "why it happens" appear as one, how much more must this be true in the **Intellectible Being**? Therefore, he who sets out to define something and takes the "why" in place of the "what" has defined it truly. 

This is because every **Intellectible Form** <note>original: "Forma Intellectibilis"</note> and its purpose are identical. By this, I do not mean that such a Form is the cause of its own **Essence** <note>original: "Essentia"</note>, but rather that when an inquiry discovers what that Form is (when understood through its own proper logic), it simultaneously understands why it exists. Therefore, since the reason for "what it is" and the reason for "why it is" are indistinguishable, there is no need to seek them separately. 

The proof that the parts of a spiritual thing do not differ is that the thing itself can take the proper name of either part. In these matters, it is not appropriate to ask by what means these parts belong to the thing. For only when parts are truly distant from one another can one ask why they are present; in such cases, the thing is not simply called by the name of one of its parts. For instance, a Man is not called an "eye" nor is he called a "hand." However, an Intellectible Being can be called by the name of any of its underlying principles. Therefore, as has been said quite often, the reason for "what" and the reason for "why" are the same in that spiritual realm—a condition that does not apply to the **Corporeal Being** <note>original: "Enti Corporali"</note>, insofar as it is physical.

<meta>This page continues the philosophical exploration of the "Intellectible" realm. <header>->BOOK<-</header>

The **Intellect** <term>Intellectus: In this context, the first created spiritual principle, often equated with the Neoplatonic "Nous" or Divine Mind</term> was produced as a pure thing, by a creation that was perfect and momentary. Therefore, its **Essence** <term>Essentia: The fundamental nature or "whatness" of a being</term> began to be, and at the same moment was suddenly completed in **actuality** <term>in actu: A state of full realization, as opposed to "potency" or mere possibility</term>, without any intervening potentiality. For this reason, to know what the Intellect is, is to know also why it exists. For since God does not deliberate while creating, when he begins a thing, he perfects it at once; as previously stated, no **potentiality** <note>original: "potentia". In Aristotelian thought, most things "become" something over time, moving from potential to actual. The Intellect is unique because it is created fully realized.</note> is mixed into its Essence.

Hence, regarding a Being of this kind produced by him, the question of "why it is" is not asked separately from the question of "what it is." For such a distinction belongs only to an imperfect thing. But if it should be objected that it is indeed possible to state why the Intellect exists, we respond that this can be understood in two ways: in one way by reason of the **Agent** <term>Agens: The active cause or creator; in this case, God</term>, and in another way by reason of the **Act**. 

Therefore, since the reasons of the Intellect do not differ at all (as mentioned before), the Intellect takes the name of both; there is no need to ask why they are present. Once it is known what the Intellect is, why it is is simultaneously known, and vice versa. For the Author indeed produced the Intellect as perfect—in act, without any mixed potentiality. Since he himself is perfect, unfailing, and most pure, he produced it through Essence as his own work and through the **Word** <note>original: "verbumque". A reference to the Logos or divine command as the instrument of creation.</note> as an operation. Such a Being is such that "why it is" within it is the same as "what it is." 

For the "Perfect Agent" is a broad concept, and is of the sort described by the **Ancients** <term>Prisci: Likely referring to the "Prisci Theologi" or ancient sages like Plato, Hermes Trismegistus, or Zoroaster</term>, whose thought we shall explain as we are able. However, the "simply perfect Agent" is that which acts through Essence alone, not through some external quality. But an **imperfect Agent** is one that acts not through Essence, but through quality. For that reason, it does not act with a pure and perfect action. Indeed, it does not begin and simultaneously perfect a work. Because the work of such an agent is of an imperfect kind, knowing "what it is" does not mean "why it is" is also known. 

Rather, once the first is known, it is still necessary to learn the second separately, as previously mentioned. Therefore, the **First Agent** is not an imperfect Agent, since it is a perfect Being above all others. Consequently, its work is also perfect. The reason for this—

It is not permitted to ask "why it is" beyond the inquiry into "what it is." 

Finally, since the production of the **Intellect** <term>Intellectus: The first and most perfect spiritual creation of God</term> is undoubtedly perfect, no one should say that it is imperfect in its dispositions. Therefore, it is not contained by them, nor does it act through them as a consequence. Again, the principles of the Intellect are most perfectly suited to it and are not subordinated in time, since they were created simultaneously with the Intellect. Therefore (as has been frequently repeated), where it is known what the Intellect is, it is equally known why it is. ### Chapter one: how the Stars operate on lower things, and that they do not perform evil.

<image-desc>A large ornamental woodcut initial 'N' in a white-vine (bianchi girari) style, featuring interlacing vine motifs against a dark, stippled background within a square border.</image-desc>

It is by no means necessary to record the arrangements of things, even those occurring to individuals, when the purpose is to deal with them in general. And as we write about these kinds of arrangements of things—namely, the reason why certain things are produced by them—we shall treat them through **Physical Causes** <term>Causas Corporales: Material or bodily causes that operate according to the laws of nature, rather than through individual soul or choice.</term>, not animate ones, nor those driven by personal will. The **Stars** <note>original: "Stellae." In this context, the author refers to the celestial bodies as instruments of divine order rather than independent deities.</note>, therefore, are like intermediaries between the art and the craftsman; they are neither like the **First Agent** <note>The primary creator or God.</note>, nor like the final matter that assists in reaching perfection, nor even like agents that act upon one another. 

In truth, they are like the good civil laws of lands, which organize the states of Cities by directing individual affairs: some of these laws guide people toward virtuous behavior by offering rewards, while others call them away from evil through the threat of punishment. The Stars are also similar to the character of a director of Citizens in timely **political actions** <term>actionibus politicis: The governance and moral management of a community.</term>; for although these actions are varied, they nonetheless all lead toward a single consultation and intend the **Good** <note>original: "bonum." A central concept in Neoplatonism, where all things in the universe naturally strive toward a state of divine perfection or "The Good."</note>. 

But if some should say that the goods of the lands are merely **signs** <term>signa: Indicators or omens that point toward a truth without necessarily causing it.</term>, we respond that if their meaning is that a sign is the path to the work, then what they say is true. Indeed, we sometimes prove the first thing from the later, such as the cause from the effect, and the simple from the composite; at other times, we learn of accidents from a principle, and the composite from the simple. Thus, from this point, we have nearly proved what was meant to be said: namely, are the Stars the causes of the evils occurring here below? Indeed, we assert that they are not, because they do not work...

### Chapter Two: That the work of fascination is twofold, and how fascination occurs.

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'O' featuring a foliate and floral design inside a square frame.</image-desc>

The work of **fascination** <term>Fascinatio: Not merely "attraction," but a technical term for the binding influence or enchantment one thing exerts over another through spiritual or natural links.</term> is twofold. One kind arises from the harmony and proportion of one thing to another. The other, conversely, arises from a difference and a multitude of powers; though these powers are diverse, they nonetheless complete a single part. 

**Artificial fascination** <note>original: "artificiaria." This refers to man-made attempts at magic or influence.</note> is deceptive, for it often fails and does not achieve its intended outcome. However, the **True fascination**—which does not deceive—is that of the wise man. By using his imagination, he imitates the **Heavens** and acts according to his strengths. Some things he accomplishes by leading through the love of one thing for another; other things he achieves by drawing through dominance. In this, he is assisted by the **innate virtues** <note>The hidden, natural properties or "occult" powers of herbs, stones, and animals.</note> of earthly things, some of which increase the love and following of one thing to another, while others increase the passion and reception of one by another. 

**Things** <note>original: "Res." This is the catchword for the following page.</note>

For these things following one after another are the foundation of **fascination** <term>fascinatio: In this context, enchantment or a binding influence exerted by one soul or object upon another through spiritual vapors.</term>, which, once understood, are vehemently preserved to exercise the power of effective love. Furthermore, the fascination that occurs through sweet words and a certain ingenious and clever speech is not the work of the speaker himself, but of the devised speech which draws one thing to another by the power of **natural love**. 

Since something is found that unites Souls that are different in their locations through a certain mutual agreement between them, there are, moreover, certain things in which the **power of love** <note>original: "vis amoris"</note> is present, so that the sensing person—even if unwilling—sometimes follows. Just as a prudent Musician sometimes voluntarily follows the consonance of his art, at other times he follows it by the gesture of his Body; for he forms himself according to that consonance, yet he does not love it by **reason** <term>ratio: The logical, calculating faculty of the human mind.</term>, but by **sense** <term>sensus: The faculty of perceiving through the physical body and its immediate reactions.</term>. 

And this is the species of fascination that the common people do not wonder at, nor do they detest it because they are accustomed to it. However, they wonder at other physical fascinations because they do not take pleasure in them, and therefore they err. And just as a Musician gladdens and entices the listener without the passion of reason, but with the affection of the sense, so too does the fascinator draw someone who is unwilling. 

Indeed, such a person is not perceiving through the **Intellect** or the **Sense**, but is only perceiving through that impression—some impetus other than a natural one—and that arises from the altering cooperation of worldly things upon a human being, beyond their previous disposition. From this, if any impression is grasped, it is understood to be made upon the **Animal Spirit** <term>spiritus Animalis: A refined, subtle substance in the body that acts as a bridge between the physical organs and the immaterial soul.</term>. For Reason does not receive that impression; indeed, it does not follow it. For if Reason were also to support the listener and he himself were to incline toward it, even then Reason would not permit the Animal Spirit to be affected by the Musician, nor by the fascinator, nor by any other inferior bodily quality. 

And indeed, when someone in the act of fascinating invokes the **Sun** or other **Stars**, praying that they might assist in the desired work, it is not that the Sun or other Stars hear the prayer. Rather, they are moved in some way, just as one member in the human body [is moved by another].

### Chapter Three: Which natures possess the power of enchantment from the Heavens, and why a just man is not enchanted.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'R' within a square frame, embellished with vine-like scrollwork.</image-desc>

Lower things, having obtained wondrous powers of **enchantment** <term>fascinandi: The act of binding or influencing through spiritual or celestial means, often translated as "fascination."</term>, have received them from the **Heavens** and work through them. Therefore, men also use clever **invocation** <note>The formal calling upon of spiritual or celestial powers through speech.</note> in their enchanting, so that it might appear that the man does it by himself. However, this is not the case; rather, they enchant through the movements and **influences** <term>influxus: In Renaissance philosophy, the "flowing in" of celestial power or spirit into the material world.</term> of the Heavens. Indeed, even if such an invocation were omitted, these natures would still enchant in their own proper time. 

The parts of the World, being naturally united, draw one another. Therefore (as said before), the enchanter who invokes works through the fitting powers of nature; nor is it a wonder that this man is heard when he utters a prayer or imprecation, for he is not a stranger to Heaven—especially a **just man**. If it is said that sometimes an **unjust man** enchants by invoking, we respond that the unjust man has drawn this kind of power from the same source as the just man. For Nature grants to men equally, not distinguishing one from another. However, another higher and nobler power exists which does distinguish between them. 

If it is said that the entire World suffers <note>In the philosophical sense of "undergoing an action" or being passive/receptive.</note> according to one part and acts according to another—which is the **Celestial** part—this part is **impassible** <term>impatibilis: Incapable of being acted upon, harmed, or changed by lower, material forces.</term>; it acts upon lower things naturally, not by accident. For every impassible agent acts naturally and without accident, and if it happens otherwise, it is beyond the intention...

Indeed, the rational soul acts upon the **sensual soul** <term>Anima sensualis: The part of the soul responsible for sensory perception and basic desires.</term>, because one part of the world acts upon another—if it has found faith in the **Prime Author** <note>original: "Autore primo"; referring to God or the First Cause of the universe.</note>. And thus, in this way, the man escapes enchantment. 

For if the distant sensual soul receives the impression of the enchanter's speech, and having been drawn near, it is joined to the enchanter through hearing and responds in some way—how much more does that same sensual soul, in this **lower world** <note>The material, physical realm.</note>, being close to the rational soul, respond and submit to it?

### Chapter Five. That something moves Man toward another, and that one too devoted to natural things is Fascinated by nature.

Finally, we also assert: that the man performing an evil work and being ignorant that it is such—if he thinks it to be good, persevering and drawn to it by Nature—is **enchanted** on account of the appearance of beauty. For indeed, seeing that earthly things are beautiful, he believed them also to be truly good and sought them out vehemently. Wherefore, desiring that which is not good as if it were good according to the **Sensual Appetite**, he is enchanted, drawn toward an involuntary thing. For the love of the enchanted person is fixed. But he who is not drawn toward earthly things, nor follows them as beautiful and good, does not fall into enchantment. Indeed, he contemplates the perpetual good, seeks and observes it, and speculates upon himself; therefore, because of this sublimity and elevation from lower things, he repels enchantment from himself. 

It has been proven, therefore (as we shall relate), that any part of this world is affected by the heavens according to its own nature and aptitude, just as one part of a **Living Body** <note>original: "Corporis Animalis"; refers to the concept of the *Anima Mundi* or "World Soul," where the universe is viewed as a single living organism.</note> is affected by another. For each part is fit to be moved by another, and each has its own character.

### **Chapter one. Why the Soul descended into the lower World.**

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'A' featuring intricate scrollwork and foliage within a square frame.</image-desc>The noble **Soul** <term>Anima: The human soul, viewed here as a divine spark that mediates between the spiritual and physical realms.</term> left the **Higher World** <note>original: "Mundum superiorem"; the realm of divine forms or pure spirit.</note>, so that it might shape and rule over those things that come after. Having performed this duty and returned, it gained this benefit: that here it truly learned the nature of good and evil through **experience** <note>original: "per experimentum"; emphasizing knowledge gained through living in the world rather than just theoretical contemplation.</note>, which it otherwise would not have known perfectly. This is not the same way that spiritual beings (who know the vices in which humans here are entangled) know them; they do not know through pleasure according to their own natures, but through the true reasons within themselves, by virtue of a dignity more powerful than this descent. For if they were to know as human souls do, they would also be corrupted by the same communion with **Bodies**, and they would attempt to be torn away from them. 

Indeed, **rational Souls** <term>rationales: Souls endowed with the capacity for reason, distinguishing them from animal or plant souls.</term> joined here to **Matter**—and therefore soiled and polluted—discern such things because of this kind of binding. If one of these souls remains pure when it is released, it will be happy in beholding the state of noble, spiritual, and principal Beings. Thus, it is made perfect in discerning the condition of both Worlds. Furthermore, although the Soul here below is submerged in the **sea of Matter** <note>original: "pelago Materiae"; a common metaphor for the overwhelming and chaotic nature of physical existence.</note> through the dominance of the senses and constrained under the limits of nature, nevertheless illumination from the **Intellect** <term>Intellectus: The higher, intuitive mind that remains connected to divine truth even when the soul is in a body.</term> does not cease. Rather, it flows into the soul constantly, because the Intellect is substantial to the Soul and is never in any way torn from it. Thus, the descent of the Soul contributed to its discerning good and evil perfectly by experience, as well as all things of this World and its own nature; provided that there remain...

For when some beautiful, illustrious, and desirable creation falls under one's gaze, a person looks around in wonder at the clear signs of its excellence. They inspect its inner workings and thereafter venerate its **Author** <note>original: "Autorem"; referring to God as the master craftsman or creator.</note>, recognizing that his work is supremely perfect and beautiful: that he himself is the **highest Good** <note>original: "summum Bonum"; the ultimate source of all morality and existence.</note>, whose power is limitless. After the Author and the Author’s first work, the remaining works also appear honored and abundantly perfect. Since the Author (who is unique) produced them, the marks of his handiwork are not hidden, as they are far from obscure.

### Chapter two. If God had not produced anything, nothing else would exist; and why many Beings were produced.

<image-desc>A decorative drop-cap letter 'S' featuring intricate floral and foliate patterns contained within a square border.</image-desc>

If the one first **Being** <term>Ens: A philosophical term for "that which exists" or "essence."</term> had remained only in his own Essence and had kept his Power, activity, and light within himself, nothing eternal would exist, nor would anything changeable or corruptible. Since neither of these types of beings would exist, the work of the one first Author would not be a beginning, a light, or a true good. 

But this is by no means the case. For since the one, first Being is a true cause, his work is also a true beginning. And if he is the true flowing light, that which receives it is also a true light; likewise, if he is true **Goodness** <note>original: "Bonitas"</note> that waters and nourishes, that which is watered is also a true good. Therefore, it is not fitting that God should exist alone, nor that he should fail to produce another noble Being...

### Chapter three. That no Intellectual or natural Substance exists that does not act; and the order of things.

<image-desc>A decorative square drop cap 'N' containing the letter N, surrounded by detailed woodcut-style floral and vine patterns.</image-desc>

No **Intellectual** or natural **Substance** <term>Substance: The underlying reality or essence of a thing, whether spiritual or physical.</term> exists without being active, except for the lowest and weakest substance, whose actions are impossible to perceive. The proof that it is impossible for natural substances to exist without being active is found in seeds sown in the earth. Unless they are crushed by their surroundings, these seeds—being spiritual and in some sense incorporeal—must necessarily act until they reach a **sprouting** <note>original: "pullulationem"; the act of budding or germinating.</note> that is similar to their species and ready to be further **propagated** <note>original: "propagaturam"; to multiply or continue the line.</note>. This occurs because **intellectual principles** <term>rationes seminales: Often translated as "seminal reasons," these are the formative spiritual blueprints that guide the growth of all living things.</term> are joined within them. Otherwise, they would not be visible; yet they become visible through their actions and reveal wonderful powers. Therefore, if these seminal principles cannot help but be active, all the more so must the eternal Intellectual Substances be active. They cannot restrain their powers and actions unless the matter beneath them is incapable of receiving their influence, or receives it so weakly that it cannot, in turn, act upon anything else. What is temporary and mobile exists like the heavens. Particular things are bordering on the motion of nature, while **Universals** <note>General concepts or essences that exist beyond individual physical examples.</note> are, according to their Substance, at rest; since the Cause of the arrangement of a single thing remains itself unvaried. Indeed, in that realm, there are no subject limits such as lines or figures, nor any other motions except from the voluntary nod of the **First Cause** <note>original: "Causa prima"</note>, which exists as the First Product; nor is it imaginable that anything existed before this, except the First Author. This is His will. Since the imitation of an external will is alteration, such change does not reach the First Cause.

### Chapter eight. That the Soul, existing in the supernal orb, still operates in the lowest; and it joins both together.

Every soul, when by its working it has filled this sensible orb with its dignities, is compelled to return to the **Intellectual orb** <note>The realm of pure thought and divine forms.</note>: which it embraces tenaciously through the aforementioned indubitable knowledge. Since that World is more noble than this one, and preserving the contemplation of that Intellectual realm, the Soul completely neglects to return to this one; as is evident to one who, having emerged from the **Fascination of nature** <term>Fascination of nature: A philosophical concept where the soul is "charmed" or distracted by the beauty and complexity of the material world, forgetting its divine origin.</term>, has returned quickly to the Intellect, having gazed upon the principles of things.

But the Soul, having returned, therefore despises lower things, because these are consumable, like likenesses of itself which do not persist, unless that Soul—acting as the cause—continually shapes them. While the Soul still exists in that proper orb, having seen its dignity, it takes and draws virtue from it and pours it into this [lower world], joining it through such a superior illumination. And thus the **unified World** <note>original: "Mundus unitus"</note> is created. We prove this opinion with a brief reason, because the Sou[l]...

### Chapter nine. That the Soul, when submerged, does not look upon higher things; conversely, once emerged, it scorns lower things.

The **Sensible World** <note>The physical world perceived through the five senses.</note> dominates us. This is because our souls are submerged within it, filled with base desires. Consequently, we neglect the announced harmony of the **Intellectual orb** <note>The spiritual realm of pure thought and divine order.</note>, nor do we obey its influence, being ignorant of the Soul’s own progress and the illumination that comes from that higher realm. This is due to the dominance of nature, which acts like a **Fascination** <note>original: "Fascinationem"; here used to mean a hypnotic spell or binding attraction to material life.</note> over individual souls in this state. Because of this, they are too weak to return to their own **Essence** <note>The true, unchanging spiritual nature of the soul.</note>. 

However, they will be strengthened to perceive that Essence, the Intellectual World, and the influx sent from it through the Soul, once we have overcome this world and become strangers to its sensory desires and natural operations. These are habits we have been accustomed to since childhood, caring only for the affairs of individual souls before they can reach the **Universal** <note>The collective or divine Soul that encompasses all things.</note>. We cannot perceive any part of that Universal realm as long as these souls exist under the power of the **concupiscible soul** <note>original: "Animae concupiscibilis"; the part of the soul driven by physical appetites and desires.</note> and the forms of the imagination. Conversely, once we have contemplated the Universal Soul, we come to scorn individual things, even though they have long been familiar to us.

### Chapter ten. That the Universal Soul rules without toil, while the individual soul rules with toil before its elevation.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'C' at the start of the paragraph, containing a floral scrollwork pattern.</image-desc>
Furthermore, the **Universal Body** <note>The physical universe as a single, living organism.</note> is the cause that joins itself to the lower world, and that world to itself. The **Universal Soul** <note>The world-soul that animates the entire cosmos.</note> rules this Universal Body by its own inherent powers and without any toil; indeed, it does not rule through the kind of deliberative calculation with which our souls manage human bodies, but rather governs through a universal **Intellectual administration** <note>original: "administratione Intellectiua"; a form of governance based on pure divine reason rather than trial-and-error thinking.</note>. This is because the Universal Body exists as an unchanging and uniform whole, lacking the diverse combinations of parts and the differing limbs found in smaller creatures. Where such diverse parts exist, they require a variable form of management; however, parts that are similar are governed as if they were a single unit. 

In contrast, the **individual soul** <note>original: "Anima particularis"; the human soul.</note>, which resides within a specific body, rules it through a laborious administration, no matter how noble that soul may be. This is because it cannot rule without the deliberative thought it requires, for it is submerged in the "ocean of nature" and mingled with the fire that rushes into the senses. From this arises pain, caused by something unnatural or overwhelming entering into this state. Indeed, it is not possible for the Soul to escape this physical condition except through great exercise of thought and **Contemplation** <note>original: "speculationis"; here meaning deep, spiritual observation or study.</note>. Through these, it immediately recovers in its administration that which had been consigned to oblivion. It then detects the hindrance that was bewitching and disturbing it—that which prevented it from gazing upon its own **Essence** and from exploring those things that help, strengthen, and carry it upward to overcome prevailing base **appetites** and corrupt imaginings. 

For this reason, the Soul (when it left the state of eternal things to pursue this sensory world) is unaware that it has moved away from perfect love and has instead put on a changeable and weak love. Furthermore, when the Soul has grown strong enough to reject these altering habits, and is no longer held captive by them, it administers its body without the pain of affliction...

# BOOK EIGHT.

## Chapter one. What the efficient cause of fire and the 
## other natural beings may be.

<image-desc>Decorative square woodcut initial 'E' featuring interlacing vine or strapwork patterns in white on a black background.</image-desc>The **essence** <note>The fundamental nature or "whatness" of a thing.</note> of fire, just as that of the earth and the other similar elements, is a certain **formative reason** <note>original: "ratio"; here meaning a rational principle or "blueprint" that exists in the mind of the universe.</note> within **Prime Matter** <term>Prime Matter: The underlying, formless substance from which all physical things are made; it has no qualities of its own until "form" is applied.</term>. Nor is fire created by the friction or the clashing of bodies acting as the **efficient cause** <note>original: "Agente"; the force that actually brings something into being.</note>, as some have mistakenly thought. Rather, fire is latent within those bodies and merely appears because of such mutual collision: for when these bodies are dry, they become intensely hot. Furthermore, Prime Matter is not fire merely in its potential state; instead, the **form** of fire only exists within it when the **formative reason** <note>original: "ratio formatrix"</note> of fire, and of other beings, brings it into effect. This formative reason is the **Universal Soul**, which exists as the same life-force for both fire and the rest of the world. Through this Soul, individual things are governed according to their specific condition, so that anything—whether among inanimate objects, plants, or animals—shines forth in its own way, while another may be in some manner harmful. Within this Soul our own soul also remains, and through it, our soul knows everything that it learns. This is, moreover, the **divine providence** <note>original: "prouidentia diuina"</note> diffused throughout the whole world, and the light by which every single thing exists and persists. Therefore **Plato** said that the Soul, acting within any simple body, produces this **sensible fire** <note>Fire that can be perceived by the senses, as opposed to "intellectual" or "divine" fire.</note> and the other **Elements**. Since the Soul is the cause, the **efficient cause** of this fire is therefore a certain fiery life; and fire...

<summary>This page argues that fire and the other elements are not created by physical actions like friction, but are manifestations of the Universal Soul's "formative reason" acting upon Prime Matter.</summary>

Within this Soul, our own soul also remains, and through it, our soul recognizes everything it learns. This is also the divine providence diffused throughout the whole world; it is the light by which each thing exists and persists.

# EIGHTH [BOOK]

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'O' containing a symmetrical floral motif with a central stem and leaves, enclosed in a square frame.</image-desc> Everything that moves in the higher sphere—whether it be the **Intellect**, the **Soul**, or something else—is moved by a **vital motion** <note>original: *motu uitali*; a movement that is inherent to life itself rather than being pushed by an outside force</note>; and it sustains that motion according to its interconnected existence. For just as an earthly traveler proceeds along an earthly path, and just as all things that sprout from the earth are earthly (even if they differ in variety), so everything that is carried along in that vital region is carried by a vital conveyance. Indeed, all things that are seen there are alive. 

Furthermore, that which is carried there moves from the beginning of the path to the end (in the specific way that "beginning" and "end" exist in that realm). I say it moves toward the end without being distant from the beginning itself. This is the opposite of how things work here on Earth, where a thing moved from the start to the end of a journey is physically separated from its starting point. For if a thing carried there were distant from its beginning upon reaching its end, it would not be **Intellectual** or **Vital** in "actuality" <note>original: *actu*; a state of being fully realized or active</note>, but only in "potential" <note>original: *potentia*; having the capacity to be something but not yet being it</note>. If that were the case, it would eventually cease through corruption, having been "born" or "created" beforehand. However, that which is Intellectual and Vital in actuality always and universally remains the same.

### BOOK [VIII continued]

[The **Intellect**] contains within itself universality itself and the very **form** <term>Form: In this philosophical tradition, 'form' (Latin: *forma*) refers to the essential 'blueprint' or internal nature that makes a thing what it is, rather than just its outward shape.</term> of things. However, the physical thing itself is not present inside the **Intellect** as if it were pressed into it; instead, the **Intellect** produces something similar to the thing, which then corresponds to it. In this way, everything past and future corresponds to something that exists within the **Intellect**, just as the knowledge in our **Soul** corresponds to the things it represents. Otherwise, if the forms in the **Soul** were different from the forms of the things themselves, we would not truly know them, nor would we grasp their truth. Indeed, the truth of a thing is the thing itself; for if truth were anything else, it would be alien to the thing, and consequently even contrary to it. For contemplative **Souls** form truth within themselves from **particulars** <note>original: *particularibus*; individual, physical examples of things (like a specific dog) as opposed to the general concept (the 'universal' idea of a dog)</note>, which, according to the specific **appearance** <note>original: *speciem*; the mental category or 'kind' of a thing</note> of individuals, is the thing itself.

Therefore, when a person has observed something and stripped away its outward form, they impress a proportioned **likeness** <note>original: *simulacrum*; a mental image or reflection</note> of it upon their **Soul**. If they see that same thing again unchanged, they recognize it, because it corresponds to the pre-existing and proportioned likeness already in their mind. If, however, they look at it a third time and it has been altered, they do not recognize it, because it no longer matches that first image in the **Soul**.

In this way, a craftsman first envisions a certain form within his **Soul**, and then creates a likeness of it in one or more pieces of **matter**. Indeed, the numerical plurality of things—the fact that there can be many versions of the same object—arises from the **matter** they are made of. Similarly, if someone else were to take a **universal** <note>original: *universale*; a general concept that applies to all members of a group</note> model from these crafted forms and later create similar objects in **matter**, there would be even more individual forms. Yet, if those particular forms were destroyed or taken away, the universal form would not be taken away with them.

Therefore, we conclude that forms are united by **abstraction** <term>Abstraction: The process of mentally 'pulling away' the general idea of a thing from its physical, material body.</term> from **matter**, and a single form is multiplied by being impressed into different materials. Likewise, **universals** are permanent, while **particulars** are changeable and perishable; for this reason, there are likenesses in the **Intellect** that are always proportioned to those other things. And if anyone should say that the rational principles of things in the **Intellect** are merely substitute instruments for those things, not differing from them in any way, we respond that (if this were the case), the form in the **Intellect** would be igno... <note>The text breaks off here; likely 'ignota' (unknown) or 'ignorabilis' (unknowable).</note>

### Chapter seven: how the Intellect is one and many.

Returning to the point from which we digressed—the discourse on how a single **universal** <term>Universal: A general concept or category (like 'Tree') that applies to many individual instances (every specific tree in the world).</term> is multiplied among **particulars**—we offer an example. For instance, consider a **Plant** or an **Animal**. Although each of these is a single concept, the name is nevertheless applied to many individuals. For the **forms** of the "acting agent" that exist in various pieces of matter differ in number; and if they exist within a single piece of matter, they differ in kind.

Furthermore, one thing can be many, such as a **Body**. Although a body is one, the "acting principle" <note>original: *ratio agens*; the organizing logic or force that shapes physical matter</note> forms many members within it. Consider the bone, the eyes, and the nostrils; although each of these is "one" thing, none of them is "one" in a simple sense. Rather, each is composed of many other parts, such as nerves, veins, and cartilages. Even a nerve (granted that it is one) is still composed of the **Elements**; and the same is true of similar things, like blood. Although blood is one substance, it is also composed of other things, and so on, until one reaches **primary matter** <term>Primary Matter: In ancient philosophy, 'materia prima' is the most basic, formless 'stuff' of the universe before it is given any specific shape or identity.</term> and **form**. Both of these, since they exist as simple entities, are each a single substance.

If we interpret the name of each: **Primary matter** is nothing other than formless substance, and true **form** is that through which a thing is what it is. Having explained these things, we see that the **Intellect**, while being "one," is not one in the same way as a physical **Body**. Indeed, it is higher and nobler than the body, as we said before. Nor is the **Intellect** "many" in the same way a body is many; rather, it is many insofar as it contains the principle capable of uniting many things. For it possesses a single form by which it is defined, and from which all internal and external forms arise. Because the **universal** unites the **particulars**, it is not taken away even if one of those individuals is removed. Furthermore, its power comes from elsewhere...

### Chapter eight: how all things are in the Intellect, and how the Intellect and also God act.

We say that all things are in the **Intellect**, yet not because things exist in it in an absolute or independent sense, nor in such a way that they are compounded with it. Rather, it is because the **Intellect** produces and preserves them. For nothing is thought to be permanent except within it, and if we take away the **Intellect**, those very things are also taken away along with their universality.

Moreover, since the **Intellect** is all things—inasmuch as it is the force bringing them about—it acts on one thing through another. But the **First Agent** <note>original: *Agens primum*; likely referring to the Supreme Deity or the "One" in Neoplatonic thought</note> (who produces these things) perfects them without a medium <term>Medium: An intermediary step or instrument used to achieve a result.</term>, and does so all at once in a single moment. Consequently, He exists as a true creator, since He acts without any other thing; He does not create something out of something else, nor does any other cause help or stimulate Him. Therefore, just as all things are created by Him, so too do they return to Him. For this reason, He is called the **First Agent**, a designation that belongs to no other, since all other things were created by Him.

For the **Intellect** actually operates as a **Second Agent** <note>original: *Agens secundum*; a secondary power that acts as a bridge between the Creator and the physical world</note>, and it effects whatever it effects through the First Agent. This is because the Intellect requires contemplation of the **First Agent** in addition to the contemplation of its own substance. Furthermore, its operation is not entirely simultaneous, nor is it instantaneous.

### Chapter nine: How all universal Living Beings are in the Universal Living Being, and how this differs from their presence in the Intellect.

<summary>This page explores the hierarchy of creation, distinguishing between the "First Agent" (God), who creates instantly and independently, and the "Intellect" (Second Agent), which produces and maintains the forms of all things.</summary>
<keywords>Intellect, First Agent, Second Agent, God, Creation, Universality, Contemplation, Living Beings</keywords>

--- Page 165 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion of the Intellect and the nature of universal principles. The previous page ended while discussing how all things return to the First Agent; this page begins a new section within Book Eight, explaining how universal "Living Beings" exist within a single Universal Life.</meta>

->[BOOK] **EIGHTH**<-

Just as all things underlying the **Intellect** are within that very **Intellect** by means of a rational principle <note>original: *per rationem*; this refers to the "Logos" or the structural essence that gives a thing its identity</note>, so too all universal **Living Beings** <term>Living Beings: The Latin text uses *Animalia*, which in this context refers to any "animated" or "ensouled" existence, not just animals in the modern biological sense.</term> are within the **Universal Living Being** by means of a rational principle. If we say, however, that there are many things beneath both types of **Living Beings**, we speak truly; however, the **Living Beings** of the lowest sphere are more imperfect and fewer than the **Living Beings** of the higher sphere. And the **Living Being** is not brought down from that abstract life without eventually reaching small, weaker **Living Beings** and existing within them—those in which, because they live a particular and limited life, the power of universal life comes to an end, since there is nothing else lying beneath them. 

What has been described here occurs when our contemplation is **Intellectual** <note>that is, focused on pure thought and abstract principles</note> rather than **Sensory**. For **Sensation** considers individual, singular things first, and only afterward looks at species and genera. But the **Intellect** contemplates the universals first, and the particular things afterward. 

This difference which we have mentioned between the supreme **Universal Living Being** and the **Particular Living Being** does not actually distinguish them except according to their form. I say that the **Universal Living Being** and the **Particular Living Beings** do not differ simply in themselves; rather, they are like the **Love** (which we have already described) in the universe, and the **Love** in the **Sensible** <note>the physical world perceived by the senses</note> sphere. In the physical world, the victory of the **Elements** from which things are composed sometimes dissolves that love; indeed, it does not even join **Beings** together except by accident, and falls short of the intention toward the primary goal. 

**Intellectual Love**, however, connects all things through will: both by a vital union and by a desire for the primary goal, which is why it is never dissolved. For there is no excess that could destroy it, because in that higher **World**, there is no controversy at all, nor is there any hatred among existing things. Instead, there is the highest **Harmony** and a communion of life, from which all lower things are nourished and given growth.

We say that the **Stellar Souls** always know they circle the earth and are alive; however, that which is perpetual and unchanging does not pass away <note>original: *non transfertur*</note>. A past day, month, or year and similar periods are merely the boundaries of **recession** <note>original: *recessio*; the movement of drawing back or the passing of a point in time</note>; therefore, **Constant Being** is not "yesterday" or otherwise "past," but is always the same. 

The human soul, however, establishes the past day, month, and year through its own motion. Just as someone making a path places a single foot upon many different parts of the ground, so the single motion of a star is divided by us—relative to its own Soul—into many parts. Time is counted in days because night follows light; otherwise, there would be no difference between past, present, and future time. Just as a falling drop—though it remains the same drop—is seen in a single blink of an eye throughout its entire descent, yet to the observer it first left the upper region, then the middle, and finally the lower; so too, past, present, and future [are distinguished] among themselves...
