The **First Author** <note>original: "Avtor primus"</note> is the highest glory, insofar as he is highest in perfection; he exists as such because he perfects every other thing capable of perfection. He perfects them because he brings them all into being. Indeed, he creates all the principles of the **Essence** <term>Essence: the intrinsic nature or indispensable quality of a being that determines its character</term> of every **Being** <term>Being: "Ens" in Latin, referring to anything that exists</term>, as the driver of the universe and of both Worlds <note>likely referring to the Intelligible/Spiritual world and the Sensible/Physical world</note>. Fittingly, he first infuses life, Power, and dignity, flowing into each thing by degrees according to its capacity. Thus, the Being closer to him is more capacious. Indeed, that thing which is the first to receive from him is closest to him in the dignity of its Substance and the perpetuity of its constancy; it exists as a medium between the First Author and all other produced things. Before all others, it receives the influx of life and dignity, which it then pours into the lower things remaining. For this primary created thing contains the light and the greatest strength of truth within a **spiritual Essence**—simple and absolute. And that which follows below it in the degree of strength and honor exists with less light and is closer to a state of perfect Corporeality <note>materiality or physical existence</note> and true composition <note>the state of being made of multiple parts rather than being "simple" or unified</note>. And this first sub-existing thing is contiguous <note>touching or directly connected</note> only to the first form through his Word. As a **Substance** <term>Substance: that which exists by itself and stands under all properties; the underlying reality</term> more perfect than all others beneath it, the influx of perfection received within it is infinite; however, the part transmitted (which is the "possible light" of the desire for perpetuity toward the following created thing, the **Second Intellect**) is finite. This is because the first created thing flows into the Second Intellect gradually, so that the Intellect itself is not overwhelmed <note>original: "turbetur," meaning disturbed or thrown into disorder</note>, and so that the light does not scatter. The infusion of this light excites the desire for eternity in every spiritual Substance, according to its ability to imitate it; however, the interruption of this flow is the cause of the cessation or corruption of the universe. Indeed, although light of this kind is fervent, great, and sublime, it is nevertheless not an equal imitation of the unity and the Word of its Creator, who exists as infinite.

## Chapter Two: How God is prior to other Beings, and what the order of Beings is.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'D' featuring floral and foliate scrollwork.</image-desc>
**God** is the **First Being**, but he is so by the priority of **Creation**. For while certain **Substances** are prior to others—such as the simple, the composite, the **Active Intellect**, and the **Soul**—they are not prior in terms of a temporal sequence <note>meaning they didn't necessarily appear earlier on a calendar</note>. Instead, as we have received this teaching, they hold a priority of **Essence** and nature: just as a general category (a genus) is naturally prior to the specific types (species) within it. Indeed, something can be prior to another without being so in time. The reason for this is: how could things that exist above time, and are themselves the cause of time, be considered "prior" in a temporal sense? It has already been proven that one thing is not called prior to another in time unless both are contained within the flow of time, and one existed at a moment before the other.

Therefore, the **Mind** <note>original: "Mens"</note> exists simply as the primary thing among the Essences. For this reason, it is called the "Prince," although it is the same as the **Word of God** <note>original: "verbum Dei"</note> and the underlying subject of the first form. Like a "highest genus," it contains all the illustrious, absolute, and pure substances. Following the Mind is the **Intellect** <note>original: "Intellectus"</note>, which is secondary in comparison to that Mind (functioning as if it were a specific type or "species" of it). This Intellect constitutes its own subject, for which it is also the appropriate form; and within this Intellect dwells a light from the **Intellectual root**, much like a ray from the sun reflected by a **Crystal**.

Furthermore, from that Intellect proceeds the Essence of the **Rational Soul** <note>original: "Anima rationalis"</note>, whose light is even more sparse, resembling the morning twilight. Because of this dimness, it is subject to forgetfulness and ignorance. This is why the soul requires learned instruction, a preserving memory, and the use of logic and reasoning to support and direct its Essence. Again, from the light of the **Rational Soul** arises the nature of the **Sensitive Soul** <note>original: "Anima sensitiva"; the faculty shared with animals that governs the five senses and physical perception</note> which...

### Chapter five: That there are three degrees of
### illumination of the Soul, and of what kind they are.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'C' featuring a bird, possibly a swan, amidst foliage and floral patterns.</image-desc>

### while the Soul is the image of the Intellect

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'C' featuring scrolling foliage and floral motifs.</image-desc> Since the simplicity and composition of **Substances** <term>Substances: In this philosophical context, these are independent beings or entities, ranging from purely spiritual ones to physical matter</term> exist as greater or lesser according to the ratio of their distance from, or proximity to, the **Divine Word** <note>original: "verbum divinum"</note>, it follows that every created thing is prior and truer in its absolute spiritual simplicity when it is closer to Him. Conversely, that which is more distant exists with less simplicity and a greater proximity to its deserved **Physicality** <note>original: "Corporalitatem"</note>. 

In the same way, the influence of light dwells in all things according to the capacity of each, following the prescribed degrees. Thus, that which is more capable is closer to the source, acting as the first recipient; it is the nearest because of the dignity of its **Essence** <term>Essence: The fundamental nature of a being; its "what-ness" as intended by the creator</term>. It stands as a medium between God and all other **Beings** <note>original: "Entia"</note> produced by Him, for it receives the influx of life from God himself. Once received, it then pours that life into another being existing below it (insofar as the first is more perfect). It does this because it exists before the lower being and is more perfect than it, and because it stands as the first imitation of God, through which the various levels of His creation are revealed. 

Thus, the Intellect also properly flows into the Soul, since the Soul is its created image, much like an expressed word. Furthermore, every operation of the Soul flows into other things, aided from above by the **Universal Intellect** <term>Universal Intellect: A cosmic, spiritual mind that serves as a bridge between the divine unity and the diversity of the material world</term>. This Intellect relates to the Soul just as fire relates to the heat that arises from it. This heat is received by one thing from another, produced by the Intellect, yet the Intellect does this without any loss or exhausting of its own power.

<margin>a</margin> The **Intellectual Soul** <term>Intellectual Soul: In this philosophical tradition, the highest part of the soul that connects human reason to divine truth.</term> existing in this **lesser world** <note>original: "minori mundo"; man viewed as a miniature version (microcosm) of the entire universe</note> understands through the process of thought. This is because its **Intellect**, being derived from the first source, falls short of that source and exists as "material"—that is, in a state of **potential** <note>original: "potentialis"; meaning the mind has the capacity to know all things but is not always actually thinking of them.</note>. And indeed, the Intellect perfects the **Rational Soul** when it produces it, just as a father produces a son. Such a Soul, in turn, perfects the **Sensual Soul** <term>Sensual Soul: The part of the soul responsible for physical senses, shared with animals.</term> because it produces it; yet, in a reciprocal way, the Rational Soul also needs the Sensual Soul. This happens when the rational soul is "awakened" by the senses to contemplate first principles. Without the senses, the rational soul would hardly be directed toward any of these principles, nor would it be shaped by the specific appearance of things. Consequently, it would not be fit to receive **universals** <term>Universals: General concepts or categories—like "Humanity" or "Beauty"—that apply to many individual things.</term> from the first **Active Intellect** <note>original: "Intellectu Agente primo"; the higher power that illuminates the human mind to allow for understanding.</note>.

That the rational soul is united to the **Sensitive Soul** is clear from this fact: otherwise, it would not respond to natural emotions and delights, nor would it seek victory or dominion. It would not require **educational discipline** <note>original: "disciplina Eruditoria"</note>, nor would it ever strive for glory. It would not be delighted by harmony or physical beauty, nor would it be inclined toward the natural state of humanity, nor would it conceive of the idea of rising higher or the joy of escape. It would by no means pursue the comforts of the body—such as health or freedom from pain—but would possess only rationality. 

Indeed, these operations belong to it because of its communion with the Sensitive Soul, which is nevertheless purer and more elevated than mere natural qualities—such as those things that can be seen, tasted, or touched, and the rest of the objects of the senses. If the soul were not united to these, it would never, while hungry, seek to be full, nor seek rest when laboring, nor health when sick, nor desire sexual union, and other similar things. Again, without the sensitive soul, the rational soul would undoubtedly be like **spiritual substances** <note>original: "Substantiis spiritalibus"; referring to purely spiritual beings like angels who do not possess bodies.</note>, which certainly do not know any of the aforementioned physical qualities. Indeed, it is a matter of experience that man feels and explores those sensory qualities, just as, conversely, the rational soul does not yet truly know the state of those spiritual substances or their **intellectual delights**.

### Chapter Eight: Concerning the Active Intellect—its nature and its relationship to the Possible Intellect.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial letter "I" featuring white foliate scrollwork on a dark cross-hatched background.</image-desc> The **Active Intellect** <term>Active Intellect: In this philosophy, a higher, constant power that acts like a light, allowing the human mind to "see" and understand abstract concepts.</term> flows into the **Rational Soul**. Indeed, its light exists as something expanded over the entire world; it directs other **Beings** and preserves all things that approach its **Essence** <note>original: "Essentiam"; the fundamental nature or "soul" of a thing.</note> through purity, whereas they recede from it through impurity. This is because the first Intellect, following the sovereign mind, flows into the world along with the **material Intellect** <note>original: "Intellectu materiali"; another term for the "possible intellect," describing the human mind as a blank slate or "material" ready to be shaped by thought.</note>, which is our very substance.

The Essence of that Active Intellect is superior to the nature of the **possible intellect** <term>Possible Intellect: The human capacity to learn; it is called "possible" because it has the potential to know all things but is not always currently thinking of them.</term>; and yet, the Active Intellect loves the possible or natural intellect as a teacher loves a student, or a father an only son, or as a male loves a female <note>The author uses these social and biological metaphors to describe the "active" principle (the giver) and the "passive" principle (the receiver) coming together.</note>. Because no other Being is fit to receive its perfect action except for the material Intellect, the first Intellect—to provide aid—inclines entirely toward it. It preserves the material intellect as its own special work, setting it above other substances. These other substances receive the influence of that active agent only individually and imperfectly, according to the purity or impurity of their own particular essence. 

The **Rational Soul**, however—which is the "second intellect" proceeding from the agent (that is, the possible intellect)—is not counted among those lesser substances. For this reason, the prior Intellect is united with it, and it preserves, governs, and illuminates the soul.

Indeed, because the aforementioned fruitful intellect lovingly embraces this sensual soul, it becomes **imaginative** and remains devoted to it.

For this reason, the sensitive soul of a human likewise desires to be joined to the **material intellect** <note>original: "intellectui materiali"; another term for the human mind when it acts as a blank slate or "receptacle" for knowledge.</note> and to be "clothed" by it. Therefore, the **possible intellect** and the **sensitive soul** of a man love one another (due to the mutual need of each) and are joined together in a **substantial union**. It is through this union that human existence is perfected and our specific rank in the universe is established. The **Active Intellect** and the **Rational Soul** relate to one another in this same way, desiring each other by a reason through which they are united and become almost a single substance.

These do not exist on their own but exist within matter. However, a certain species of this kind remains active in all "intellectual forms," much like rays of **Light**, which, while inherent in an illuminated body, persist in the soul of the agent. ### Chapter Twelve. That the entire universe is perfect, and consequently what the nature of its First Author is.

The entire universe contains all things, nor can anything higher add anything to it, since it is supremely perfect. Such a **being** <term>Being: In this philosophical context, "being" (ens) refers to anything that exists, whether physical or spiritual.</term> does not admit any addition in the first place. For any addition (if one were to be made to the whole universe) would be either a **natural being** <note>original: "Ens naturale"</note> or not. 

It cannot be a natural being, because the totality of the universe itself constitutes nature. How, then, can that which is already contained be added to the container? Likewise, since everything that falls under the possibility of nature also falls under the activity of some agent, and since nothing in the whole universe acts without the **First Author** <note>A common philosophical term for God as the primary cause of all things.</note> creating the **Active Intellect** <term>Active Intellect: The power of the mind that illuminates truths and allows us to understand abstract concepts.</term>, it follows that whatever is possible is capable of being brought into effect by God.

Therefore, such an addition is either necessary to the world, or it is not. If it were necessary, yet the world lacked it, that would be a defect. But a wise Agent does not produce a defective work. If, however, the addition is not necessary, then if it were added, it would be superfluous. One must not ascribe superfluous action nor deficient power to the **First Author**. 

Furthermore, such an addition is either a part of the world or it is not. If it exists as a part of the world, it is no longer "outside" the world. For the demonstration has already been established that nothing exists outside the world, because all things are contained within it. If that addition were outside the world, it would be either created or uncreated. If it exists as something created, it is already a part of the world. Consequently, it is not external. If, however, it were uncreated, it would follow by the same logic that the entire universe could exist without **Creation** <note>original: "Creatione"</note>. 

But if, returning to the first division, one were to say that this addition is a "non-natural" being, how could that happen? For a non-natural being is not possible, seeing as every other possible thing is a being [such as...]

<summary>This chapter presents a logical argument for the perfection and completeness of the universe, asserting that it requires no additions and reflects the perfect wisdom of its Creator.</summary>

Nothing in either world <note>Referring to the physical world and the spiritual/intellectual world.</note> exists without a **primary Author** <note>original: "Autore p̃mario"; referring to God as the First Cause.</note>, nor are the beings of the universe subject to anyone but Him, and to Him alone because of His dominion and preservation. Indeed, such a Word does not immediately form anything except the intellect, nor is the intellect formed except by the Word.

### Chapter sixteen: An epilogue of the foregoing.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial letter 'I' containing stylized foliage and branches within a square frame.</image-desc>
It has now been proven, therefore, that between the **true Author** and nature there are several intermediaries, of which the **Agent Intellect** <term>Intellectus Agens: In this philosophical system, the "active" or "agent" intellect is the highest part of the mind that acts as a bridge between divine truth and human thought.</term> is the first; the **rational soul** is the second; and the **sensual soul** <note>Also known as the sensitive soul, responsible for processing sensory information from the body.</note> is the third. 

Furthermore, the first intellect after the divine is joined to His **Word** <note>original: "verbo"; referring to the Logos or the divine expression of God’s mind.</note> by an unthinkable union, being closest to Him; thus, both are one. Yet, their union is not like the union of the **first agent intellect** and the **second potential intellect**; for although this second intellect is from that first Agent according to its substance, it is far lower in rank. 

Indeed, the rank of this second intellect is the first rank of **mobile being** <term>Mobile being: A philosophical term for anything that can change or move. Here, it refers to the human soul, which "moves" as it learns and thinks.</term>, depending on the first intellect. The rank of the first intellect is one of **rest** because of its absolute nature, for it does not need any external perfection—the very thing that makes the other [the soul] "mobile." That which is **immobile** <note>Referring to the Agent Intellect/Divine Word, which is perfect and unchanging.</note> entirely contains the mobile and all its parts; and that which contains is prior to that which is contained, and superior in dignity. It is self-sufficient in the simplicity of its substance, even through the multiplicity of the other. 

For there always exists something moving on the outside, and the soul, because of its lack, is mobile toward multiplicity. And while one mobile thing is moved and another is at rest, the **Word** (which is the **agent intellect**) exists as neither mobile nor resting, but is abstracted from both. 

It has also now been proven that among created things, the primary is the **first or agent intellect**, and the secondary is the **second intellect**, which is called the **rational soul**, placed by God (as previously mentioned) on the boundary of **both worlds** <note>The "boundary of both worlds" refers to the soul's position between the eternal, spiritual realm and the temporary, physical world.</note>. But if anyone should ask: who then was the Author who brought forth the first agent intellect? We answer: God.

### Chapter seventeen. That the expressed Word is properly the Cause [as] creator; but God is not properly the cause of the same.

<margin>u</margin> The **expressed Word** is called the **Cause of Causes**, and this was the opinion of the **wise men of Babylon** <note>This likely refers to the "Chaldean Oracles" or ancient Zoroastrian wisdom, which Renaissance philosophers believed anticipated Christian truths.</note>, since all Beings are produced by it. Even the intellect itself is made fruitful by it, and this is because of the union of this Word with the **first Author**, by whom the Word itself and all other existing things are truly procreated. Indeed, that is called a **Cause** which is an effector <note>An "effector" is the thing that actually carries out an action or produces a result.</note> with an expression similar to the existence of the thing Caused; therefore, if nothing else had been created, such a Word would not be called a cause. 

And for this reason, no other lower thing is so fittingly called a **Cause**, since nothing is produced with a similar expression without the aforementioned Word. And since nothing receives the expression of its own existence from itself (for though it exists, it does not proceed to the expression of its own existence by its own power), it is in no way fitting that anything should be named or be the cause of itself. Just as it is false that something which is **Prior** should become **Posterior** to itself, or that something surpassing a certain class should be surpassed by it. 

Furthermore, it happens that the **Agent Intellect**, which is such a Word, is called the **Cause**, because it is full of the **seeds** <term>Semina: Often called "seminal reasons" in this philosophy; the hidden blueprints or potential forms of all physical things held within the divine mind.</term> implanted from lower things; if it lacked these, it would not be fittingly named the Cause—indeed, its very existence would cease. For it does not happen that anything depends on one extreme while that extreme does not exist; otherwise, it would happen that there would be a **Cause** without a **thing Caused**, and vice versa, a thing Caused without a cause. If this were the case, all Beings would be disordered; if this were granted, the power of seeding and the mastery of a more absolute power would be taken away. Therefore, the **Agent** and the **Patient** <note>In philosophy, the "Agent" is the one doing the action, and the "Patient" is the one receiving it.</note> toward/

<summary>This page explores the role of the "Expressed Word" (Logos) as the intermediary "Cause of Causes" that bridges God and the physical world. It argues that while God is the ultimate Author, the Word is the functional cause that contains the "seeds" or blueprints for all created things.</summary>

However, we experience these things as unequal, both by reason of **action** and **passion** <note>In traditional philosophy, "action" refers to the power to cause change, while "passion" refers to the capacity to be changed or acted upon.</note> in certain cases, and by reason of a single or manifold **Medium** <term>Medium: The middle ground or intervening substance through which a cause exerts its influence on an effect.</term> in others—or even no medium at all in many cases, such as those Beings of abstract and perfect power. Therefore (as has been said), a **Cause** is named in relation to the **Effect**. <note>original: "Causatum"; literally the "caused thing."</note> 

If someone should say that while the Cause and the Effect agree in their correlation but differ in substance, how then is the cause joined to the effect? We respond that between the cause and the effect there is a certain conjunction through a kind of **radiation** <note>original: "radiationem"; here describing an invisible flow of influence or energy from a higher source to a lower one.</note> and a common proportion, without which it is impossible for one to be the cause of the other. 

Take, for example, a person being the father of a son. Although one of them exists before the other, there is nonetheless a certain conjunction between them. And even though "sonship" resides in the son and "fatherhood" in the father, this does not take away all communion <note>original: "communio"; a shared connection or commonality.</note> between them. As it is with these "Fathers" of correlation, so it is with the rest. 

In this way, this conjunction exists between the **Elements**—which are the cause of "mixed" or composite bodies—and the composites themselves, such as **Minerals**, **Plants**, and **Animals**. Furthermore, such a communion exists between an individual of one species and an individual of another, such that the alteration and transformation of one occurs because of the other. There is also a placement in a proper Region and an ascent, both by dignity and by the position of one above the other; for example, among the elements: **Water** is above **Earth**, **Air** is above **Water**, and **Fire** is above **Air**. Each of these, established in its own place, remains at rest. 

We see this also in animals, such as the **head** being above the **feet**, and in plants, such as the **branches** being above the **roots**. Furthermore, the animal is more sublime than the plant, and the plant more than the mineral; thus, there is a proportion between one and the other. If there were no such communion among the aforementioned things, it would be impossible for one of them to exist as the cause of another. 

In the same way, the **revolving heavens** <note>original: "caeli circumlati"; the celestial spheres that ancient and medieval science believed rotated around the Earth, driving all physical change below.</note> are the cause of the elements being altered, transformed, and acted upon. There is a manifold conjunction between them. They agree both in that they are mobile in space, and in that they are things with quantity and defined limits. And...

# BOOK

If there were no proportion <note>original: "proportio"; here meaning a relationship of compatibility or scale</note> between them, the **Elements** would not be acted upon by the **heavens**, which is nonetheless false; since nothing is generated from the elements except through the **Impression** <note>In medieval cosmology, an "impression" is the process by which celestial bodies exert influence or "stamp" their qualities onto the physical world.</note> from the heavens themselves and their movements. For the heavens are the **Cause** of natural forms, and these forms are the cause of **generable composites** <term>Generable composites: Physical objects in our world made of combined elements that are subject to creation and decay.</term>—between which there is such a communion.

Furthermore, **matter** and **form**—of which the motion of one is conceivable, while the other is at rest—are both the Cause of the **Composition of the heaven**, and between these and the heaven there is a very great communion. This is because the heaven is carried around, while the **form** carries it around; since there, matter and form are imperceptible, just as they are here.

Moreover, the **universal soul** <term>Universal Soul: A cosmic principle that animates the entire universe, distinct from individual human souls.</term> has a proportion to this kind of matter and form, being the Cause of both—and more stable than the **particular soul** <note>The "particular" soul refers to the individual soul of a single living being, like a person or animal.</note>—because the universal soul uses the description of spiritual light, while the particular soul uses corporal light, as it is immersed in matter.

Likewise, the Universal Soul is the cause of the **Motion of the spheres**, but the cause of the **rest of the Poles**; in the same way, the particular soul is the cause of the movement of the **organs**, but the cause of the rest of the **Powers**. <note>Just as the poles of the world remain stationary while the sky rotates, the core faculties or "powers" of the soul remain stable while the bodily organs move to perform actions.</note>

Again, **Matter** and **form** fall under Nature, insofar as matter cannot exist without a supporting form, nor likewise can form exist without a subject matter.

Furthermore, the **Agent Intellect** <term>Agent Intellect: A higher, universal mind that illuminates human understanding, allowing us to grasp universal truths.</term>, which is universal (as previously mentioned), is the cause of the universal soul and thus has a manifest communion with the soul. For indeed, whatever kinds of seeds are implanted in the Agent Intellect, such also exist in the rational soul; for the soul does not act unless its essence receives from the forms of the Agent Intellect.

Again, there is another communion between this Intellect and the aforementioned soul: that the Intellect is both something particular and something universal, and similarly the soul. And thus also the Intellect is one and the same as the **expressed word** from the Power of the **First Author** <note>original: "Autoris primi"; refers to God as the ultimate Creator and source of all things.</note>, whose will and precept of wisdom is the same as that which is begotten in the same degree of Essence. And the Agent Intellect is Created by the First Author through this kind of precept and will.

...completely indifferent to it. It is neither produced from matter nor from an external example <note>original: "exemplo Exteriore"; referring to a pre-existing blueprint or Platonic ideal outside of the creator</note>, as is the case with other created things. Therefore, we gather that there is always some kind of communion <note>original: "comunio"; a shared nature or relationship</note> between a **Cause** and its **effect**; otherwise, without this relationship, it would not happen that one becomes the cause of the other. For truly, since God does not have this kind of proportion to the **Creature**, it is impossible for Him to be strictly called its **Cause**. Yet, He is the **Author** and the **Producer** of the thing **emanating** <term>Emanating: The philosophical concept that all things "flow out" from a single divine source while the source remains unchanged.</term> from Him.

Nor is such a communion necessary between the agent and the act; for the condition of **passivity** <term>Passibility: The capacity to be acted upon, to change, or to be affected by external forces.</term> does not occur in the agent. But if any such thing occurs, it appears in the thing itself emanating from Him. Furthermore, a **Cause** imprints some quality similar to itself upon the **effect**. Something common is always found between the Cause and the effect, just as **heat**—the natural and essential quality of fire—is common to the air, water, and stone warmed by that same fire.

But it is impossible for the world to exist from the **First Author** as heat exists from fire. For heat is like the soul of the fire; however, the world is by no means related to its Author in this way. Thus, also, since the **soul** is described and expressed by the intellect closest to the **Divine Word** <note>original: "uerbo diuino"</note>—which is the **Author** of all created things—the description or quality of the caused soul proceeds from something similar in the **Agent Intellect** <term>Agent Intellect: In medieval philosophy, the active power of the mind (often seen as a universal force) that allows us to understand truths and gives form to the physical world.</term> which acts as the existing Cause.

Furthermore, if God were the cause of the **Creatures** themselves, His knowledge would be similar to their knowledge. This is false. For it is already known that God created beings without any other being or external pattern. Nor does any likeness of Him exist in any celestial or elementary thing. Again, therefore, the sublime God (as stated) is not truly the cause of a specific created thing, but the **Author of the Cause** itself, which is His work. For, as mentioned before, He lacks the necessary communion with the creatures themselves.

### BOOK

<margin>a</margin>
The Primary One <note>original: "Vnus primarius"; referring to God as the absolute Monad or source</note> established the **Word** <note>original: "uerbum"; here used in the philosophical sense of the *Logos*, the first manifestation of divine intellect</note>, which is the **First Created**, to be the **Cause of the Beings** proceeding from it. And yet, this [Word] is not truly "one" in the highest sense, because it does not enact the essence and existence of **Creatures**—an action that is beyond its power—nor does it undergo duality or numerical equality. Instead, it remains one and is truly abstracted from them. For it is not "one" by the foundational unity of number <note>original: "unitate principiaria numeri"; the mathematical '1' that begins a sequence</note>, even though number is also somewhat abstractable from essence, because this type of unity also exists necessarily in all corporeal particulars. To these particulars, the **Word** itself gave unity in two modes: to some it gave a unique unity, such as to the earth, the air, the sun, the moon, and other similar things. Each of these is a unique, singular individual, indivisible into many things of the same species; hence it is said that all earth is a single earth, and so on for the others.

To other things, however, it granted a **Multiplied** unity, and this also in two degrees: one degree exists in things like fire or stars, consisting of natural individuals—for example, minerals and animals; the other degree exists only as numbered particulars, where unity is called "first," "second," "third," or "fourth." These are abstractable from natural things, even though they are numbered.

Then one comes to spiritual things, which are **Multiplied** through a renewing and vivid creation, reaching as far as the **intellect** created by the divine Word. This intellect exists as "one" by a unity that contains implanted seeds <note>original: "unitate contentrice seminum insitorum"; referring to the *rationes seminales*, or the spiritual blueprints of all created things</note>; yet it is multiplied through those many abstractive and productive aspects of creatures.

But the true **Creator** is found to transcend numbers, being abstracted from the divisibility of **Creatures**, and is not **Multiplied** by implanted active or exemplary forms <note>original: "formas insitas activas : uel exemplares"; the internal patterns or external "blueprints" used by a craftsman</note>. Therefore, He is "one" with a unity that differs from Natural, numerical, or spiritual unity. Such a unity of His cannot be grasped except through abstraction and the negation of **Expressed** unity <term>Expressed unity: The way we normally understand 'one' as a count or a single object in the physical world.</term>. For he who thinks God himself is "one" simply because He is not two or three, is ignorant of such a primary **Author**. Indeed, such a person is merely imagining an **Expressed** number,

...named by the pre-numbering of its unity: from which (as has been said) it is abstracted. This, therefore, is the **Difference** <note>original: "Differentia"</note> between **numerical unity** <note>original: "unitatem numerariam"; the mathematical number one used for counting</note> and the true unity that is proportioned to the supreme creator.

If anyone should ask why the intellect is so singular and the master of other **Creatures**, we shall answer that its **Author** is a Being: one, true, simple, and containing all things—both the composed and the uncomposed. According to this principle—as the renewer of **Being** <note>original: "Entitatis"</note>—this same Author brings about the **Agent Intellect** <term>Agent Intellect (Intellectus agens): the active part of the mind that transforms sensory information into abstract thoughts</term> and everything within it, for individuals and for the multitude of all things.

Number is also not the principle of things, as some have mistakenly thought. For "one" is prior to "two," and two is where number begins. However, "one" does not exist as a number; rather, it measures number. Furthermore, since this is so (as stated before), the **Rational Soul** <note>original: "Anima Rationalis"</note> is also a number by way of imitation and likeness of the unity of the **Agent Intellect**. This is because the primary and celestial essences are not corporeal, nor are they subject to physical growth; instead, they exist as spiritual beings without any measurable boundary. Otherwise, they would be thick, solid, and possessed of surfaces—which is how the senses (albeit falsely) imagine them to exist.

Evidence of this exists in the **seminal reasons** <term>seminal reasons (rationes seminariæ): the invisible, spiritual "seeds" or blueprints that govern the growth and form of living things</term>, such as those of plants. These reside in moisture but do not exist in a visible or apparent way; they are hidden and invisible. How much more so, then, is the **Word** <note>original: "uerbum"</note>—which is the **Agent Intellect**—and its essential number invisible.

Furthermore, we are not currently speaking of "countable number," which is obvious and evident, but of "natural number." This is the **Essence** <note>original: "Essentia"</note> contained by another, such as the **dual unity** <note>original: "unitas duaria"; a philosophical concept where a single essence contains a duality of powers</note> of the **celestial world** <note>original: "Mundi superni"</note>. It dwells within the intellect and within absolute agent reason. It does not strictly imitate divine unity, but rather results in a certain number which exists as the form of the individual things created by the **Intellect**. This Intellect truly contains and preserves all **Beings** <note>original: "Entia"</note>, and was itself first formed by that **One** under the appearance of a lower Essence. And so, this duality is a unique Essence.

### Chapter nineteen. In what way God—since He is supremely one—creates many other beings, and in what way [He creates] things that are intelligible in their specific kinds.

<image-desc>A large decorative initial 'Q' containing detailed scrolling foliage and vine motifs within a rectangular border.</image-desc>

We must inquire concerning the **Agent Intellect** <term>Agent Intellect (intellectus agens): in medieval philosophy, the active power of the mind that allows us to understand abstract concepts</term>: by what reason it is understood by any being, and in what manner it was created by the **First Author** <note>original: "Autore primo"; referring to God as the primary cause</note>, as well as what the perpetual state of one who contemplates it might be. Furthermore, we must ask—since the mind is naturally inclined and desires most greatly to know this when nothing prevents it, and because it is a matter over which the wise have been troubled and have quarreled among themselves—namely, in what way Nature, being a single, absolute, and entirely non-plural **Being** <note>original: "Ens unum"</note>, could have created many other beings without departing from the unity of its **Essence** <note>original: "Essentia"</note>, and without any loss of that unity; indeed, even with the strengthening of it. For although all other things flow from the One, plurality does not for that reason exist within that One. Once we have stated what kind of thing this is, let us also demonstrate it through proof. To accomplish this to the best of our ability, we first implore help and assent from the First Author Himself—not with the mouth only, but with a suppliant gesture, and with a heart abundantly, incessantly, and wholly turned toward Him. We pray that He may illuminate our mind and remove the folly that grows over our souls because of the body. For in this way, we hope that we shall prove this kind of arrangement, which belongs to the one true and honorable Good; for He Himself sends forth light for those who seek Him truthfully and sincerely.

First, therefore (as is most eagerly explored), the One True Being created many beings in this manner: there first occurs to His contemplation a certain unique Being. He established this before all other things; this established being then returns to His Essence. It recognizes that such beings were fashioned as turbid copies <note>original: "turbida"; literally "cloudy" or "disordered," suggesting that created things are less pure than their divine source</note> that decline from that same source. Since this is so, every created thing is moved by a longing for the Being itself. Otherwise, in no way...

In Neo-Platonic thought, the soul is "doubled" when it splits its attention between the divine realm and the material world, losing its singular focus on the One.</note>, you will lose this kind of contemplation. Which [contemplation] nevertheless—if you have not meanwhile been defiled by bodily filth—you will receive back upon turning again toward the star of **Jupiter** <term>Jupiter (Iouem): the planet associated with the higher intellect and divine order.</term>. You will be rendered **adjacent** <note>original: "conterminus." Sharing a boundary or border.</note> in light just as before and almost **consubstantial** <term>consubstantial (consubstantialis): sharing the same essential nature or "substance."</term> with it; and likewise, you will be ignorant of all things except those by which you were disturbed during your separation. Otherwise, as a stranger to that Planet (since Jupiter will then shrink from you), you will never reach the supreme sphere. 

Wherefore it is necessary that all other men who intend to contemplate its supernal essences should conduct themselves toward the Lord of the Planets in this way (as has been said). Furthermore, greater effort must be given by everyone to contemplate the **super-celestial World** <term>super-celestial World (Mundum supercælestem): the realm beyond the physical stars and planets, identified with the realm of pure Ideas or the Divine Mind.</term> than the celestial one, since the knowledge of the former is more noble than that of the latter; which [celestial knowledge] is nonetheless a distinguished and **pre-illuminating** path to it, and without which, as a middle stage, no one can undoubtedly attain the supreme. Of the most beautiful Good, upon which no sight can be sufficiently fed, and with which the observer must be clearly one and of the same name; and he who, having entered the light of the **Intellect** <note>original: "Intellectus." In this context, it refers to the highest part of the soul capable of direct spiritual intuition.</note> through such a penetration, becomes like a shining lamp to that which it resembles.

If, then, the senses are ignorant of the aforementioned qualities, how much more so regarding intellectual substances, which are distant and very foreign to them? Therefore, the senses also do not acknowledge the **Intelligences** <term>Intelligences (Intelligentias): divine, non-corporeal beings or governing spirits that inhabit the celestial spheres.</term>. But if the Intellect were to deny these, it would deny itself. Otherwise, it would be a bodily substance. Also, if it happened to withdraw itself from Intellectual Reason, and considered intellectual essences as if they were bodily, it would never penetrate the supernal sphere and its minds. These, on the other hand, it transcends when, looking back at its own essence, it has gazed within perfectly.

## BOOK TWELVE.

### Chapter one. That the body of man is mortal, but the soul is not; and that the body of a living being is the instrument of the soul.

<image-desc>An ornamental woodcut initial 'I' decorated with intricate interlacing vine and scrollwork patterns within a square border.</image-desc>

**A**t present, we must consider whether both parts of man are corruptible <note>subject to decay and death</note>, or whether only one is corrupted while the other persists forever. We must investigate what this nature is, and to do so perfectly, we must search by means of natural reason. Man, therefore, is not something "simple" <note>in philosophy, a 'simple' thing is indivisible and pure, like a soul or an atom</note>, but rather consists of a soul and a body which exists as a joined **instrument of the soul** <note>original: "organum animae"</note>. The body is different in kind, and although it is most excellently united to the soul, it is not joined to it inseparably, nor is it consistently firm in itself. For the body itself is a composite <note>made of many parts</note> and not simple; and every composite thing is eventually resolved into those elements from which it is composed. 

Consequently, the body does not endure, as is also evident from experience. Indeed, we see bodies corrupted in various ways, sometimes by external forces and sometimes by one another—especially when the **noble soul** <note>original: "anima nobilis"</note> has left them. Conversely, if the body endures, it persists by the support of the sublime soul, and without it, the body neither stays together nor exists as a single unit. For the body is resolved back into the matter and form from which it was constituted once the soul that contained it departs. Likewise, the body is a "quantity" divisible into tiny parts, and this very divisibility is a form of corruption. Therefore, since the body is only one part of man and not both, only that portion is not incorruptible. Rather, one part will be corrupted—namely that which exists as the **instrument of the mind** <note>original: "instrumentum animi"</note>. The mind requires this instrument, though not forever, but only for a time. Otherwise, if the instrument were destroyed, the mind itself would be destroyed at the same time; which indeed...

[This corruption] does not occur when the mind still persists in its own state, firm and unconsumed, since its nature does not admit any decay whatsoever. The powers of the soul also require suitable instrumental members through which the soul itself flows. The proof of this is that the soul, with its various powers, follows the **complexion** <note>original: "complexionem"; referring to the "temperament" or the balance of physical humors in the body</note> of the body. Conversely, many operations happen to the body because of the soul using it as an instrument, such as sadness, fear, desire, joy, and sorrow. Therefore, this **mutual exchange of accidents** <note>original: "accidentium comerciū"; "accidents" are non-essential qualities or states like emotions or temporary conditions</note> and the reciprocal alteration of soul and body indicate that it is necessary for the body to be a fit servant to the ruling soul. 

This is further proven by the fact that if any animal dies (as happens), it never gives birth to another to which that same soul could be fitted. Thus, every animal always has its own specific soul, and conversely, every animal soul has its own specific body. For a prepared soul responds equally to a prepared body. Therefore, it is necessary for the physique of a **courageous man** <note>original: "animosi"</note> to be different from that of a **cowardly man** <note>original: "pusillanimis"</note>, just as the iron tool of a carpenter is different from that of a shoemaker. 

And so the **soul of a lion** <note>original: "anima leonis"</note>, being courageous, has wisely fitted for itself a physical body suited for the occasion—such as solid bone for strength and a toothed jaw for biting. The dog's soul has a lightly-footed body for speed; the horse's a hard-hoofed one for battle and ready for other actions. The soul of an ox also...

## Chapter Two. What the composition of the human body is like, and for what purpose.

<margin>c</margin>
Since the human soul is nobler and wiser than the rest, and therefore closer to the divine substance, it prepared for itself a body more noble than those of other animals, and better and more suited in its members for exercising the **arts** <note>In this context, "arts" refers to any skilled craft, technology, or specialized human activity, from carpentry to painting.</note>. Since the soul requires many different organs for the many tasks it performs, and could not fashion all of those together within a single joined body, it composed within the body one organ suitable for fabricating those many separate instruments: namely, the **Hands**. Indeed, if it had only a single organ fit for only a single use, it could not manufacture the other necessary tools. It also established an upright body, to which it added feet along with the hands, so that it might be able to imitate many other species of animals—almost countless in number—with varied gestures, and to represent many of their movements. If it retained only a single natural movement, it would be unable to do this. 

For indeed, all the works of the beasts are in some way suited to man: such as the **lordship of the lion** <note>original: "leonina Dominatio"</note>, for which he uses armor, a shield, a citadel, and even more instructively, the **Ballista** <term>Ballista: A heavy siege engine used in antiquity and the Middle Ages for hurling large stones or bolts.</term> and the **battering ram** to destroy walls and repel harmful things with missiles. Likewise, for battle, he uses the horse; but also speed like that of the hare, and natural precaution (like that of the sheep). And these actions, performed through instruments, are more powerful than the brute powers of animals. Likewise, by the power of the **Intellect** <note>original: "Intellectus"</note>, man performs certain exquisite directing works, beyond his natural thought (since the power of natural works is also present in beasts...

### Chapter Three. That the human soul has no innate skill, nor a connatural bodily form.

<margin>a</margin>
The Soul of the Beast (as previously mentioned) gave its animals both the necessary instruments for their actions and natural instincts useful for protection from harm, according to the condition of each. But the human soul bestowed neither of these upon man. It only established a versatile body in place of many fixed organs, and granted **teachability** <note>original: "docilitatem" — the capacity to be taught</note> instead of innate skill; it provided this in place of natural instinct. For if it were otherwise—namely, if the soul carried knowledge from nature with it—it would not seek this lowest world; for indeed, it would not need to learn through **abstraction from sensible forms** <note>The philosophical process of gaining universal knowledge by observing physical, "sensible" objects</note>, unless one were to answer that the soul indeed has its own natural knowledge, but since it is veiled, it cannot uncover it except through education, nor can it recover from forgetfulness unless...

...stirred by these lower things—which is surely not its nature. For it does not contain any bodily form of this kind, such as a protective covering; otherwise, it would not admit any other form. ## Chapter four. That the human soul does not need a bodily organ, and that it is simple, and for that reason incorruptible.

<margin>a</margin>
The Human Soul carries out some less-noble actions for which the body is undoubtedly necessary, such as oratory and the other arts, which it does not perform without the limbs that serve as their instruments. However, it carries out most actions through the power of **Thought**, such as deliberative and contemplative discourse—moving from visible things to those that are hidden. Other actions it performs through the more noble **Power of the Intellect**, according to its capacity and without the need for discourse. For both of these latter types of action, the soul has no need for a physical organ. Every form that does not require a bodily instrument to act is **incorruptible**, since it is **simple** <note>In philosophy, "simple" means not made of parts; since it has no parts, it cannot be broken apart or "dissolved"</note>. Such a thing is not **dissolved** into other things, but remains firm and indestructible.

The mind is simple because it is not composed of parts, since it is the receptacle of simple and purified forms. It reaches for these forms equally; it does not receive one more than another, nor one faster than another through consideration, just as a mirror receives images, or the air receives colors, sounds, smells, and other sensible forms. It does this indifferently and without disturbance, conveying them to the senses and preserving them according to the nature of each; and this operation belongs to the mind naturally and always. Furthermore, everything that is a receptacle for simple forms is **incorruptible** <note>original: "incorruptibile" — meaning it cannot decay, rot, or be broken down because it has no physical parts to separate</note>; and that which is simple and absolute remains the same unto itself. The mind, moreover, possesses both these qualities, and therefore it remains incorruptible.

### Chapter five. That the mind is immortal because of its infinite power for learning, and because it does not possess innate knowledge.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'R' featuring interlaced vine or floral motifs within a square border.</image-desc>

Now, everything that behaves in this way remains perpetually like itself—or rather, it becomes better, which is more accurate. If, by proceeding in this way, it increases its **power** <note>original: "potentiam" — refers to the soul's potentiality and its strength of will</note> and does not reach an end, it possesses an excellence that is uninterrupted and unceasing, containing a boundless force. Consequently, it is indissoluble and incorruptible, just as (conversely) that which is finite—like the body—is dissolved and corrupted. And as vision is the perfection of the eye, so **intellection** <note>original: "intellectio" — the active realization of the mind's potential when it understands a concept</note> is the perfection of the soul. As the eye is indifferent to all visible things, so the soul is toward all things that can be understood; and just as the eye would not actually see unless it had been fit for seeing, so also the soul would not actually understand unless it had been prepared beforehand for understanding.

## Chapter six. That the soul is absolutely simple, and for that reason immortal; and that it is simple in two ways.

The soul (as said before) is equally receptive to all forms by drawing them away from things perceived by the senses; for this reason, it does not have any such form within its own substance, but only the receptivity for them. And this is its first and proper form. Indeed, the soul itself—insofar as it is a soul—is defined by this receptivity. 

As has been often said, if any other single form were already present in the soul, it would not receive all the others so indiscriminately. For that existing form would resist the others as if they were weaker, being "foreign" to its nature. Furthermore, since the soul lacks a specific, fixed form of its own, it is therefore **simple** <note>original: "simplex" — in a philosophical sense, this means the soul is a single, unified thing that cannot be broken down into smaller physical parts</note> in itself. Since every composite thing has a certain proper form of its own, and the soul (as stated) does not contain one, it is therefore uncomposed, and consequently simple and absolute. One of these arises from communion with the body, but the other two require very little assistance from the **instrumental support** of the body. These two are: drawing conclusions from fitted principles, and moving oneself from one known thing to the knowledge of another. This pertains to the dignity of the soul and constitutes its own **proper operation** <note>original: "operatio propria" — the specific function that defines a thing's nature</note>.

### Chapter Ten: That the Soul is not corporeal. By reason of intellection.

[IMAGE: A decorative woodcut drop cap 'R' featuring floral motifs and scrolling vines.]

Again, there exists one reason at present why the **rational soul** <note>original: "Anima rationalis"</note> is not corporeal. For clearly, if it were so, when it understood, it would understand either through a few of its parts, or several, or all. And if indeed the soul understands through a few or several parts, the remaining parts, being ignorant, would cease to function. But if it is said that the soul understands through all its parts, and not in the other ways mentioned above, it is still necessary that each part understands what the others do; wherefore it follows that a single soul would understand a single thing multiple times, unto infinity, which is false.

Likewise, how could the soul require all its parts to understand? For if a body knows, it knows only through **contact** <term>contactus: the physical touching between the sensor and the thing sensed</term>; therefore, only the outermost part of the soul touching the object would understand, and thus all the remaining parts would not understand in any way since they do not touch it. If it is said again that the soul is a **perfection** <note>original: "perfectio" — here meaning the "form" or "actualization" of a body</note> which knows through many of its parts, we respond that this is false, because when we know a single thing, we do not know it through many parts.

For indeed, various powers of consideration know things that are different in essence—such as **touch** and **sight** <note>original: "tactus & uisus"</note>—where the object of one is different from the object of the other. And touch indeed knows many things falling within its scope, and sight likewise comprehends diverse things under its own single mode of sensing. Furthermore, if the soul understands by the contact of certain parts, if it touches a smaller part of a body, it will not understand it, since the soul itself is larger; and if it touches a larger part, it will also not understand it...

### Chapter Eleven: That the Rational Soul is not simply a Body, nor even the most subtle one.

If anyone should still stubbornly assert that the **mind** <term>animus: often used in this period to refer to the seat of the intellect or the "spirit" of the soul</term> or the **rational soul** <note>original: "animam rationalem"</note> is subject to **corruption** <term>corruptionem: the process of decay, change, or falling apart into constituent elements</term> because it is the thinnest body of all, it must be considered and properly investigated. ### Chapter Twelve. In what way all simple and mixed bodies are animated.

### Chapter Thirteen. That the Soul is not a body, because every such thing is composed of matter and form, but that it is its form. And concerning other reasons.

Finally, the soul is not a body, as it seemed to some based on their discourse. If our adversaries were to object that we only experience that "like knows like" <note>original: "simile cognoscit aliud simile"; a common ancient philosophical principle suggesting that the perceiver must share the nature of the thing perceived</note>, and since the Soul contemplates bodies, it must therefore follow that it is a body—at least a **subtle** <note>that is, refined or ethereal</note> one, unmixed even if composite—we respond that this reasoning is worthless. This is because all knowledge is produced by some **agent** <note>a "doing" force or cause</note>. Every sensation and piece of learning is a kind of **passive experience** <term>passio: in this philosophical context, it refers to the state of being acted upon or receiving an impression from an external source</term>. Furthermore, like is not acted upon by like. For one whiteness is not acted upon by another, but rather by its opposite, such as blackness or another color. Likewise, in the act of sensing, the sense does not become identical to the thing it senses; otherwise, the eye would actually turn white when seeing whiteness. Thus, the one who senses, and likewise the one who knows, is not acted upon by something identical to themselves, but rather they receive **perfection** <note>attainment of a fuller state or "completing" of the potential to know</note> from the things themselves. Therefore, it is not necessary for the soul to be a body simply because it knows bodies.

Furthermore, regarding the reason mentioned earlier—that since the Soul is formed by the mixing of indivisible bodies, it seems to be a body as well—we respond that this does not follow. The Soul is not made from those mixed bodies as if they were its parts, nor is it made by the mixing itself as if the mixing were the agent of its creation. Rather, it is only made *in* the mixing—that is, at the moment of the mixing—proceeding from an **external Author** <note>referring to God as the creator of the soul</note>.

Moreover, it is an error to assert that the soul is a body, because it would then follow that the soul (which is so noble) would be far less noble than it is. This is because an essential quality is **form** <term>Forma: the defining principle or essence that gives a thing its specific nature</term>, while a body is, in a sense, **matter** <term>Materia: the physical substance that has the potential to receive a form</term>. A form of this kind is certainly more noble than such matter. Matter is capable of growth, diminution, dissolution, and change; it is even capable of being altered. However, the **substantial form** <term>Forma substantialis: the core identity of a thing that remains constant through its existence</term> remains the same in its own state, unvaried and unchanged, from the beginning of its appearance in matter until the end.

Additionally, if one were to insist on the reasoning already mentioned—that the soul is a body because it knows bodies—we respond by turning the argument back on them: if this were the case, and the soul only knew things by virtue of its "bodiliness," then the Soul would *only* know bodies. It would therefore be ignorant of many other things, not...

Moreover, this is so because the soul understands many incorporeal things; and it was already proven earlier that it knows bodies through a means other than corporeality. Likewise, if the Soul were a body composed of other bodies, by what other active nature was it so composed? For it is undoubtedly impossible for something to be the **efficient cause** <note>the "maker" or agent that brings an effect into being</note> of itself; otherwise, it would exist both before and after itself. Furthermore, the cause that creates a body must be distinct from the body itself, just as the first cause is the most noble of all. There is nothing in this world more noble than the Soul; therefore, the Soul is that which acts upon bodies, from which it is concluded that the Soul itself is not a body.

### Chapter Fourteen: That the Soul is neither the shape nor the composition of the body.

Furthermore, since it has been said by some that the Soul is the **shape** <note>original: *figura*</note> of the body, it would follow that multiple souls would be formed in a single living being, given that many limbs are present within it. Each of these limbs possesses its own specific shape, differing from the shape of the others. And if it is asserted by others that the Soul is a **composition** <term>complexio: in medieval philosophy and medicine, this refers to the specific "temperament" or mixture of qualities and humors that make up a body part</term>, it would likewise follow that many souls exist in one living being. This, however, is false, because each individual limb is likewise allotted its own peculiar composition, distinct from the composition of any other. If, in order to avoid this conclusion, it is argued instead that the Soul is indeed a composition—not of the members individually, but of the whole body—the result is that when the body itself fails, the Soul must also fail. This would return us to error and ignorance; on the contrary, we experience the opposite result: namely, that while the body slides into decay, the **Mind** <note>original: *Animus*; while *Anima* usually refers to the life-force, *Animus* here refers to the rational or intellectual spirit</note> remains a survivor, unharmed. Indeed, even as the body is worn down and weakened, the Mind is often strengthened. Therefore, we observe that the Minds of the elderly and the decrepit are often more clear-sighted and active, even when their bodies are evidently weaker.

### Chapter Fifteen. That the soul is not an image expressed by matter, and that it is not a body.

Perhaps some will propose that the Soul is a **likeness** <note>original: *simulachrum*; here meaning a representation or image</note> expressed by matter. Should this be suggested, we say it is false, because matter certainly cannot form the essence of the Soul, nor can the Soul in any way flow out from the essence of matter. Without a doubt, whoever posits that matter emits the substance of the soul—which it previously contained within itself—also establishes that all bodies are naturally animated. This, however, is contrary to the very nature of corporeality and matter, for it is impossible for matter not to be a receptive potential for another **perfection** <term>perfection: in medieval philosophy, the "act" or "form" that completes a thing's existence, bringing it from potential to reality</term>; and such perfection is nothing other than **form**. This form exists as the light or the "act" of the power of a composite thing as it is moved from one state of composition to another.

Likewise, the Soul is not a body, because it is impossible for a body—whether simple or mixed—to be stable. Indeed, every such thing is by nature dissolvable and able to be returned to the matter from which all composite bodies are made, insofar as they are bodies. Just as all bodies would perish and be reduced to nothing if they were inanimate, so too if the soul were some kind of body—as some have thought—all Souls would likewise fail and decay.

Furthermore, the Soul does not always obey the nature of the body and matter; on the contrary, it opposes and resists them. This is apparent because the Soul, when one body fails, generates another by converting one form back into matter; otherwise, the successive generation of things would cease. Therefore, the Soul is neither a body nor a likeness of the body's matter.

Moreover, since the entire world is posited to be a single animated body, if the Soul were also considered to be corporeal, the world itself would be "animated" in name only; in reality, the Soul would be removed from it. For if it were so, since every body is resolvable and for that reason corruptible, the Soul...

### Chapter sixteen. That the Soul is not a body, neither subtle nor dense, and universally belongs to no such genus.

...bodies <note>The Latin text begins with the fragment "-pora," completing "corpora" (bodies) from the previous page.</note> among us remain firm and alive so long as the **Soul** is within them; 
but when the soul departs from them, they die and are corrupted. Thus, the entire corporeal world, insofar as it persists, does so because the **Soul** is always in it and always remains constant.

Even those who argue for the corporeality of the **Soul** are witnesses to this; later thinkers, compelled by the truth and driven by the facts themselves—though later perverting the truth—asserted that the **Soul** is a fiery spirit <note>original: *spiritum igneum*</note>. 
Indeed, they applied this descriptive reasoning to the **Soul** because they perceived that it is not fitting for a noble power (such as the **Soul**) to be inferior to fire. 
They also conjectured that it is impossible for the **Soul** to exist without a certain receptacle <note>original: *conceptaculo*; a vessel or housing</note> in which it may reside. 
Wherefore, from these suppositions, they gathered that the **Soul** is a fiery spirit or, most especially, an airy breath, since such a body is the most subtle and fertile of all. 

After this, it was necessary for these theorists, following their first confession, to say that while a body is indeed preserved by the receptacle or container <note>original: *contentorium*</note> in which it resides, the **Soul** is in fact such a container for the body—and not, conversely, that the body is the container for the **Soul**. 
It is through the **Soul** that the body exists, since the soul is the cause of the body. 
The cause, by its own very Essence <note>original: *Essentia*</note>, is sufficient unto itself and does not need the "effect" <note>original: *causato*; the thing produced by the cause</note> in order to exist; rather, the effect truly needs the cause in order to exist and to persist.

...if they could show that it is adjacent to some known body; having tried to defend what they had previously asserted, and proceeding further, they posited that the **Soul** is indeed a body, but one different from those that are manifest <note>Visible or obvious to the senses</note>. They called it a highly active type of body, naming it "spirit" <note>original: *spiritum*; in this context, it refers to a subtle physical vapor or breath rather than a non-material ghost</note>. However, they erred, because spirit is distinct from the **Soul**, since we say that all other spirits (of which there are many) are not **Souls**. 

But if they respond that the **Soul** is a spirit by the power of another soul, we ask what this power might be: namely, is it some kind of body, or is it a quality in a body? If the first is granted, it follows that the **Soul** is not the spirit which possesses such power, according to the arguments previously devised. If the second is posited (since a "quality" is a predicate <note>A characteristic attributed to a subject</note>), then that quality is not matter, since every predicate exists within a bodily subject. Therefore, the **Soul** exists as a nature other than a corporeal <note>physical or bodily</note> one. 

To confirm this, we further assert that it would be impossible for the **Soul** to be a body of any kind, whether it is called "thick" or "thin." We prove this in another way: since every body is either hot or cold, moist or dry, rare or dense, black or white, or something in between; and if a body is hot, it only heats; if it is cold, it only cools. If it is light, it makes things light; if heavy, it makes them heavy; if it is black, it blackens; and if white, it whitens. For it is not the nature of a cold thing to heat, nor a hot thing to cool. Thus, every body, insofar as it is a body, performs only one type of work. On the other hand, we experience that the **Soul** performs various operations. Therefore, from this we learn that the essence <note>original: *essentia*; the fundamental nature</note> of the soul is different from corporeal substance <note>original: *substantia corporea*; physical matter</note>. Because of this, no one can deny that truth.

<margin>¶</margin> Since the **Soul** in this lowest world is distinguished by certain virtues, the intellectual world <note>The realm of pure thought and divine forms, above the physical world</note> also does not lack such things; for example, **Rectitude** and **Justice**. Indeed, as often as one pleases, these kinds of virtues are sought; therefore, it is not at all ambiguous that they must exist in some other substance. Otherwise, why would the **Soul** choose an impossible thing? Why would it seek what can never be found, or desire what is possessed <note>original: *habitam*; suggesting the soul desires virtues because it recognizes they are held by higher beings</note>? 

Since these virtues exist in others, they certainly exist in the **Active Intellect** <note>original: *Intellectui agenti*; in medieval philosophy, this is the "engine" of thought that radiates knowledge into the human mind</note>, which is more sublime and noble. It is this Intellect that sends these virtues into the soul when the soul contemplates it. However, the Intellect suspends this flow when the soul is turned away and directed toward the senses; hence the soul remains in a base and humble state. Furthermore, that **Intellect** always preserves these distinctions <note>original: *insignia*; literally 'insignia' or 'marks of honor'</note>, because it never departs from the vision of the **First Author** <note>God, the ultimate source of all existence</note>, nor does anything interrupt it, since it is closest to His word. 

Nor indeed do these kinds of virtues merely exist in that Intellect; rather, they exist with the highest rectitude, for they suffer no defect, since they proceed immediately from the **Prince-Author** Himself. When the **Active Intellect** receives them, it then expresses them according to the manner in which they were infused. In the primary essence <note>The nature of God</note>, however, these virtues are of an even more exalted kind, because that essence is their creator. Nor do they exist in Him as if in an instrument, but as in their **Author**; nor do they exist as if in something else—indeed, they are not even said to "be in" Him, except because they flow from Him as effects, and this happens unceasingly.

and unceasingly; and for this reason, He is properly called **Super-essence** <note>original: *superessentia*; a term for a reality that exists beyond the standard definitions of "being" or "essence"</note>. It is also present in individual beings, shaped according to the capacity of each species. Their essences are assigned according to their fitting condition; for the **Active Intellect** <note>The "engine" of thought in medieval philosophy that radiates knowledge into the human mind</note> received a more noble essence than the **Rational Soul**, and the soul more than the heavens, and the heavens more than changeable bodies. This is because the more distant a produced thing is from the source—and the more intermediate steps it passes through—the more lowly the received essence will be. For the **Primary Author** <note>God, the ultimate source of all existence</note> indeed exists unmoved in His essence; He is not strictly "perpetual" <note>existing forever within time</note>, nor temporary, nor located in space. Rather, perpetuity, time, and place exist and persist because of Him. 

And just as the center of a circle exists in itself, while the lines drawn from it to the circumference—and the circumference itself with its points—exist within that center, so also all essences, both intellectual and sensible, are established and consist in the **First Agent**. Upon Him they depend, to Him they return, and Him they desire. And we return to Him like lines moving from the circumference back to the center. 

And if anyone should ask: "In what way do essences remain in the First Author?" (given that form remains in matter, and matter in form, and an **accident** <note>term: *accidens*; a philosophical property that is not essential to a thing's nature, such as its color or weight</note> in a substance), we answer that "remaining in another" happens in two ways. One way is how a form remains in matter, an accident in a subject, or a subject in its natural form. But another way is remaining in something else as in an **agent** <note>The cause or performer of an action</note>; for example, light remains in the thing that shines, and a ray in the thing that radiates. In this way, the rest of the simple essences remain in their efficient cause. Therefore, the **Active Intellect** remains in the **Primary Author**, and in this same Author, the **Rational Soul** remains through the mediation of that Intellect. However, the **Sensitive Soul** <note>The part of the soul responsible for sensation and movement, shared with animals</note> of man remains first in the body; and second, also in the **Active Intellect**, though by means of the **Possible Intellect** <note>The human capacity to receive and store knowledge</note>. Likewise, the **Rational Soul** has authority <note>original: *ius*; literally 'law' or 'right'</note> over the **Vegetative Soul** <note>The basic level of the soul responsible for growth and nutrition</note>, just as it does over other natures.

If anyone should ask what our final state will be? Since (as was recently stated) we human beings are—according to the **Soul** <note>original: *Animum*; the rational spirit or life-force</note>—derived from the **First Essence** of the Author of all things; yet the noble powers of that soul would not exist for us if we were turned away from that same First Author, and from the **Active Intellect** <note>The "engine" of thought that illuminates the mind</note> and the **Potential Intellect** <note>original: *intellectu possibili*; the capacity of the human mind to receive knowledge and forms</note>. 

Indeed, there are many people who, always lacking these virtues, are ignorant of them and deny them when they hear of them, thinking them to be fabricated vanities and fictions. We respond that our ignorance of ourselves and of other things arises from the fact that we are led to learn only by **sense-perception** <note>original: *sensu*; information gathered through the physical senses like sight or touch</note>. 

Hence, when exploring for the sake of knowing, we say: "We experience this thing; but that thing, we do not." We do not set aside our own thought, but rather we gather our learning from it; yet, thinking we have experienced everything, we assert that nothing exists which does not fall under the senses. Therefore, compelled by this narrow view, we do not acknowledge the **Potential Intellect**, nor the **Active Intellect**, nor the **First Author**, nor other similar essences. 

And if a person seeks out some persuasive habit of mind regarding such matters, it is mistakenly thought to be true science—even if it is false—for such a person joins these higher things to the physical senses and asserts that the soul, the Active Intellect, and the First Author are **corporeal** <note>original: *corporeos*; having a physical body or material substance</note>. 

In truth, the virtues are preserved by the soul, the soul by the Active Intellect, and the intellect by the **Primary Productive Essence** <note>God, as the ultimate cause of all effects</note>. And certainly, the Soul is not a **Body**, but the cause of the body; likewise, the Active Intellect and the Sovereign Essence are not bodies. Already the ancients harmoniously proved, by appropriate reasoning, that the Soul and its noble powers are not bodies, since they do not fall under the senses. For in what way could they be bodies? And we, leaning toward sense-perception, do not perceive the Soul or its virtues through it; for indeed we, sometimes turned away from sense and turned toward...
