## Chapter One: What kind of Being the Active Intellect is, and in 
## what manner it creates many beings, though it is one unchanging Being.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'E' featuring white interlaced strapwork and foliage against a dark, textured background within a square frame.</image-desc>
The One Absolute Being is the cause of all other created things; it neither exists within any of them, nor is it anything like them. However, it is the cause of all other created Beings insofar as they are Beings, since all such things proceed from it. Thus, the essences of things of this kind exist more firmly within it, and to it they return. It also exists as an absolute essence, as the true cause of causes and the **foremost creature** <note>original: *creatura princeps*; in this philosophical system, the first thing brought into existence by God, often identified with the First Intelligence or Active Intellect</note>. But if anyone asks in what way it happens that other creatures, many and various, are made by this one simple, unchanging, and non-multiplied Being? We respond that it is because such a One Absolute Being truly contains all other creatures; since it was created by the **Author** <note>original: *Autor*; referring to God as the ultimate Creator</note> without any other created thing existing before it. Therefore, it is also closest to Him; for which reason it gazes upon the primary Author Himself and, consequently, possesses an action also closest to Him. And thus, from this One Absolute Being, all other creatures have **emanated** <note>original: *emanarunt*; literally "flowed out," a term used to describe how creation results from the divine source like light from a sun or water from a spring</note> insofar as they do not exist as equally absolute essences. I say again briefly that such many things are not made by it except according to how it knows all those things encountered in contemplation; wherefore they emanated from it as things previously **ordained** <note>original: *fata*; things spoken or destined</note> within it. Therefore, the Author is the Primary Being. He, who is the **Word** <note>original: *verbum*; the divine logos or creative speech</note>, created the **Mind** <note>original: *mens*; here synonymous with the higher intellect</note> or the immediate **Active Intellect** <note>original: *intellectus agens*; the power that illuminates the human mind to allow for understanding</note>; from this Mind afterwards flowed all other creatures of the world, both of the higher and lower realms.

### Chapter Two. Why the Active Intellect is perfect and unequal to God; likewise why God is supremely perfect: and in what manner the ordered production of things occurs.

The One Absolute Being exists as perfect and pure, whereas the sensible world is imperfect and impure, having been produced by it. However, the **Active Intellect** <term>Active Intellect: In medieval and Neoplatonic philosophy, the first and highest intelligence created by God, which acts as the source of light and form for all other things</term>—which is that very One Absolute Being—was perfect and pure, because it was created as a unique being by the one true Being, who is supreme in perfection. Indeed, this [Supreme Being] does not require anything else, nor does He receive anything from any other. Rather, on account of His highest perfection and self-sufficiency, and the power and majesty of His unity, another thing was newly created by Him. Although this supremely perfect Being, as the primary source, creates this other perfect thing—namely, the Active Intellect—it is nevertheless impossible for a created, secondary Being to be equal to that primary one. 

For that which is created always falls short, and in no way exists on an equal level with its **Author** <note>original: *Autor*; referring to God</note>. It is, nonetheless, perfect within its own degree, bringing to perfection the next thing that follows. This is because the one true Being, who is supremely perfect, looked upon His own self while creating it, having before His own contemplation His true essence, which is most full of the light of wisdom. 

The Active Intellect, however, in the act of creating, gazes upon the Word of the Author closest to it; the **Universal Soul** <term>Universal Soul: The *Anima Mundi* or "World Soul," the spiritual principle that gives life and form to the physical universe</term>, as the fashioner and mother of all forms, contemplates the Active Intellect while it acts; and Nature, the producer of individual forms in matter, looks down upon the Universal Soul. For the one true Being first created the Active Intellect as the essence closest to His own Word; and this Intellect is the first being to receive [influence] immediately from the primary Agent. Thereafter, it produces nothing without first gazing upon its one Author, by whom it is also determined as one

He is understood to be one not only because He is not counted by any species of number, but because nothing foreign is added to His very **essence** <note>original: *essentiæ*</note>. He exists as one abstracted from all **Plurality** and numerical multiplication, in whatever way such things might happen to a created thing.

### Chapter six. The nature of the hierarchy of creation.

<margin>a</margin>
One primary Author <note>original: *Autor* (transcribed as *Vtor*); referring to God as the First Cause.</note> created one Being: and He decreed that it should preserve substances lacking forms among us; wherefore we are unable to apprehend their essences. Then, through that Being, He created the first forms, which possess essences without matter/which the thinking faculty cannot recognize by any example/stripped of matter. Afterwards, He further procreated substances naturally adorned, down to the final thing capable of being generated.

The **Intellect**, therefore (after the Author), is the First principle of every other created being, and existing everywhere, it preserves all those things. And the **Universal Soul** <term>Universal Soul: In Neoplatonic thought, the *Anima Mundi* or world-soul that connects the spiritual realm of ideas to the physical world.</term> is the principle of every spiritual and corporeal form, existing itself also as a form stripped of matter, and being sufficient in itself—on account of the influence it receives—to contemplate all things. Its work (which is nature) appears formed in natural matter.

Finally, there exist **crafts** <note>original: *artificia*; products of human skill or art.</note> similar to natural formations, insofar as they are composed of them. For if a craftsman is to make something, he requires formed matter from which to make it. For in what way could he suspend the shape of art in matter without form? Or form without matter? This is indeed impossible; for example, a potter about to shape a jar or some other earthen vessel, first considers and mixes the earth/and desiring the work/then shapes the jar itself according to his ability. Afterwards, he also fires it to harden it; nor is it doubted that the clay is the matter of the jar. Thus it is with air and fire; and so art behaves in this way.

The **Universal Soul**, however, has obtained the power of creating form in matter that is naturally simple and formless. For it does not happen that it creates forms except in this kind of pre-created simple matter. The **Agent Intellect** <term>Agent Intellect: The "active" part of the mind that makes potential knowledge actual; here described as a bridge between the Creator and the Soul.</term>, likewise, since it is the work most proximate to the primary Author/by contemplating Him/has the perfect power of renewing the universal soul. <margin>a</margin> Every soul made natural and sensible things at the same time and bounded them; it established for them their own proper grades <note>original: *gradus*; refers to the specific level or "rank" an object holds in the hierarchy of existence.</note> according to right reason. Otherwise, the Soul would not be anywhere at all. If that were granted, then it would be above and below and everywhere without any division; yet it is not spread out like a universal Being, otherwise it would occupy all places at once. [Man] stands on the border of both worlds, as a substance almost halfway <note>original: *substantia fere media*; the idea that the human soul is the "horizon" or bridge between the material and the spiritual.</note> between the sensible <note>things perceived by the senses</note> and the intellectual. One thing is also beneficial to know: that all natural things are somewhat dependent on one another, ordered in a sequence. When a later <note>or lower-order</note> thing is corrupted, it returns to the nearest preceding thing, until it reaches the Heavens; then it returns to the **Universal Soul**; and then to the **Agent Intellect**, through which all other Creatures exist. This Intellect itself exists in the **Principal Author**, who is the **creative Word** <note>original: *uerbum creans*; echoing the concept of the Logos in the Gospel of John.</note>, to which all things finally return, as we have many times repeated; for by Him they were created and in Him they persist.

### BOOK [THIRTEEN]

<image-desc>A large decorative drop cap 'O' featuring a complex interlaced knot pattern within a square frame. The knot is composed of several looping bands forming a symmetrical, circular design.</image-desc>

**ALL** other created Beings (as we have said before) exist within the **First Intellect** <term>First Intellect: In this philosophical system, the first and highest mind created by God, containing the blueprints for all existence.</term>, which the **Sovereign Author** <note>original: *Autor princeps*; referring to God as the ultimate creator.</note> made and established as their origin and as the source of all various substances. This same First Author planted the "reasons of forms" <note>the underlying logical patterns or "blueprints" for all physical shapes and types of things</note> into the **Universal Soul** <term>Universal Soul: Also known as the *Anima Mundi*, the spirit that animates the entire universe.</term>. He produced these forms and the Intellect in a state of perfection according to their rank—not through a gradual passage of time, but in a single, completed moment of action.

The **Agent Intellect** <note>the "Active Mind" that illuminates human understanding</note> and the **Universal Soul** were never "in potentiality" <note>original: *in potentia*; a state of "could be" or "not yet finished."</note> before they were "in act" <note>original: *in actu*; fully realized and functioning.</note>. This is because God perfected those **Absolute Essences** so they could serve as the causes for all remaining creatures. It is false and impossible to say that the **Agent Intellect** ever existed in a state of mere potentiality, for this reason: it contains "non-Being" no less than "Being," since it is the substance that brings both into effect.

<note>The author is using a technical Aristotelian argument here: if "Being" is defined as matter that has been given a specific form, and "non-Being" is defined as formless, raw matter, then the Intellect must be something else entirely. It cannot be made of matter or form because it is the thing that *creates* and *understands* them.</note>

For if "Being" is defined as material form—that is, a thing composed of matter and form—and "non-Being" is defined as formless matter, there is no middle ground between these three. The Intellect is none of these things. If it were "Being" in that material sense, it would follow that some other "Being" existed before the Intellect, and the Intellect would not be a single, absolute thing.

On the other hand, if we said the Intellect was "non-Being" (raw matter), it would not be capable of thinking; it would instead be something that is *thought about* <note>original: *intelligibilis*; an object of thought rather than a thinking subject.</note>. An object of thought is not the same as the Intellect itself, though the Intellect grasps it when it is stripped of its physical traits. Therefore, since it has been proven that the Intellect is the principle of all Beings, it is impossible for it to be a material thing or a "potential" thing. Rather, it stands apart from all such categories.

Thus, in the sequence of created things, the **Universal Soul** follows the **Agent Intellect**. The Soul, through its own desire, ascends toward the Intellect to receive its own perfection—which is the **influx of light** <note>original: *influxum lumi[nis]*; the spiritual energy or knowledge that flows down from the higher mind to the soul.</note>.

...from the Intellect. Nevertheless, you should know that the Soul does not approach the Intellect through the reception of its influence in such a way that it merely imitates or looks at it from a distance. Nor is the Soul simply extended into the contemplation of the **Agent Intellect** <term>Agent Intellect: In medieval philosophy, the "Active Mind" that illuminates the human soul, allowing it to understand abstract truths.</term>; rather, it is united with it and greatly sublimated.

Because of this union, the Soul does not lack the necessary light from the Intellect. Indeed, by reaching the Intellect in this way, the Soul attains its own perfection, rest, and stability. **Plato** provided an example of this, saying that the Intellect is like the indivisible center-point of a circle which contains all its angles and sides, such that all lines originate from that point and exist within it. The circle itself represents something that surrounds and contains the forms placed within it.

### Chapter Two. That the Intellectual Man exists together with all perfections from the First Author.

<margin>a</margin>
The **First Author** <note>original: *Autor primus*; referring to the ultimate Creator or "The One."</note> created the **Intellectual Man** <term>Intellectual Man: The "Ideal Man" or the perfect, non-physical blueprint of humanity that exists in the mind of God.</term> with all fitting properties simultaneously in a single moment. He did not create one property before the other, nor did he create them through a sequence of time, as is the case with the **Sensible Man** <note>the physical human being perceived by the senses, who grows and changes over time.</note>.

For this reason, all the perfections proper to the Intellectual Man were present from the very beginning. No new qualities are added to him later as if they were accidental arrivals; rather, he exists in the **celestial sphere** <note>original: *orbis supernus*; the higher, spiritual realm of ideas.</note> as pure and absolute. Whatever condition was attributed to him at the start is never later taken away.

Otherwise, if the Intellectual Man received his perfections one by one over many moments, he would be subject to "generation and corruption" <note>original: *generabilis & corruptibilis*; the cycle of being born, changing, and eventually dying or decaying.</note>. 

Furthermore, things that start out diminished and require later additions are produced by a diminished and slow-acting agent, such as **Nature**. However, the beings of the celestial sphere come from the Absolute Author, who is supremely pure and is, consequently, an instantaneous agent. Therefore, those forms are perfect and pure, and for that reason, they are equally excellent; indeed, no form is even counted among them unless it possesses a total firmness of existence.

It uses Plato's analogy of a circle's center point to describe how all forms and perfections originate from and are contained within the divine Intellect.</summary>

However, anything that falls under **generation and corruption** <term>Generation and corruption: The philosophical process of things coming into being (birth) and passing away (decay or destruction) in the physical world.</term> comes from a temporary efficient cause. Because natural things are of this kind—even if their origin was perfect—they are subject to being born and being destroyed. Since this is the case, we must first ask regarding these things *what* they are, and then *why* they are. These two lines of inquiry do not exist at the same time for physical things.

However, perpetual substances were produced without deliberation <note>original: *sine consultatione*; meaning the Creator does not need to "weigh options" or "think it over" because His action is instantaneous and perfect.</note>. Indeed, they are produced by a **Perpetual Author** who is not "thinking" in a discursive way <note>original: *minime cogitāte*; in medieval philosophy, this suggests God does not "think" through a process of logic, but possesses all knowledge instantly.</note>, because He is supremely perfect and suffers neither increase nor decrease.

If anyone should object that the primary agent could have made something and then added something better afterward to perfect it, we respond: if that created Being <note>original: *Ens creatum*</note> had been first established in one way and then had another good quality added later, it would follow that it was not perfectly good at the start. Such a thing does not befit the **First Agent**—that He should perform a work that is good but not perfect. Since He is the primary and supreme Good, nothing of a fitting goodness should be lacking even once from His work, as it is closest to Him.

We respond that it is through that form of the **Intellectual world** <term>Intellectual world: In Neoplatonic philosophy, this is the "higher world" of pure ideas and forms that serves as the perfect blueprint for everything in our physical world.</term> in which all things exist. If someone says again that there is such a great imitation present in a living creature as is sufficient for it to protect itself from harmful things, we say that while this is true, nevertheless terrestrial substances are preserved by the **primary form** <term>Primary form: The original, perfect archetype of a thing as it exists in the divine mind.</term> of the high sphere. Wherefore, man exists there not only as an intellectual being, but also as a sensing being. He does not possess the power of sensing simply as an addition to his power of understanding so that he might be fit for **generation** <term>Generation: The process of physical birth and living in the material world.</term>; rather, he has it because, in that higher state, both of these perfections are appropriate.

Indeed, in that celestial sphere, nothing is merely sensitive in potential, as the **master-philosophers of Babylon** <note>original: "archifophi Babiloniæ"; likely a reference to the "Chaldean" sages or ancient Eastern philosophers who were highly respected by Renaissance thinkers for their ancient wisdom.</note> agreed. For the contrary would be absurd: that the power of the Soul should only be fully realized here below, when in fact the Soul becomes more ignoble as it descends, becoming in some way subject to decay. To this we add: if the Soul in the Intellectual region did not have the power to sense, by what reasoning would it be able to tell the difference between things that can be sensed and things that cannot?

### Chapter four. That there is a certain "simple" man, and a certain "composite" man; what each is, and that the simple man is partly celestial and partly terrestrial. <note>original: "Caput quartum. Quod sit homo quidam simplex/ quidam autem compositus/ & quid sit uterq; ac quod homo simplex quidam supernus/ quidam infimus."</note>

As we are about to explain the state of the **intellectual man** <term>Intellectual man: The ideal or spiritual human being that exists in the realm of pure thought, serving as the blueprint for physical humans.</term>, let us describe the nature of the **sensible man** <term>Sensible man: The physical human being that can be perceived by the senses.</term>. Since it is impossible to know the physical man perfectly, how can we hope to understand the man of the higher sphere? Perhaps a thought arising here suggests that this physical man is actually that higher one. Setting forth the beginning of our proof, we ask whether the sensible man is an **Image** <note>original: "Idolum"</note> of the **particular Soul** <term>Particular Soul: The individual soul belonging to a specific person, as opposed to the soul of the entire universe.</term>, existing beyond that Image of the **Universal Soul** through which man is a living creature; or whether the Universal Soul itself is "man," while the particular soul operating in the body is not. 

And thus, perhaps man is a **rational animal** <note>original: "Animal rationale"</note>, not something composed of Soul and body, nor the Soul itself merely joined to a specific body. Therefore, when the "lower man"—who is composed of a rational soul and a body—is defined, it is impossible for this man to be exactly like that higher man whom we call "intellectual" and "formal" <term>Formal: Relating to the 'form' or essential essence of a thing rather than its physical matter.</term>. For this reason, such a definition will not be entirely true, though it may be plausible, because it does not lack the essential principle of man—namely, the **form** through which he is a **Being** <note>original: "Ens"</note>. 

Since this is the case, that definition is not yet of the true, simple, and formal man, but of the **composite** one. A composite must be defined not only by its form but also by its **matter** <term>Matter: The physical substance that, when combined with 'form,' creates a tangible object or person.</term>. However, for the "simple" man, it is enough to be defined by form alone. Thus, the true man must be defined only by the form through which he is "man," which is inseparable and necessary; just as it is said "man is a rational animal," where "animal" stands for **life**, which does not exist without the Soul being poured into it. The whole man, however, is divided into the body and the Soul, which is the form. Hence, it cannot be avoided that the true man is either the **Intellectual Soul** <note>original: "Anima Intellectiua"</note> or he is the work of that Soul. And if the first is granted, it follows—

### Chapter four. That there is a certain simple man and a certain composite man; what each of them is, and how the simple man is both celestial and internal.

...[it might be seen] that man would be an **intellectual soul** <term>Intellectual soul: The highest part of the soul, responsible for pure thought and understanding.</term> having entered even a body other than a human one. However, this is false. Indeed, one does not join the Soul under this name "man" unless it exists within a human body in the way it does now. Since this is the case, what prevents "man" from being called, on one hand, a certain composite of Soul and body, and on the other, a **rational animal** <note>original: "Animal rationale"</note> or a "reason"—that is, the work of the **rational soul**? For it is impossible for such a work to be produced by any other agent.

For just as the **active principles** <term>Active principles: Or "rationes agentes," the formative spiritual forces that direct the growth and life of an organism.</term> in seeds prove that each individual seed is not without its own specific soul, and vice-versa. The souls in those same seeds prove that life dwells within those principles; and this is no wonder, since these are the works of **vegetative souls** <term>Vegetative soul: The most basic level of soul, responsible for growth, nutrition, and reproduction.</term>. In this same way, the **sensory souls** <term>Sensory soul: The level of soul responsible for perception and movement.</term> are even more illustrious and manifest; and even more so do the rational souls behave, in that these active principles of life are all the more present in them. Therefore, the rational soul, before it is within the body (according to that formal definition), was the "man proper." But when it existed within the body, it formed an **image** <note>original: "simulacrum"</note> of another man—namely, the **sensible man**—which it fashioned to the best of its power into the likeness of the true man. It is like one who fashions a figure of the human body: he imitates the body to the best of his ability. And just as such an effigy is indeed a likeness of a man, but more ignoble because it lacks the conditions of a man—namely, life—for it has neither the power of movement nor any other potency; so too this sensible man, whose form is an imperfect rational soul, is a likeness of that first, divine, and true man. Indeed, the Soul has attempted to make the physical man resemble the true man through light, because it bestowed upon him the principles of the **primary man** <term>Primary man: The divine, celestial archetype of humanity.</term>, but imperfectly, as they are few and limited to particulars. For in the primary man there exist powerful, illustrious, and clear senses, far more so than in this physical being who exists only as his shadow.

## Chapter Five: What the lower man must be like in order to contemplate the celestial.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'O' with floral scrollwork and symmetrical foliage patterns within a double-lined square border.</image-desc>
It is necessary that a man who is to contemplate the **primary and true man** <note>In Platonic philosophy, this refers to the "Ideal Man" or the spiritual archetype of humanity that exists in the divine mind before physical birth.</note> should be distinguished by great probity and dignity. He must also possess powerful senses so they are not obscured when illustrious rays from the **celestial man** <note>original: "homine superno"</note> shine upon them. For indeed, the primary and true man is a clear light, and within him exist all the distinguished **human principles** <term>Human principles: (original: "rationes humanae") The divine blueprints or logical patterns that define what it means to be human.</term>. And he is that man whom Plato defined, except that he added to the prescribed definition by saying: Man is a **rational animal** <note>original: "Animal rationale"</note>—that is, a life or **rational Soul** <note>original: "Anima rationalis"</note>—to which the body serves as its own work. For the body serves this Soul first; but it serves the noble divine Soul second—namely, through the mediating **sensory Soul** <term>Sensory Soul: The part of the soul responsible for perceiving the physical world through the five senses, acting as a bridge between the physical body and the higher intellect.</term>, which the rational Soul accompanies. This rational Soul provides a higher life, not by descending from the **celestial sphere** <note>original: "orbe superno"</note> to the lowest, but by infusing it. For the rational Soul does not fall down from that intellectual world into this one, but is joined to that Soul which hangs from it. Therefore, although the reason of this earthly man is imperfect, yet when it is sublimated by its origin from that high source and its union with the same, it becomes stronger. For this reason, some have said that the **particular mind** <note>original: "Animus particularis"</note> is a part of the **universal mind** <note>original: "Animus uniuersalis"</note>.

...is different from the sense of this base man, because there perception is higher; since one sense exceeds another, just as one sensible object exceeds another. Furthermore, sensation also exists in the **Soul** <note>original: "Animae"</note> existing in that higher realm, since there are **universal bodies** <term>Universal bodies: In this context, the perfect, archetypal forms of physical things that exist in the divine intellect.</term> there, just as there are particular ones here. And the Soul perceives those higher things, just as a man perceives these lower things; he is secondary, being a **likeness** <note>original: "simulacrum"</note> of the primary. Likewise, this corporeal man senses more through the body, but that spiritual man understands more through the intellect. Since the **active principles** <term>Active principles: (original: "rationes agentes") The creative, formative forces that organize matter according to a divine plan.</term> are present in that primary man, he still transmits his light to the secondary man, and even to the third man of the **lowest world** <note>original: "mundi infimi," referring to the physical, material universe.</note>. Since this is so, the operation of both prior levels exists within the corporeal man, of whom he is the figure. For this same man performs some work of the **rational man** <note>The soul using logic.</note> and some of the **Intellectual man** <note>The soul using direct intuition of divine truths.</note>, although both are imperfect and diminished, since he is a likeness, and even a likeness of a likeness. Now therefore it has been proved that the primary man senses with a higher sense than the lowest man, and that higher things do not receive influence from lower things, but vice versa: lower things receive from the higher. Indeed, they depend upon them, as they follow the same qualities and are similar to them; wherefore this man takes his strength from the celestial man. And although he also senses, it is not in the same way as that one, who senses purely, perceiving higher things. For there, sight perceives universals, but here it perceives particulars because of its weakness. That higher man stands forth as much more powerful, because he encounters objects that are more illustrious and distinguished than the corporeal man, who exists imperfectly as one who looks upon base and minimal things, which are but **images** <note>original: "Idola"</note> of those higher things; wherefore this Intellectual man is robust and possesses the kind of sense we have described.

### Chapter Five: What kind of person the lowest man must be to contemplate the one above.

<image-desc>Ornamental drop cap 'O' decorated with floral and vine motifs within a square frame.</image-desc>

It is necessary that a man who is to contemplate the **primary and true Man** <note>The "primary and true man" refers to the ideal, archetypal form of humanity that exists in the divine or intellectual realm, as opposed to the physical human being.</note> should be marked by great integrity and worthiness. He must also possess powerful senses so that they are not overwhelmed when the illustrious rays from the **supernal man** <note>original: "homine superno"</note> rise upon them. Indeed, the primary and true man is a clear light, and in him exist all the distinguished principles of humanity. And this is that man whom **Plato** defined—except that he added to the prescribed definition, saying: **"Man is a rational animal"** <note>original: "Homo est Animal rationale"</note>, that is, a life or a **rational soul** <note>original: "Anima rationalis"</note>, which the body serves as its own work. For the body serves this Soul first, but it serves the noble **divine soul** <note>original: "Animæ diuinæ"</note> second—namely, through the mediation of the **sensual soul** <note>original: "Animā sensualem"</note>. This sensual soul is accompanied by the rational soul, which grants a superior life; yet it does not do this by descending from the higher sphere to the lowest, but by **infusion** <note>In this philosophical context, "infusion" suggests that the higher soul radiates its influence downward without actually leaving its perfect state or "falling" into the material world.</note>. For the rational soul does not fall from that intellectual realm into this one, but is joined to this soul which hangs from it. Therefore, although the reason of this [earthly] man may be imperfect, it becomes stronger when it is sublimated through its origin from that exalted soul and its union with the same. For this reason, some have said that the **particular mind** <term>Particular mind: (original: "Animus particularis") The individual human intellect.</term> is a part of the **universal mind** <term>Universal mind: (original: "Animus uniuersalis") The cosmic or divine intellect that encompasses all individual thoughts.</term>.

**S**hould anyone ask—since it has already been stated that the lowest sense within us proceeds from the high—what must be said regarding other Animals? Specifically, in what manner did God produce them? Did He first think upon the form of the horse and other **Brutes** <note>original: "Brutorum"; in this context, "brutes" refers to all non-human animals.</note>, and then produce them in this **sensible world** <note>The "sensible world" is the world we perceive through our five senses, as opposed to the "intellectual world" perceived by the mind.</note>, but not in the Intellectual one? We respond that we have previously proven by sufficient reasons, demonstrating that God created all things without **consultation** <note>The author argues that God does not "deliberate" or "think through" options like a human, but creates through an immediate and perfect expression of His nature.</note>. Indeed, He first established the sublime world and placed upon it, without the need for thought, all perfect and pure forms—being produced as they were with their own proper essences apart from **accidental qualities** <note>original: "accidentia"; these are non-essential traits, like a horse's specific color or age, which do not exist in the perfect eternal template.</note>. Afterwards, He truly created this sensible world as a mere **image** <note>original: "simulacrum"</note> of that incorruptible one.

Since this is the case, when He created the horse or any other animal in the **supernal world** <note>The "supernal world" refers to the higher, celestial realm of archetypes.</note>—in which He placed all species of Animals in a more elevated way, pure and perfect—He did not create those animals only there, but also these lowest ones here. Otherwise, His power of creating would suffer a defect. But this cannot be, since no power can extend to all things except the first power, the most powerful of all and the **creatrix** <note>The source uses the feminine form "creatrix" to describe the creative power of the First Principle.</note> of all others; she is neither moved to a place nor enclosed by a place, since she is infinite. 

However, one might object that **rational Animals** <note>meaning humans</note> exist in the intellectual world because they are noble; but who could imagine that a multitude of irrational beasts are also there, especially the most ignoble ones? We shall respond that the reason for this is that the first **Author** <note>The "Author" refers to the Creator or the First Principle.</note> is entirely one. His essence—which is the same as His existence, as we have said many times—created a single Intellectual World. But because it is unbecoming for the unity of the thing created to be equal to the unity of the Creator (for they are not the same thing), the first Created thing then creates many things. For the creation is posterior to the Creator, who is entirely one; it is neither prior to Him nor equal to Him. Therefore, it is not equally one, and is thus many. For unity is immediately opposed to **plurality** <note>original: "pluralitati"</note>, because it is one.

**S**hould someone object, saying that while it is indeed possible for noble Animals to be placed in a noble world, it is impossible for "ignoble" animals to be there—such as **irrational creatures** <note>original: "irrationabilia"; animals that lack the human capacity for reason</note>. We say that the Intellect in that realm is varied. Since the human intellect is above the brutish one, there is no doubt that human thought differs from the thought of a beast. Indeed, they find that even the thoughts of beasts are in many ways rational, as their **thinking faculty** <term>cogitativa: the specific power of the soul used to process sensory data and form judgments about the physical world</term> acts as their own intellect for each individual beast, through which they discern things grasped by the senses. 

But the thinking faculty of a human offers a thing perceived by the senses to the Intellect; if the Intellect confirms it, it will admit it, but if it does not confirm it, it will reject it. And sometimes, turned toward the senses, it will confirm a perception; then, returning again to itself, it ruminates upon it many times until it believes the truth of the matter has become manifest.

Who would understand the horse unless the **thinking faculty** <term>cogitativa: the power of the soul that processes sensory information and forms judgments about physical objects</term> of the primary horse were the **Intellect**? <term>Intellectus: the divine or cosmic mind that contains the perfect archetypes of all things</term> For the Intellect and the thing understood are the same; wherefore the Intellect understands only that which is intellectual. And just as a particular life does not exist without an **absolute life** <note>original: "uita absoluta" — refers to the pure, undiluted essence of Life from which all individual living things draw their existence</note>, so also a particular intellect does not exist without the absolute intellect, but is derived from it.

Therefore, we also assert that the intellect of no beast exists without the absolute intellect. Moreover, the absolute intellect, when it enters into a human, is made a particular intellect distinct from itself; likewise, when it enters into a horse, it is made both particular and different from the human one. And so it is in the remaining animals: for as many times as the intellect descends <note>This "descent" describes the process of a divine idea taking on physical form, which the author views as a step toward a less perfect state</note>, so many times it becomes less noble. 

Thus, the more the **vital power** is weakened, the more it fades. From this arises a result: an obscure and less noble animal. When such a creature's natural wit is weak, the Intellect, acting as a compensation, makes its limbs strong to achieve a balance of power—as, for example, in dogs, whom it perfects in this way to some extent to make up for a lack of vital vigor. Indeed, it is necessary for every animal to obtain a certain perfection from the life-giving intellect. If anyone should object to this, arguing that some beasts are found to be imperfect and unable to repel harmful things, we respond that such cases are few.

### Chapter Ten. That the lowest earth is a participant in life, and the heavenly earth even more so.

<margin>u</margin>
Whether the earth of the heavenly sphere is alive is something we can discern once we have observed this lowest earth, because this physical earth is an image <note>original: "Idolum" — a reflection or phantom-copy</note> and figure of that higher one. For in this earth, a certain life exists and a "reason" <term>ratio: the logical or vital principle that organizes matter</term> that drives life. The proof of this is the earth's changing form; indeed, the earth grows, assimilates matter, and increases the size of mountains, which are terrestrial by nature. In the midst of such mountains, there also exist many passages, caverns, streams, and other features created by the Soul <term>Anima: the "World Soul" that animates the entire universe</term> which produces such forms. This is the "formative reason" <term>ratio formatrix: the internal blueprint that directs natural growth</term> of the earth: working within, it shapes a tree according to its underlying nature, or even a branch cut from a tree. Therefore, from these things we conclude that the "reason of the soul" <note>original: "ratio animae"</note> exists within the earth, even if it is of a subordinate <note>original: "servilis" — meaning it serves the higher forms and is the lowest in the hierarchy of life</note> nature. Since it is impossible for the earth not to live while performing such miraculous works, and if it exercises the works of life, it undoubtedly possesses life. And if this sensible <term>sensibilis: perceptible by the physical senses</term> earth lives, how much more does that primary, heavenly earth live? For this physical earth is secondary, having arisen from that one.

### Chapter Eleven. What the state of being is like for those in the heavenly sphere.

<margin>a</margin>
We likewise assert that all beings <term>Entia: existing things or entities</term> of the heavenly world are illustrious, as they exist in an exalted light. For this reason, each one of them perceives all others through its own essence and within the essence of the others. Consequently, in that realm, all things exist in each individual part and in the whole, and the light that has arisen within them is infinite. Therefore, any one of them is also "greatest" (in a majesty whose power is infinite) and pure. And vice-versa—for example—the sun in that realm is every star, and every star is the sun. However, that which excels above the others is called the "sun," while that which does not excel is named a "star," and so it goes for each of them.

...is perceived in another coexisting part. Indeed, the universe is seen in the individual, and the individual in the universe. There, motion certainly exists, but it is hidden, because it has neither a beginning nor an end; nor is it different from the thing that moves, but is the moved thing itself. And there also is perfect rest, which is not defined by physical motion, for it does not contain such motion. In that place, too, there exists an absolute sense, since nothing remains imperceptible to perception. Moreover, everything existing there is firm, even the earth. For it does not exist in the way that these lowest things <note>referring to physical matter on our world</note> do; rather, that heavenly substance is similar to its lower kindred <note>original: "congeneri" — of the same origin or type</note> but excels it in degree. Nor is there any higher place in which it exists, because it subjects "place" to itself and is exalted above it. 

Similarly, the Intellect and the visible heavens exist there, along with the light of the stars and an even higher radiance. In the physical spheres, each of these is located outside the other, existing in only a single part rather than the whole; but this is not how it is with the parts of the spiritual heavens, where each part is simultaneously the whole. For when you look at a part, you will perceive the whole, and when you look at the whole, you will perceive the part. For sight, directed toward one part, penetrates all things because of its subtlety <term>subtilitas: the refined, non-physical quality of spiritual perception that allows one to see through the surface</term> and speed. It is as if, for example, someone looking at the earth could see through into all its lowest depths. 

Likewise, the contemplation of the higher world does not tire the intellect, nor does it bring about a feeling of being "full" or bored; for it suffers from no lack. In that place, the observer does not merely look at a single part, but at all the best things, in which he rejoices. If he were to see only a single part, it would be neither the best nor a source of joy. Moreover, the essences existing there are incorruptible and never-failing. Nor does the observer lose his desire when looking at these things, as usually happens with physical sights; instead, the more he contemplates, the more he desires and wonders. He does not grow weary in his looking, but is continuously strengthened. For the substances existing there, life is not laborious or afflicted, but truly sweet; for they are pure and immaterial <term>immateriatae: existing without the heavy, restrictive, and decaying nature of physical matter</term>.

### Chapter Twelve. By whom the Beings of the heavenly sphere were created, and the nature of the divine word.

<margin>h</margin>In this way, the Beings of the heavenly sphere were created by that primary word, which is the Sovereign Substance <note>original: "Substantia princeps" — the first or highest reality</note>. Nor indeed was it so that the Essence existed first and its intellection <note>the act of conscious understanding</note> was produced later, as occurs in secondary substances; rather, both were created at the same time, for the act of understanding itself is the Intellect. I add, however, that the Intellect understands itself first, and secondly its own act of understanding; just as the planet Jupiter reflects upon those images and figures impressed by the higher realms, which exist between the celestial and terrestrial worlds. Therefore, those things are arranged with admirable qualities, which none but the most fortunate of men can penetrate through a great effort to contemplate such things. 

But above all exists the word of divine wisdom. It is the most powerful of all things, such that who is able to comprehend its majesty as sovereign and its power? Or who can behold the true essence of that same Word, in which all things are visible and from which the power of creation is derived? For this Word is the sovereign power and act, next after the first created being, which is then the single cause of all other intelligible creatures—that is to say, immediately. Through these intermediate beings of the sensible world, as much as all of them are contained in that first created <term>Agent Intellect: in medieval and Renaissance philosophy, the "active" part of the mind that translates potential knowledge into actual thought</term>; these are works proportioned to it. The Agent Intellect itself is a work proportioned to the supreme Author; by turning toward and contemplating an even more universal Intellect, it is sublimated and becomes the universal cause procreating all other subsequent, ordered Beings.

Through constant contemplation of the mind, one becomes wise, but not through exemplary reasoning or the indicative signs used in the manner of the logicians <note>original: "dialecticoꝝ" — referring to practitioners of dialectics or formal logic</note>. We, however, hardly strive to contemplate that brilliant beauty because the Senses dominate us; nor do we accept through belief anything except physical Beings. For this reason, we also believe that we only learn by deducing conclusions from several assumed principles. This, however, is not true in every field of study practiced here, for self-evident principles are learned without the need for deduction from other sources; they are, in fact, the primary principles themselves. Therefore, higher realities are understood even more directly, not as conclusions drawn from principles. Truly, in that realm, truth is perceived absolutely and entirely without error or deception, because it is not seen through a secondary medium. Since these things are simple in nature, nothing foreign or accidental is mixed with them—unlike what happens with earthly things, which are not perceived in their true state.

Therefore, whoever doubts that the Heavenly World is as we have described it has turned away from it. Yet, since some of us have achieved the "victory of the Soul" <note>original: "uictoriā Aiæ" (animae) — a state of spiritual transcendence where the soul overcomes material limitations</note>, we demonstrate that it is indeed so. And for this reason, we say again that the King of Babylon <note>Likely a reference to an ancient sage or a figure from Hermetic tradition</note>, having beheld that world with his mind, later recalled and reported: "In that place, nothing exists inside another thing." Yet he did not explain how this is possible, leaving the story unfinished; here, we begin the task of completing it.

All things come about through some form of knowledge, whether it be acquired or innate. Acquired knowledge imitates nature, insofar as the knower is guided to make themselves like something in nature. Innate and connatural knowledge, however, is not diverse but unique. If it resides in the <term>Agent Intellect: the active part of the mind that, in medieval philosophy, makes understanding possible by illuminating concepts</term>, it exists there primarily and of its own accord; it cannot be acquired by learning from some prior source. If anyone asks where such dignity comes from in this aforementioned intellect, we say it comes from its own proper nature; and having reached this point, we shall seek no further explanation. Indeed, if anyone should deny that knowledge is innate to the Agent Intellect, we argue in rebuttal that if the Intellect had to acquire its knowledge, it would have to learn it either from something higher or through its own essence—which is impossible. For the Agent Intellect was not made by the Divine Word with an essence such that it *is* its own knowledge, in the way that the Word itself is. Rather, the knowledge of the Agent Intellect is a quality within it, not its very substance. For knowledge...

## Chapter Fourteen. That among celestial Beings, one is not essentially nobler than another; and why the Egyptians used Hieroglyphic letters.

<margin>1</margin>
Among the Beings of the higher World, none is substantially nobler than another; rather, all things there exist according to the most perfect form. This is just as the forms existing in the mind of an architect are equal in their creative power, though they differ from the finished works—for example, from the figures inscribed on a wall. Therefore, the Ancients called such celestial forms "Exemplars," which Plato described as being the substances or essences of lower things. And the wise men of Babylon and Egypt, with sharpness of mind, looked within and embraced the forms <note>original: "spēs" (species) — the archetypal forms or ideas</note> of the Intellectual World. They did this through knowledge handed down from elsewhere or discovered by themselves—a knowledge which they claimed for themselves by their very profession. Indeed, when they were about to explain something, they used spiritual <note>original: "intellectuaria" — referring to direct, intuitive understanding</note> teaching rather than human <note>discursive or rational</note> teaching. Unlike some others who, when consulting them, did not seem to have learned firmly enough from opinions expressed in speech, they wrote down the concepts received in their minds (as we read by eyewitness account) onto stones through figures <note>hieroglyphs</note>. They did the same in all sciences and arts, placing them in temples like pages to be read; and these served them as useful books. This they did to show that the immaterial Active Intellect <term>Active Intellect: In ancient and medieval philosophy, the spiritual power that creates and illuminates all things according to their divine blueprints</term> created all things according to the specific reason and likeness of each essence. This was a most excellent and beautiful lesson. Through this, I wish it were also shown by what method they reached those wondrous and hidden forms; for in that way, their knowledge would be even more worthy of praise—a condition that happens to only a few men.

# BOOK

<margin>Since</margin> Since the Knowledge of the Egyptians concerning heavenly things is to be admired: how much more, therefore, is the wisdom of the prince <note>referring to the "First Principle" or God as the source of all things</note> who created such substances in the highest sphere. Nor should it be investigated why those Beings were produced as such: since they themselves exist as the highest <term>reasons</term><note>original: "rōes" (rationes) — here meaning the rational principles or archetypes that define what a thing is</note> in dignity, and are pure essences; God created many of them without the need for [discursive] thought. Nor is the beauty of lower things absolute; for these were made by an agent <note>the Creator or Demiurge</note> looking back at those aforementioned perpetual reasons which proceeded from the first Author, beyond the thought of any other principle of beauty. 

And indeed, who would not admire the power of essence in that most noble and supreme Being? It created all other things without consultation and according to its own nature; its primacy is the Reason of reasons. Nor, for that reason, does Essence itself need to look outward to explore such things—namely, external beauty. Indeed, its own primacy is sufficient for itself. This we also say in imitation of our ancestors, who harmoniously asserted that this World was made not by itself, nor by chance, but by a most wise and noble <term>architect</term><note>The "Architect" is a common Neoplatonic metaphor for the Divine Intellect that shapes the universe</note> who is abstracted from every created reason. 

Yet again we must ask, regarding the construction of this World, whether the agent pre-thought in Himself all the things to be done. Did He think of individual things: creating first the earth at the center of the sphere; second, the water above; third, the air higher than the water; fourth, the fire more sublime than the air; fifth, then the heavens containing all things; and sixth, afterwards, the plants and animals of diverse species—yet all fitting together in an inanimate harmony—by establishing the exterior and interior members in a manner suited to their functions? 

First, therefore, if the forms of the things of the World had been thought of individually by the divine mind in order to perform the works correctly, God would have created one after another as a model. But that does not suit the most wise Author and the most noble substance above all others. Nor, secondly, is it right to say that God pre-thought the things to be created in Himself and only afterwards created them. For in that case, the things thought of are either outside of Him or within Him. If they were outside of Him, then they existed before they were created; if they were within Him, then He does not need a pre-thought of them, since they are themselves...

It contrasts the supreme wisdom of the "First Principle" with the secondary, derived beauty of the physical world.</summary>

possessing these things, they are thus the principles. God likewise created **cogitative reason** <note>the faculty of discursive, step-by-step thinking</note>; nor did He "pre-think" it, for otherwise there would be a process stretching to infinity <note>an "infinite regress," where every thought requires a prior thought to conceive it</note>, which is false. Furthermore, a human artisan, pre-thinking a work intended to be an imitation of what he has conceived, makes that work through instruments. But the **Supreme Founder**, when about to make something, does not imitate any created thing as a model; rather, He creates the new form itself as something capable of being imitated, without any other model. Nor does He use any creaturely instrument for this task. For nothing external assists Him; instead, He brings it into being from His own inherent power.

Therefore, it is proven that God—whose name be exalted—created the universe without consultation or discursive thought. Thus, the arguments of the adversaries have been shown to lack solidity. God first created a single substance: namely, the **Active Intellect** <term>intellectus agens</term><note>In medieval philosophy, this is the "bridge" between God and the human mind, often described as a light that makes knowledge possible</note>. Into this, He infused a shining light, the most excellent of all created things; for the Active Intellect is closest to Him in such light, power, and simplicity. Through this medium, the **higher world** was created, consisting of pure intelligences and souls. Through this same medium, the lower sensible things <note>the physical world we can perceive with our senses</note> were afterward renewed and contained under similar forms—except that the beings of the higher world are pure, perfect, and unmixed. Otherwise, they would not be perpetual if they were capable of being dissolved or if they were joined from the primordial form down to the very last.

For **Matter** <term>Hyle</term><note>original: "Hylæ" — the Greek term for the raw, formless substance of the universe before it is shaped</note> is first formed by a common form; afterward, it receives the Elemental form, and then other succeeding forms. For this reason, no one can look beneath it to see its true essence, as it is clothed in many hidden and imperceptible forms.

### Bernardino de' Guidotti of Vicenza, Professor of Arts: greetings to those eager for learning.

# THE THEOLOGY of Aristotle the Stagirite <note>Aristotle was known as the Stagirite after his birthplace, Stagira.</note>, who of all philosophers that are, have been, or shall be in the years to come, is easily the most eminent and discerning prince: otherwise called his Mystic Philosophy, according to the teachings of the Egyptians. It was brought forth from the most abundant Greek source into the Arabic idiom by that most faithful interpreter, Abenama the Assyrian <note>original: *Abenama Assyrius*; likely the 9th-century translator Abd al-Masih ibn Na'ima al-Himsi</note>—that is, a Saracen, for those we call Saracens today were once called Assyrians, just as those now called Tartars were once Scythians. Furthermore, Moses Rouas <note>likely a Jewish scholar from Cyprus</note>, most skilled in the Arabic language, flew from the Arabic into the Latin at Cyprus. Peter Nicholas of the Castellanis of Faenza <note>original: *Petrus Nicolaus ex Castellanis Fauentinus*</note>, a philosopher and a notable regulator of the human body <note>a physician</note>, organized it precisely into chapters and restored it into the Roman speech. Finally, Lucas Gauricus <note>a famous Renaissance astrologer and mathematician</note>, the foremost of astrologers, a doctor of arts, and not ignorant of holy theology, applied the final polish to this most celebrated volume. But as for those errors he could not purge, I pray you ascribe them not to him, but to the rustic printer <note>original: *Calcographo*</note>. Expect, moreover, other monuments of ancient philosophers nearly any day now, never before opened to the Latins, which Rossi the antiquarian <note>original: *Roseus antiquarius*; referring to Francesco Rosello</note>—a man of letters not without merit, a most diligent and fortunate searcher of hidden things—discovered at Damascus while he was journeying by sea and land to the Eastern regions. He will soon see to their publication with the support of the most pious Pope Leo X <note>Giovanni de' Medici, reigned 1513–1521</note>, who has always been accustomed not only to cherish those endowed with virtue but to decorate them with the most ample rewards and honors. May Almighty God favor his wishes according to his desire.
From the premier city <note>Rome</note>, on the Calends of June <note>June 1st</note>, in the passing year of the Christian liturgy, 1515.

---

### Eulogy by Francesco Macino of Faenza, Priest and Rhetorician.

->Read these Memphitic <note>Egyptian</note> decrees of Aristotle in eloquent words,<-
->Whoever you are: believe in the true and ethical God.<-
->You other authors, yield your labors by right.<-
->This one noble work stands above all.<-
->Yield your right as well, you modern wise men:<-
->The elegant Nicolaus <note>Peter Nicholas of Faenza</note> is knowledgeable.<-
->He writes the hidden theorems of sublime wisdom<-
->And teaches that they can be held in this easy Latin breath.<-

### A poem by Giovanni Pietro Fereti, Doctor of Civil and Canon Law and Canon of Ravenna.

->What heaps of the inner secrets of wisdom Abacomactus <note>A variation of the name Abenama</note> the Arab<-
->Brought forth from the shadows of the illustrious Aristotle.<-
->These sacred gifts, long sought by our Latin<-
->Philosophers, the pious care of my Rossi <note>Francesco Rosello</note> provides.<-
->Like a second Triptolemus <note>A figure from Greek myth who brought the secret of grain and agriculture to humanity</note>: a portion of this well-earned<-
->Greenery of the Muses is born by his help.<-
->For compare the divine discoveries of others:<-
->There is none to be found equal to these merits.<-
->The Heavens shine in order for you, Francesco;<-
->Have an immortal age in the peace of Pope Leo.<-
->Let the world receive this with varied applause: and to him alone<-
->Let it owe an immense debt, he who brought such great goods.<-

->**Reader, correct these errors.**<-

In the short letter of Roseus of Ravenna, where "most famous" <note>original: *clarissima*</note> is read, let it be corrected to "most famously" <note>original: *clarissime*</note>.
In the letter of the philosopher of Faenza <note>this refers to Pietro Niccolò Castellani, mentioned on the previous page</note>, where you find "more of things desired" <note>original: *magis optarum*</note>, read "desired" <note>original: *optatum*</note>; and read "open to the Latins" <note>original: *latinis apertos*</note>, not "open of the Latin."

Finally, in Book 7, where in the upper margin—due to the laziness of the printer <note>original: *impressoris ignauia*</note>—it is written 37, let it be written 35, and vice versa.

Very often, most learned reader, you will find letters turned upside down or swapped; also many words that should be written with a diphthong <note>a vowel combination, like 'ae' or 'oe'</note> which are not, or vice versa. Likewise, where a relative word was printed as an adverb, and the opposite: you (if it does not trouble you) will be able to refine and correct these with exactness. Indeed, this applies to whatever has come forth from the root word "separate" <note>original: *separo*</note>: such as "separated," "separable," "inseparable," etc., which you will see for yourself have been wrongly noted.

<meta>Following the previous page’s list of typographical corrections, this page presents the formal preface and dedicatory poems for the work. It introduces the scholarly team behind the translation and publication of this "Theology of Aristotle"—a text we now know was actually based on the works of the Neoplatonist philosopher Plotinus, though Renaissance scholars believed it to be Aristotle’s "mystic" philosophy.</meta>

## Bernardino de Guidoctis of Vicenza, Professor of Arts, to those eager for the good life.

# ARISTOTLE
### The Stagirite <note>Aristotle was born in Stageira, hence the title "Stagirite."</note>, easily the most eminent and refined prince of all philosophers who are, were, or shall be in the years hereafter. His *Theology*, or mystic Philosophy, according to the dogmas of the Egyptians, was brought from the most abundant Greek source into the Arabic tongue by a very faithful interpreter, Abenama the Assyrian <note>original: *Abenama Assyrius*; this refers to the 9th-century translator Ibn Na'ima al-Himsi.</note> (that is, a Saracen; for those we call Saracens today were once called Assyrians, just as those now called Tartars were once Scythians). Then, Moses Rouas <note>likely a reference to a medieval translator from the Arabic-to-Latin tradition</note>, most skilled in the Arabic language, translated it from Arabic into Latin at Cyprus. Pietro Niccolò Castellani of Faenza, a philosopher and no obscure physician <note>original: *humani corporis moderator*, literally "governor of the human body"</note>, arranged it precisely into chapters and restored it to the Roman speech. Finally, Luca Gaurico, the "Alpha" of Astrologers, Doctor of Arts, and not ignorant of holy Theology, put the final polish on this most famous volume; but whatever errors he could not entirely purge, I beg you to ascribe not to him, but to the rustic printer <note>original: *Calcographo*; referring to the manual labor of typesetting which often introduced errors.</note>. Wait, moreover, for other monuments of ancient philosophers never before opened to the Latins, which our Roseus <note>referring to the editor/antiquarian responsible for finding the manuscript</note>, this antiquarian not without knowledge, a most diligent and fortunate investigator of hidden things, gathered at Damascus (while he journeyed by sea and land to the eastern regions); soon he will see they are published <note>original: *spumẽda*, literally "to foam forth," implying a fresh publication.</note> with the support of the Divine Pope Leo X, most pious, who has always been accustomed not only to cherish those endowed with virtue but indeed to decorate them with the most ample gifts and honors; to whom may Almighty God grant his prayers according to his wish.

-> From Rome, prince of cities, on the Kalends of June; in the year of the Christian liturgy 1519. <-

---

### Eulogy by Francesco Macini of Faenza, priest and Rhetorician.

> Read these Egyptian decrees of the eloquent Aristotle,
> Whoever you are; believe in the true and eternal God.
> Let the remaining works of the author yield by right;
> This one noble work stands out above all others.
> Yield also by right, you modern sages;
> [Yield to] the elegant and knowledgeable interpreter Nicolaus <note>referring to Pietro Niccolò Castellani</note>.
> He writes the established theorems of sublime wisdom,
> And teaches that it can be done with an easy and Latin spirit.

### A poem by Giovanni Pietro Fereti, Doctor of Both Laws and Canon of Ravenna.

> The heaps of the inner chambers of the wisdom of famous Aristotle,
> Which Abenama the Arab had suppressed in darkness;
> The sacred gifts long sought by our Latin philosophers,
> The pious care of my Roseus now provides.
> He is another Triptolemus <note>A figure from Greek myth who flew across the world in a chariot to teach humanity the art of agriculture.</note>; thus a portion of this springtime
> Is born for the greening Latin land through his help.
> For compare the ancient divine discoveries of others;
> None is to be found equal in merit.
> Francesco, the sky shines in order for you, being appeased;
> Have an immortal age in the peace of Leo <note>referring to the era of Pope Leo X</note>.
> Let the world receive this with various applauses: and let them
> Owe immensely to the one who brought such great goods.
